ADVANCE, AUSTRALIA! Sons of the giant Ocean isle, In sport our friendly foes so long, Well England knows you, and we smile, When you outmatch us many a while. So fleet you are, so keen, so strong You, like that fairy people set Of old, within the circling sea, Far off from men, might well forget This elder nation's toil and fret, - Might heed not aught save game and glee! • But what your fathers were you are, In lands the fathers never knew, 'Neath skies of alien sign and star, You rally to the English war, Your hearts are English hearts, and true! Ay, now, when first the shadow falls On England, and the touch of Fate, You answer ere your Mother calls, You leave your ocean-girdled walls, And face our foemen in the gate. --Daily News. A. L.

A PUZZLE. We two had a row, Somehow. Perhaps she was fretful, and I didn't care, Or perhaps I did something that she couldn't bear, Or perhaps a depression advanced in the air; But however that be, the disturbance was there, And a storm began to brew. At first it muttered, And hard words were uttered; Then harder and harder, until things grew Supremely unpleasant for each of the two, And I came to think We had reached the brink Of the grave of a friendship whose loss we should rue, So I begged her pardon—what less could I do? She declared she was sorry—l hope it was true. And the tempest's frown • Smoothed slowly down. And it rumbled and sighed, • And whispered and died Away. Yet all I can say To this very day • ' Is—we two had a row Somehow. _ But I couldn't make out What brought it about, And I don't know now.

A TERRIBLE ADVENIIME.—The Italian and Swiss papers relate some striking incidents to which the recent avalanches *have given rise. A man of the name of Rapelli, an ex-Marshal of carabineers, lived with his wife and his children in the village of Groscavello. The wife waa an Invalid, and while her husband and their little girl were he her bedroom two Sundays ago an avalanche fell on the village and crushed the house. Rapelli was killed, and the child, one of whose feet was caught be- tween two joists, was,thrown head downwards, without any possibility of extricating herself. The mother, though saved from destruction by a beam, had one of her arms so tightly wedged under it that she could only just touch the child's head with the tip of her fingers. After hanging in the position described for thirty hours, continually crying to her mother for help, she died in convulsions. Mdsie. Rapelli would probably have perished of hunger and cold if a hen had not come within reach of her free hand. She seized and strangled it, plucked it with her teeth, and placed the feathers under her neck, which was in contact with the snow. Then she devoured the fowl just as it was. After re- maining thus imprisoned nearly sixty hours she was got out by a rescue party and carried into a stable hard by, where a short time ago she still lay in a condition bor- dering on idiotcy. The cause of these disasters (a cor- respondent points out) is well known. There is nothing like forests for stopping or breaking the force of an avalanche, and the slopes of the Italian sides of the Alps have been almost completely denuded of their timber. The Swiss owe their comparative immunity from the catastrophes which have wrought so ranch havoc among their neighbours to the care they bestow onthe preserva- tion of their mountain woods. hsnraitsTiox.—The main cause of nervousness is indigestion, and that is caused by weakness of the stomach. l o one can hive sound nerves and good health without using Hop Bitters ts strengthen the stomach, purify the blood, and keep the liver and kidneys active, to carry off all the poisonous and waste suttee of the system. A smart lawyer in Wilmington, North Carolina, had the misfortune to lose a suit for a client who had every reason to expect success. The client, a plain old farmer, was astonished by a long bill of costs; and,hastening to the lawyer's office, said, "I thought you told me we should certainly gain the suit?" "So I did," said the lawyer; "but, you • see, when I brought it there before the judges, they said it was coram non)udice." "Well, if they said it was as bad as that," replied the old farmer, "I don't wonder we lost it ;" and he paid the costs, and a big fee besides, without another murmur. • A Inlay CONSCIENTIOUS REPORTER.—II IS a breach of confidence for a member or an officer of the Senate to disclose the transactions of a secret session until the re- moval of the injunction of secrecy by a formal re.solu tion of that body. Still, newspaper correspondents generally manage to find them out in some way. So well known was their accomplishment in this direction that senators would oftentimes go to the reporters for information as to what had been done in secret session, instead of the reporters to the senators! Once a senator, going to the Senate rather late in the afternoon, met a correspondent coming from the Capitol. The law-maker asked what was being done in the Senate. "Oh. nothing important," was the answer. "They havo just gone out of executive session, and are now discussing the subject they had up yesterday:" The senator was evi- dently interested in some nomination or other business, and so he persisted and asked the correspondent what action had been taken in executive session. The news- paper man coolly eyed the senator for a few, moments, and then cautiously remarked, "Well, you Congressmen are getting to be such free talkers, I think I'd better not tell you —Si. Nicholas. QUAINT OLD PROVERBS ON DrIARRIAGE.—Hot love is soon cold. Wedlock is a padlock. A ship and a woman are ever repairing. Sweetheart and honeybird keep no house. A man's best fortune or his worst is his wife. I A gossip is seldom a good housewife at home. Happy' is the wooing that is not long in doing. In the hus- band wisdom, in the wife gentleness. Husbands are in heaven whose wives chide not. Marry your sons when ; you will, your daughtere when you can. He who Would the daughter win Must with her mother nrst begin. He who marries a widow will often have a dead man's head thrown in his dish. The foot on the cradle and the hand on the distaff is the sign of a good housewife. Maids want nothing but husbands, and when they have them they want everything. Houses and riches are the inheritance of fathers, but a prudent wife is from the Lord. Be a good husband, and you'll get a penny to spend, a penny to lend, and a penny for a friend. Is the good man saith, so say we. - But as the good woman saith, so must it be. PRESIDENT GRANT'S Lirrtz STOUT.—" By the way," he went on," I remember an incident that clearly illus- trates his (General Grant's) character. When I was Secretary of the Navy some) hundreds of the sailors of the better chow came to me and asked to have some rank given them. They didn't care about an increase of pay, they said, but they wanted relative rank. I couldn't do anything for them, but they came several times, and were rather importunate, and I finally led a delegation of them over to the White House and let them present their petition to President Grant in person. They told him what they wanted;and argued for a redress of their grivances plainly, but/forcibly. At last an old . satswain came to the front, and hitching up his Irons- sers and turning over his incumbent • quid, he said: 'Mr. President, I can put this 'ere matter so's you can see it plain.- Now, here I be—a parent; in fact, a father. My son is a midshipman. He outranks me, don't you observe? That ain't right, dont you see?' Indeed,' said Grant, who appointed him a middy;?" The Secre- tary here,' the bo'sun said; and encouraged by the ques- tion he went on: It ain't right, don't you see, that I should be beneath 'im ? Wy, ef I was to go onto his ship the boy I brought up to obajence would boss his own father! Jest think of that! An' he has better quarters'n me, and better grub, nice fura'ture, an' all that; sleep.a in a nice soft bed'n all that. See?' Xeei tin rvg- tlent said ; 'yes, the world is full of inequalities. I !Knew of a case SIM similar to yours.' fhe old bo'sun chuckled quietly, and gave another hitch to his lower gear. I know of an old fellow,' said Geneial Grant, 'who is postmaster of a little town in Kentucky. He lives in a plain way in a small house. He is a nice old man, but he isn't much in rank. His son outranks him ttaVre than your son does you. His son lives in Washington, in the biggest house there, and he -slirrounded by the nicest of furniture, and eats and 'rinks anything he takes a notion to. He could remove his father from office in a minute if he wanted to. But he dosen't want to. And the old man—that's Jesse Grant, you know—doesn't seem to care about the inequality in rank. I suppose he is glad to see his boy get along in the world. The old bo'sun looked down at the carpet and tried to bore a hole in,it with his toe, and his com- rades all laughed at him joyously, and slapped him on the back, and filed out in great glee.! It was the last I ever heard of the petition or the petitioners. The old bo'sun flung his quid into a Spittoon as ho left. Probably he had concluded to give up thinking."—Ex-Secretary Robeson.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

ragout° AMONGST Dram ram Tnais.—We observe that this practice has still its adherents, but we feel sure they cannot specify any reason in defence of it beyond the fact that their forefathers did the same before them. ti3o far as we know the practice originated with the view of turning the 'weeds under, and the operation is for a time successful. But we invariably see an equally bountiful crop spring up the following season. We find the land more free from weeds when left undisturbed beyond tating a hoe and scraping the surface into the spaces between the rows of trees. The frequent traffic over them spaces between the rows obstructs the pro- gress of weeds there. On heavy soils some cultivators make awactice of excavating a trench eight inches or a foot deep between the rows early in autumn and throwing the soil on either side over the roots of the trees. This answers the purpose of a 'top-dressing, and maintains as well the soil in a drier state round the, nets. It must be admitted that this is a very reason- aiiie practice. These channels serve as a receptacle for weeds in the summer time, when the ground is hoed and 'the weeds are raked into them. 'The act of digging amongst bush fruit trees cannot fail 'to destroy all roots to the depth the spade enters, and these are always re- garded as the best. The colder 'the climate the more should these surface roots be encouraged, as roots so situated are in a warmer medium, and the trees willconse- quently be more productive and the fruit of finer flavour. Apart front the mischief arising 'from the operation of digging, the labour that it involves should be taken into consideration- where great breadths aro grown. The best plan to follow for the sakaof keeping down weeds, as well as benefiting the trees, is to mulch Over the rdots any time from now to May with half-decayed manure, old leaves, or decomposed bark. The latter is destruc- tive to surface-rooted and delicate vegetation when fresh, but after it has decayed most things will root in it.

BROAD BEANS.—A soon as the soil can be gat in a suit- able condition broad beans may be sown in drills four to six inches deep, and three feet between the rews. Two or one rows of seeds may be placed in each drill, but if the first method is selar:sed the distance between the seeds should be greater, or about four inches each way. Though beans delight in sail of a stiff nature, providing it is well manured, the early crop is best on lighter soil, for the seeds are not so liable to perish, and the produce will be ready much earlier. We gave last a list of the most suitable varieties for -sundry purposes. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Dahlias should be frequently examined now, or it may occur that when required for the-front garden they may be found useless. When they -have to be preserved in dry. cupboards in the dwelling- house they are apt to sbrrvel and lose their vitality. Should there be any symptoms of contraction, the roots may be dipped in water, and after remaining for a while to drain, they may be replaced, or, if there is a choice of position, preference should he given to one not so warm , and confined. If they are preserved in warm, damp cel- lars they are incited to make premature growth, which, if in the hands of the gardener, would be converted into cuttings, but for which the cottager lacks accommoda- tion.. He must, therefore, maintain his plants in a dor- mant state as long as possible, and if they are i exposed to warmth and moisture they should be removednto a dry, airy place, from the reach of such frosts as we may reasonable expect. IVlES.—AmOOOst the many varieties of ivy there is one in particular that should have a place, where ivy is grown in covering a residence. The leaves are purple, and therefore contrast well with the green varieties. We are informed by a correspondent in a contemporary that the variety originated with the late Mr. Thomas Wil- liams, of Ormskirk, who found it wild, with unusually deep purple leaves, which under cultivation became still darker. THE WlNDOW.—FueHsies.—We find some of these, though in comparatively low temperature, are showing indications of growth. They lave been pruned and placed in a light position. Like many others, we kept these plants too dry during their season of rest. The result was that three parts of each shoot would be dead, which at the time appeared a matter of little conse- quence, as we were in the habit of pruning them still shorter, but there is no doubt that-the energies of the plants were considerably impaired. Seeing how well the plants look out of doors after an unusually mild winter, and possessing vitality to the very tip of their shoots, the question was forced upon us—Why keep these plants dry when under cover? Since then, we , make every effort to green them moist without watering unduly, which, accompanied with warmth, excites them , Mto growth, After all the leaves drop off in the autumn, ; •

TIIE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY. HEN VOOPEL The old-fashioned system of permitting hens to choose their own nests and rear their chicks in their own way had the very decided advantage of saving a great deal of trouble and thought. ' The result, such as it was, came to be regarded as all that could be expected. If a good hatch, that was a proof of the admirable system; if a bad one that was just into, and could not be avoided. Whether the chicks were early or late, it was ' all a matter of luck, which term is often made the ex- cuse for that which is gross neglect But the advan- tage was far out-balanced by the disadvantages. Chicks had to be taken when they could be got, and very sel- dom, indeed, were they at the proper season. Hens in their wanderings would fight, and their progeny would be the unhappy victims of their enmity. In short, the poultry breeder was the sport of his fowls, who but sel- dom did their work at the time that best suited his con- venience or wishes. So it came about that this method had to be given up, and it became necessary to make other arrangements for rearing the chickens. Hence the introduction of coops, the object of which is to con- fine the hen to a given place, and at the same time to permit the chicks their liberty. Thus a dozen broods of young birds can be reared in a place which would not hold a couple were the hen allowed to wander about with them. The requirements of a coop are that it shall give shelter to the inmates, that it shall be warm and com- fortable, that it shall protect them from marauders at night, and that it shall be easily moved. If only to be used in the chicken-house, as described by us a week or two ago, it makes little matter of what shape it is. A bottomless box, with wooden laths or wire bars at the front, will answer just as well as anything. But if it has to be put out in the open, then there must be some- thing very much stronger and offering more protection. The ordinary Sussex coop, which at one time was almost universally employed, is triangular in shape, and presents at the front the appearance of an inverted V. This generally stands about 24 or 27 inches high in the centre' and is the same width at the ground. The sides and back are solid, but the front is made of upright laths, one of which slides up, so as to allow the hen's exit when that is thought desirable. Of course, the y laths, as in all coops, are sufficiently cod to allow the chicks to pass through. ThiS coop usually has no floor, and in such dry districts as Surrey and frussex a floor is net neetled, in any COOP; but wherever the ground is at all cold" or damp, a floor is an indispensible adjunct to any coop, of whatever kind it may be. Till§ Coop may be regarded as an old-fashioned one, but it is none the worse on that accbunt. Its chief fault is that the front does not give much space for a shelter flap being fitted thereon, and this is very useful.either on wet or sunny days. A wire run, of eourse made the same Shape, can be fitted to it, and some time ago we saw one of which one side was made of galvanised iron sheeting, which when placed either to the wind or the sun made a very perfect shelter indeed. Spratt's Patent made a very nice COOP of this kind without run, and those who wish to I buy rather than make their o*n coops, will find' two or three kinds in their price list, which we have pleasure in here mentioning. , • Another kind- of roof is the square one, which may have either a roof sloping from front to back, or gabled, either of which does equally well. The size depends upon the hen, but we have always found that two feet square was a useful size. All coops should have solid sides and backs, and the design does not in any way affect this point. And the front should be wire bars or wooden laths. If the former are employed, all but two should be fixed in the upper and lower frames, but these two, the centre ones, should be rather longer, and both in one piece, the bend being on top, so as to form a handle. The ends, which will then come to the bottom frame, should be fixed into a loose piece of wood long enough to nearly touch the next bar on either side of the two. A piece of tin carried loosely round the bar, and then tacked to the wood at both ends, will keep the door in position and prevent the hen getting out when she is not wanted. If wooden laths are used it will be sufficient to make the centre one longer and loose, and I then it can be lifted right out. A flap should be made to fit at top of the front for shelter, and be arranged to I lie flat or at an angle, and another may be placed at the I feA to close up at night, t wwthioer for athe-ult caw Cllot wire run i 8 11 611- ployed this iat,7 very Well find their way in. il n When from the nature of the soil a floor is hecessarY, it is important that it be properly made. A mere fixed floor to a coop is very bad, as it absorbs the damp from the earth, making the hen and her brood cold and un- comfortable, and giving rise to colds and other diseases. Not only so, but a fixed floor cannot be cleaned properly, and on that score is very objectionable. A floor should, therefore, be movable and be raised two or three inches above the ground. The best method is one that we have adopted for years, and it is 'perfect in all ways. The I boards forming it are nailed on to a couple of pieces of three-inch scantling, and fit entirely within the coop, the I side resting upon the scantling. In this way the inside i I of the Coop s kept perfectly dry, for however hard tt,e rain comes down it does not splash in, and yet bv if tin the coop the floor is at once accessible ftf a Another advantage is that the coop n t Used either with or without the floor, as theXthie of year and season may make it desirable. Wilere the ground is sufficiently dry we prefer not to use a floor, and where not the boards should ha kept well coVered with dry earth and straw. Daily, moving to fresh ground is essential, as is very careful attention to cleanliness. It should be well whitewashed out between every `orood occupying it, or Insects will become a trouble aid annoyance to hen and chickens both.

The most important o:ding at the presea time is to look well after the breeding pens, and the hsAchers. The former want to be very carefully fed, and to have plenty of exercise. Heavy or liberal seeding is sure to result in a large proportion of =fertile eggs, and that happy means should be sought when the fowls shall have enough to at but not too muck Rich food must be 1 adjured hut a little stimulating powder may be used now and again when 'the weather seesus to require it. The best condition for beeding is wi,on tho fowls are rather thin, yet perfectly healthy, and when they are alWays ready for their meals when feeding time comes. I Should any bird—cock or hen—appear out of sorts, it Should be removed forthwith, as ailing fowls can never produce healthy chicks. And .in case of unfertile eggs, If this state of things continues, it will be better to give fewer-or more bens as the case may seem to require, but if that kilt another cock bird should be obtained.

- THE DYNAMITE OUTRAGES IN LONDON.—The two men, Cunningham and Burton, charged with being concerned in . the dynamite outrages in London, were brought up at Bow- street Police Court, London, on pionday, before Sir James Ingham. Mr Poland (instructed by MnPollard, Mr Stephen- son, and Mr Coffe) prosecuted on behalf of the Treasury ; the prisoners being represented by Mr Q,uilliam, Of Liver- , pool.—P.C. Charles East said that on the day of ths explo- sion, about one o'clock, he saw Cunt.ingharn come from the ticket office, and go towards the White Tower. He was posi- tive as to his identit' :, and he fixed the time of the explosion at exactly two o'clock. He picked .him out from among other people.—Thomas Gallagher and the constable deposed to seeing Cunningham at the Tower about one o'clock on the day of the explosion, but prisoner had no bag or parcel visible.—P.C. Deyonald was on duty at the Reception-room of the White Tower, and saw toe prisoner pass out to the parade ground about a quarter of an hour before the'explo• sion. He was the last to leave the Recoption-room before the explosion took place. and was preceded by several who appeared to be ordinary visitors.—Cross-examined : It would take ten minutes to get to the gates.—lnspector Abberline (previously examined) added that when.qeestioned prisoner denied haviog bad a brown box, or saying he borrowed it of a friend- He gave the name of James George Gilbert at first. Witness was present when Burton was taken into cus- tody and his things searched, maps of London and guide books to the Tower and Houses of Parliament being found. He also had nearly .£l5 upon him, and a piece of the New York World for the 16 h of last Novensber.—Cross-ex. &mined There were other guide books in Burton's box.— Miss Elliot proved that Burton lodged with her at Lime. house from May to September. At Whitsuntide he went to Paris, and when he left he said he was going back to America, being interested in the Presidential elections. She saw him again on Christmas Day evening, when he said he had just returned from America. She did not remember him saying his expenses to America would be paid, as the contest would be closed.—Ralph Bainbridge, bookkeeper to Henry Beeman, cabinet maker, Limehouse, said Burton worked for them, but only drew £3 2s 9d between May 16 and September 2of last year. He returned in January, and in that month only received 153—Frederick Daitz, the fore- man, knew Barton had purchased a brown box, which he said he should use as a tool chest. The box produced was about the ordinary &re of a cabinet maker's tool chest. It was usual for cabinet makers to have such a chest. Prisoner was regarded as a good but slow workman,—Prisoners were again remanded for a week.—Mr Poland said he should then go to a different branch of the case.

MCBDER IN IRELAND.—Two relatives named Hurley quarrelled at Cork on Monday, and one intl:cted fatal in- juries upon the other. The murdered man is Michael Burley, and his nephew, Timothy Hurley, is in custody. Frequent, quarrels have taken place between members of the Burley family as to the ownership of a small plot of land adjoining their respective farms. Litigation recently took place, and it was during the levying of the costs in the ease on Monday that the nephew kicked the uncle and in. flicted injuries which canoed cissith. TEE ULSTER CONSERVATIVES AND THE OPPOSITION LEADERS.—It is eald that the relations between the Ulster Conservative members and the Opposition leaders continue somewhat strained. On Monday afternoon Viscount Crich- ton presided at a meeting of the Ulster members at West- minster. The subject discussed was the action to be taken upon the proposed Vote of Censure. It was resolved that a deputation should seek an interview with the Marquis of Salisbury, and their course in the forthcoming division should depend upon his lordship's reply. It was further decided to support Sir John Lubbock's motion in favour of proportional representation, and also the motion of Sir John Hay for a reduction of the representatives of Ireland to 90 members.

BRIJNNER, MOND, AND Co, LIMITED, WINNINGTON. The eighth half-yearly ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the above company was held at the Law Association &ORIN Liverpool, on Thursday week. Mr. John ems&ld, J.P. (Warrington), the chairman of the Board of Directors, presided. There was a large atten- dance of ehareholders, amongst others present being—Mr J T Brunner, Mr L Mond, Mr H Branner, Mr E Milner, Mr J P Brunner, Mr H Coghill, Mr W G Reiland, Sir J A Picton, Mr H Neumann, Mr W H Verdin, Mr T Irvine, Mr W Blain, Mr W H Andersson, Mr W B Marshall, Mr FJ Hawkins (solicitor to the company), Mr T W Read (auditor to the company), Mr J Handley, Mr G G Walrusley, Mr D C Keeling, Mr J 11 Kerane, Mr A W Chalmers, Mr P D Carr, Ac. The Secretary (Mr T H Forgan) having read the notice convening the meeting, The CHAIRMAN said he bad to congratulate the share- holders upon the satisfactory balance sheet of the company, copies of which they had already received. He could as- sure them that the profit shown on the balance sheet had been honestly and truly earned, and he thought he might venture to say that their prospects for the current year were as good as they had turned out to be in the past. Considering that trade throughout the country was se de- pressed, it was very satisfactory to see a oencern like that plying its ordinary shareholders a dividend of 20 per cent. (Hear, hear.) He moved the following resolution That the Directors' report and statement of accounts be adopted, and that a dividend be paid the holders of the preference shares at a rate of seven per cent, per annum on the amount paid no on such shares, and that a dividend be paid the holders of the ordinary shares at the rate of 20 per cent, per annum on the amount paid up on such shares' free of income tax, for the half-year ended 31st a cemberlBB4." Mr H CooHILL seconded the resolution, which was un- nanimously adopted. _

The following lean extract from the report of the Direc- tors :—The balance sheet and profit and lose account, certi- fied by the auditor, and now presented, show a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working of the half-year ended on the 31st December, 1884, of £64,706 17s 3d, which, with the amount of £29,647 8s 5d brought forward from the previous half-year. makes a total of £94,354 5s Bd. The Directors propose to deal with the above balance as follows :—Dividend on the preference capital, at seven per cent. der annum, £8,077 ; dividend on the ordinary capital, at 20 per cent. per annum, £47,260 ; amount to be written off patents account, £5,244 108 ; amount to be placed to the reserve fund, £7,500; balance to be !larded forward £26,282 15a 8d ; total, £94,354 53 Bd. . _

CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETING.

SPEECH OF SIR GILBERT GREENALL. On Monday evening the aminel meeting of the Conserva- tives of South-East Ward was held in the National School- room, Church-street, Councillor W J Burgess presiding. There were also present the Tory candidate for the borough. Sir Gilbert Greenell, Bart., Mr James Croston, JP, Man- chester ' • Captain Reynolds, Alderman Webster, Councillors Bolton, Hutchinson, and Whittle, and Messrs H Greenall, J Smethurst, G Woods, J Roberts. R Isherwood, Marsh, J I) Ruckton, J V Taylor, A W Brundrett, W M Adams, and J Hampson, ie Coneetyethe ageet, T 1.16 CHAIRMAN said that no one who reflected for a moment upon the preeent position of affairs in this country would suppose that there was any lack of material for any one to speak upon the situation from a Conservative stand- point. The difficulty was not to find what the Government bad done that was ill, but to discover a bright page in the dark chapter of its five years' existence. (Applause) After criticising the general policy of the present Government, Mr Burgess said that all previous mistakes and blunders had been obscured by the miserable, hesitating, halting, im- becile policy that had been shown in respect to Fgypt and the Soudan, a policy that had cost us some 50,000 lives, millions of treasure, and some of the best and noblest of Englishmen. The war in which we were engaged, he said, need never have beea entered upon if Her Majesty's Minis- ters had known their own minds, and had from the fl-st acted with firmness and decision. The truth was that hesi- tation, v'.lllalioe, pd procrastination hid been the watch; P ri e words of the Ce;.svernmOll. (Applause.) Sir GILDORT GREENALL then addreseei the meeting, lie said :—My friends and neigh'„oure, I came down this evening very, very indeed to come and appear amongst you, but I had nought, and I think now, that as I have to many and. 'frequent opportunities of addressing you, 1 and as I kriq'ef well enough to-night that you will want to heat anything that Mr. Croston will tell you, I had thought that it was wiser, better, and more polite—if I may use the expression—to you, not to detain you by any remarks of my own. I know well enough, intimately, lam glad to say, with confidence and affection I know him—l mean ' your chairman. (Applause.) I have frrquently heard your chairman speak. He is a good chairman. (Hear, hear.) He is of the right stamp. He speaks plainly, and he speaks with courage. Now, if any qualities are wanting in speakers at this time of day it is clearness and integrity of view and a resolute determination to express those views in plain and direct language. (Hear, hear.) It is not easy for any Englishman in these days not to raise his protest against the Government of this country. (Hear, hear.) It is not straightforward, I should tell an untruth if I said that I thought this country was at this day rightly governed and sufficiently and honourably supported. We have terrible things to think of. Just for one moment think of Gordon. Just for one moment regard Gordon's fate. I say this, Gordon has been mercilessly destroyed. (Hear, hear ) Gordon has been mercilessly neglected. (Hear, hear.) Gordon in speaking a right and true tone to his country- men was not listened to. (Hear, hear.) Gorden was neglented, Gordon I &wider perished—can I say the eord—Gordon is a man that England has suffered to be murdered. (Applause.) And now let me say a word for Warrington. There is something very good, there is some- thing perfectly true, in the breeding of people in Warring- ton. Earle—Earle—General Earle, as brave a man, as fear- less a man, as grand a soldier, as ever put on the Queen's uniform, that man was where an Englishman, an English officer, an English gentleman, will always be—ha was in the front rank, and he lost his life in leading on the forces against the enemy. (Applause.) Now, Earle came from a Warrington family. (Hear, hear.) I have the honour and the plfasure of an acquaintance with the family of Earle. They have lost a noble branch of their family, but if lost to them be lives amongst his country- men. (Hear, bear.) What Earle has done, where Earle died, will never be forgotten by a single man whom I have now the honour to speak to. Well, we have lost one who a short time ago would have appeared amongst us. the brave, the grand, the noble Colonel Burnaby. (Applause.) Now, my friends, I will pass on. I might have gone on and have spoken in this strain for some time—(cries of "Go on") —but Mr. Croston is here. But, you and I, my friends, we are English. (Hear, hear.) You and 1, my friends, love our country. You and I, my friends, wish our country and those who lead and govern our country, we wish them never to be as her Majesty's Ministers have been for the last twelve months or more, we wish them, we wish our- selves—never to be.too late. Well, it is very pleasant for me to come amongst you ; it is very pleasant to me to have the affectionate reception you always give me. I know you thoroughly and well; I know my aim and my object pretty well, and my aim and my object is to belong to you and to deserve to belong to you. (Applause.) Mr. CROSTOW then spoke on "Conservative and Radical Rule: a Contrast and a Warning," denouncing the policy of the Liberal Government in strong terms. In reply to a question from the audience if his name was " Crosfield," he said no. He was none of that kith or kin, but was, always had been, and hoped he might remain, a Church- man and a Conservative. Referring to the speeches that he said he had seen reported in the Warrington Examiner, Mr. Croston said that one was an address by the gentleman who was at present supposed to represent Warrington in Parliament and another by a gentleman who aspired to that position. These gentlemen he said, in endeavouring to throw a little dust into people's eyes, undertook to explain what the Conservative party was and he noticed that Mr. Crosfield undertook to explain the meaning of the word "Tory," and said that it was a name given in 1680, or thereabout, and that its meaning was " a robber." He was surprised to find that gentleman going back to ancient his- tory, but it was useful sometimes, as it proved that for 200 years the party of which Mr. Crosfield was such a fitting ornament bad lived by traducing the character of, and libelliug and slandering better men than themselves. Why did not Mr. Crosfield at the same time explain the meaning of the word " Whig 7" because they had it on record that the meaning of that word was " whey "—sour milk. (Laughter.) When they remembered the sourness of disposition of the party to which Mr. Cros- field belonged, whether rell7,lons or political, be thought that they would admit that " sour milk "was a correct des- cription of him or his friends. Mr. Croston then referred to a speech made by the gentleman for whom Mr. Crosfield took the chair—a gentleman whom he described as an indi- vidual of limited education and unlimited imagination— and said that he was surprised that Mr. Crosfield should have by his presence countenanced, sanctioned, and en- dorsed the untruths that were uttered. (Applause.) The meeting concluded by the usual votes of thanks.

Da Worms, in criticising the speech of Mr. Gladstone, maintained that it had in no sense justified the policy of the Government, which he described as one con- tinuous chain of vaccillation, change, and failure. Sir GEORGE CAMPBELL expressed gratification at the speech of Mr. Gladstone, and strongly advocated a cessa- tion of hostilities in the Soudan.-.-Colonel DAWNAY was of opinion that the motion of Sir S. Northcote did not suffi- ciently express the indignation felt by the large majority of Englishmen at the policy of the Government, and hoped that one of the final acts of the present Parliament would be to depose the present Government from office. Mr. SIMIERLAND expressed his conviction that the Government was not to blame. Mr. BRODRICK commented on the divergencies of the ' Ministerial supporters, and painted out that in their lobby would be found the apostles of peace alongside of those whose blunders were responsible for forcing upon us a North African Empire. Mr. Pacroer contended that it wag a mistake on the part of the Government to send out General Gordon, and ridiculed the idea that it is necessary for this country to fight in the Seti lan in order to maintain its prestige. Sir H. GIFFARD asked for information as to what was to be the policy of the Government in the future, and, having argued that General Gordon had been sent to Khartoum en- ' tirely on the responsibility of the Government, com- plained that they so long delayed to attempt to rescue him tram the position in which they had allowed him to be placed. After a few words from Mr. Redmond, the debate was ad- journed on the motion of Mr. GOSCHEN. After other business the House adjourned at 1245. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. THE OFFICE OF Exectrrtoeren.—Earl COWPER called at- tention to the mismanagement attending a recent attempt at the infliction of cepital punishment, and asked whether it is not now the opinion of her Majesty's Government that there should be a public executioner for the whole of the United Kingdom, appointed and removable by one of her Majesty's Secretaries of State. The noble earl, referring to the unfor- tunate scene at Exeter on Monday, said that the Home Sec- retary had been placed in a great difficulty. He had to choose between two evils, and he had chosen the lesser of the two.—Lord MONSON regretted that the Earl of Dalhousie was prevented through indisposition from being present to answer the question. What he was requested to s ty, in answer to his noble friend's question, was that the Secre- tary of State had taken steps to have a strict investigation made into all the facts It did not yet appear that the fault rested with the executioner.
. Their lordships adjourned at fiva minutes past five o'clock.

It was arranged that immediately after qaestions Mr. Gosclaen should resume the debate on Sir Stafford North- cote's vote of censure. But the House proposed and the Parnellites disposed. When at twenty minutes to six ques- tions were answered, Mr. Gladstone moved that notices of motion should be postponed till after the order for debate on the vote of censure, Mr. Redmond noisily protested against the attempt to supersede a motion which he had put down on the paper for last night. The Speaker, after twice warning him, ordered hint to resume his seat. At half-pelt six, the discussion on Mr. Gladstone'a motion having proceeded in most disorderly fashion for nearly an hour, the Speaker rose and said : "It is my duty to inform the House that I consider this subject has been adequately discussed, and that it is the evident sense of the House the question should now be put." This was the application of the Closure Rule, which, after lying dormant for two years and a half, was for the first time put in operation. Mr. Gladstone approached the table, but was received with such a storm of cries and jeers from the Parnellites that he was unable to proceed. Amid less articulate cries were sheuts of " This is Liberal policy!" Mr. O'Brien, who made himself prominent in the disturbance, cried out threateningly, "We will remember this in Ireland." The Speaker, immediately rising to his feet, was heard above the din to say, "Mr. O'Brien, I name you as disregarding the authority of the chair." "Name away!" the Parnellites cheerily answered, and continued their shouting. Mr. GLADSTONE again approached the table. He moved that Mr. O'Brien be suspended from the service of the HOII9O. The Speaker was about to put the question, whea Mr. Sexton rose amid renewed uproar, in which the House generally and angrily joined. For some moments the I speaker and Mr. Sexton were on their feet, the latter shout. log net that he rose to a point of order. Eventually he was enabled to make known his point of order, which was that the Speaker had not named Mr. O'Brien with the full formula. "You only said' Mr. O'Brien,' " Mr. Sexton defiantly shouted. ' '•

The Speaker proceedel to put the question that Mr. i O'Brien be suspended from the service of the House. The [ division bell rang, and members trooped in from all the ad- jacent rooms. The lobby had already been cleared, mem- bers being attracted by the vociferous shouts plainly heard through the glass doors. On a division the suspension was decreed by 244 votes against 20. " So the member for !Leßow will withdraw," said the Speaker. "Certainly, Mr. Speaker," Mr. O'Brien retorted ; "1 [ will leave the place with much more pleasure than I ever ' entered it." Thereupon he vanished through the crowded doorway. The main question to postpone the orders of the day as put and carried, but not mail after a lengthened and some- what angry discussion on points of order. THE VOTE OF CENSURE DEBATE.

In the ala.s.en-ce. of Mr.Goschen,thedebte upon the pro- posed Vote of Censure was resumed by Sir J. LUBBOCK, who argued that the intention of the Government to overthrow the Mandi was inconsistent with Lord Woleley's procla- mation that he had gone to restsre peace in the Soudan. His contention was that we had no right to attack the tribes in the Soudan unless we intended to remain there. He would support the Government in any line they might de- termine to be necessary for defending Egypt from the Mandi, but deprecated the extension of military operations beyond the limits which were adopted as the permanent frontier of Egypt. —The debate was continued by Mr. Stuart-Wortley. Mr. Borlase, and Mr. Long.—Mr. ARNOLD hoped the debate would mike members look to the future and endeavour as far as they could, in the light of the papers before them, to give their best counel and aid to the Government in the difficult position in which the affairs of Egypt were now placed. A series of mistakes had been made in regard to Egypt, but they had not been made by the Government alone. Mr. TREVELYAN consi- dered the important point, after they received the news of the fall of Khartoum, was whether the decision to push on the war was a justifi tble one.—Mr. GOSCHEN implored the Government to let. the House know what their ultimate ob- .

i.e.-cis were. He wished to know if it was one of the objects of the Government to assist in suppressing the slave trade ; and whether the Government meant, after breaking the power of the Mandi at Khartoum, to establish an orderly Government. We must stand by the tribes which had stood by our troops in the Sandal', and any scheme which did not offer some security to those tribes would be unsatis- factory in the highest degree. He was not prepared to sup- port a policy of breaking the power of the Mabdi without otricter declarations from _the Government than bad yet been made—The debate was adjourned until Thursday, on the motion of Mr. CItiPLIN, and the Hoase rose shortly before one o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. . . .

A House was not made until twenty minutes to one o'clock. The North Wales Narrow Gauge Extension. Bill was read a first time. PRIVATE BILL LEGISLATION.—Mr. CRAIG SELLAR, in moving the second reading of the Private Bill Legislation Bill, said the subject had been considered bye committee of both Houses, by joint committees, and by a royal Commis- sion, and outside Parliament the evils of the present system bad been an unfailing source of discussion by learned societies, chambers of cominerco, and muni- cipal corporations in England, Scotland, and Ireland. As an illustration of the haphazard character of the present system, he mentioned the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, with which Parliament had played shutlecock attl battledore for 114 days, and hal ended the matter by leaving the pro:voters exactly where they were to begin-with. A system which produced such results was satisfactory neither to suitors nor to the public, and did not redound to the credit of Parliament.— Sir J. PEASE proposed to refer opposed private bills to Joint Committees of both Houses. Alluding to the Ship Canal scheme, he said when people did not know what to do it was better to do nothing, and no doubt that was the prin- ciple upon which the committees on the Ship Canal bad acted.—Mr. GREGORY recommended a reference of such bills to a committee of four, consisting of two from each House.—Mr. Sadamst-Boom thought private bill commit- tees enjoyed the confidence of suitors and the public to a greater extent than would be felt in the decisions of judges selected in the manner proposed.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, while sympathising with the objects of the bill, thought there were strong reasons why the question should be left open for the decision of the new Parliament. Should that course be taken the Government would do their best to assist Parliament to arrive at a satisfactory solution of the question.—Sir LYON PLAYFAIR remarked that thia suggestion would be only adding to the delay which had

MOWBEAY advocated the second reading of the bill and its reference to a select committee.—Upon a division' the motion for the second reading was rejected by 160 to 55. Sir J. PEASE proposed to amend his amendment by the addition of the worth., "without further inquiry and con- sideration" after" unwilling;" but Mr. BIGGAR objected, and, it being after a quarter to six, the debate was adjourned. THE MOTION OF CENSURE.—Lord GEORGE HAMILTON gave notice that on the vote of censure, in the event of Mr. Morley's amendment becoming the substantive question, he should move to leave out all the words after "thin" in the first line, in order to add "the Government has failed to indicate any policy which justifies the confidence of this House or the country." (Cheers) The House adjourned at five minutes to six. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tlinusnev. The Lord chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. VOTE OF CENSURE.

The debate upon the Marquis of Salisbury's proposed Vote of Censure caused the House of Lords to be crowded. —The noble MARQUIS moved—" That this House, having taken into consideration the statements that had been made on behalf of Her Majesty's Government, is of opinion that (1) the deplorable failure of the Soudan expedition to attain its object has been due to the undecided counsels of the Government and to the culpable delay attending the com- mencement of operations; (2) that the policy of abandon- ing the whole of the Soudan after the conclusion of military operations will be dangerous to Egypt and inconsistent with the interests of the Empire." Lord Salisbury complained that throughout there had been an unwillingness on the part of the Government to come till the last moment to any definite decision, and that there had been an absolute terror of fixing upon a settled course, The conduct of the Government had been an alternation of periods of slumber with periods of rush. He contended that from the an- nouncement of the abandonment of the Soudan and the mission of General Gordon all our subsequent troubles had arisen. He did not accept the theory of treachery; but supposing it to be time, if British troops had been in Khartoum with Gordon treachery would have been Impos- sibk What, be asked, were our prospects for the future ? The Government would not say whether they were going to evacuate the Soudon or not. They would not say who, was going to occupy it. The advantages desired could be obtained if England would lay down a determined policy and adhere to it. But a coast tent policy could only ba conducted by a Ministry which wad capable of unity of counsel and decision of pur- I pose.—Lord WENTWORTH moved his amendment declaring that the Government should not employ British forces to occupy the Soudan, or to prevent the exercise by the Egyp- tian people of their right to select their own tiovernment. —Lord NORTHBROOK replied to the criticisms of Lord Sol- isbury.—The debate was continued by the Dqke of Rich- mOnd'anctGordon, the Marquis. of Handy, Lard Stanley of Alderley, Lord Brabourne, Lord Thurlow, the Earl of Jersey, Lard Baty, Lord Morley, .the Marquis Of Waterfo:d, and Lord Darby. _ _ _

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. QUESTIONS —ln the House of Commons the HOME SEC. RETARY, referring to the newspaper reports of a meeting of conspirators in Paris with the avowed object of destroying buildings and sacrificing human life in this country, said he had reason to balieve there was no foundation for the sensational paragraphs which had appeared.—Lord E. FITZ • MAURICE assured Sir If. Holland that the whole report of a native revolt at Quitto, on the Gold Coast, was an exag- geration, for nothing mo-e bad occurred than a serious police affray.—Questions were put by Irish members re- specting the judicial rents fixed by the Land Commis- sioners, and Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN stated that there was no intention on the part of the Government to amend the Land Act. A short statement was made by the PRIME MixisrEn on the subject of the Italian expedition to the Red Sea. Replying to a question whether the expedition was intended to co-operate with the British forces, the right hon. gentleman said Italy was in the most cordial relations with this country, but there was no plan of military co-operation between the two. —ln reference to the French notification that they intended to treat rice as contraband of war in the )perations against China, Lord E. FITZMAURICE said the Government, after consultation with the law officers, had determined that they could not assent to the right claimed by the French.—Mr. CAINE informed the House that the Government had no present intention to exercise the power of retaining time- expired men in the navy. THE ADJOURNED DEBATE.

The adjourned debate on the proposed Vote of Censure was resumed by Mr CFIAPLIN, who maintained that all the difficulties of the Goverm,ent in the Soudan had arisen from their determination to ignore their responsibilities, and that whatever might have been the original policy of the Government, nothing could condone the treachery to- wards General Gordon. He held that two things were absolutely essential to be done, the first being that we must get rid of our Prime Minister, and the second that we must largely increase the military and naval forces of the noun- try.—Sir W. Hancontrr, replying to the assertion that the Government ought never to have advised the evacuation of the Soudan, said that was a decision the Government saw no reason to regret, and General Gordon left Eng- land fully accepting that policy. The Government were asked why they were going to Khartoum. It was because that was the only manner in which the evacuation of the Soudan could be safely accomplished consistently with the safety of Egypt. Dealing with th inquiries of Mr. Goschen, he asked how the Government could pledge themselves as to what they would do after operations which must depend upon circumstances with which they were not acquainted. He contended that the proposals of the Opposition were all in favour of a more direct and prolonged intervention in Egypt, and repeated ' that the Government adhared to their pledge to leave that country as soon as they possibly could. The Conservatives, if they came into power, would find that Europa would not release them from the pledges which her Majesty's Govern- ment had given.—Sir 14. CROSS denounced the policy of OS I Government as" stupid," and said it was absolutely neces- sary that we should remain in Egypt.' With respect to the Suakim-Barber railway, he asked what the Government pro- posed to do with it after they bad overcome the Matadi.— , Professor BRYCE regarded the making of the railway to 1 Berber with gre it apprehension, as it would involve the per. mament occupation of that part of the Soudan. On the motion of Sir M. H. BEAM the debate was ad- journed till Friday. SUNDAY Cr.ostNo.—Sir J. Pnese brought in a bill for ' closing public-houses on Sunday, making exception for the sale of beer during certain hours, and for the Metropolitan 1 district.

The home team had the piay pretty much their own way, and at the call of time were declared the winners by seven goals to nil.

_ NEWTON (A TEAM) T. KIRIDILE.—These teams met on the ground of the latter in Stanley Park, Liverpool, and Newton, who played one man short, were defeated by one goal, three tries, and several minor points to one minor point.

WARRINGTON EXCELSiOR V. WIDNES STLR OF HOPE.— This return match was played at Warrington. The game ended in a victory for the Excelsior by 1 try, 2 disputed tries, and 7 minor points to nil. The home team forwards played excellent, dribbling in fine style. WARRINGTON V. ECCLES —On Saturday these clubs met at Eccles, and a good game resulted in favour of Warring on by one goal, two tries, and two minor points to one goal. Teams :—Warrington : T Walsh, back; J T Massey, T Barnes, and W Speaktnan, three-quarter backs ; E Gilbert and J E Warren, half backs; H Ashton, W Hayes, F Turner, W Povey, Frank Turner, J Robinson, J Jolley, W Ddlon, and J Rigby, forwards. Eccles: W Parker, back ;J Worth- ington, L Brittain, and J Wignall, three-quarter backs ; R Willis and E Vickers, half backs ; R Evans (captain), A Berry, C haw, G Crook, F Potter, J E Fletcher, C Holt, J Shrewsbury, and W Holmes, forwards. RUNCORN RECREATION V. NEW BRIGHTON VICTOICIA.—On Saturday the above club paid a visit to Runcorn, arriving very late, and with a short team; but they obtained the services of G Wainwright, Andrew, and Riley, on the Run- corn club, and Lewis and Wilson, of the Recreation. The bull was kicked off down bill by the Recreation, and after a series of scrimmages in the visitors' 25-, the ball was pasvd to W Faulkner, who dropped a neat goal. At the call of time the Recreation were declared victors by one goal and three minor points to two minor points. All the subs played well for the visitors, as did Edwards and Wylie and W Faulkner and A Clare for the Recreation.

RCNCORN (2so TEEM) V. WEsTax PoiNr.—The return m..tch between these teams was played at Runcorn, on Saturday, when the home team won by one goal, four tries, and fifteen minor points, to Weston Point nil. Tbe tries were obtained by Andrews, Whitby, Clarke, Wainwright, and Wocd (full Pick). Teams:—Runcorn, Woods,. back; Lunt, Riley, and Wainwright, three-quarter hicks; Whitby and Antrobus, half-backs; Clarke (captain), Janion, Cox, Gittens, Dunbavand, Andrews, Raffe, Ford, and Orme, for- wards. Weston Point: Brown, back; Mather, Gittens, and Cawley, three-quarter backs; Stubbs and Rostock, half- backs ; Jeffs, Atherton, Kennedy, Cartwright, Griffiths, Hulse Corker, Abrams, and Sherlock, forwards.

Si. HELENS V. Si. HELENS RECREATIOZS.—These Old rivals met on the St. Helens ground on Saturday, in the pre- sence of a good number of spectators. The weather was anything but favourable for football, a strong wind blowing from goal to goal. The time had to be divided into four twenties. St. Helens Recreation always manage to whip up a strong team for this match. Last Saturday was no ex- ception to the rule, and, atter a very tough struggle, the result was a draw. the Recreation scoring five minor points to one minor point, but just before the finish of the third twenty St. Helens had hard lines in not scoring a try. Teams :—T Rodgers, back ; J Gregson, W C Haselden' and .1 Dearden, three-quarter backs ; Finney (c apt tin) and .1 0 S Edwards, half backs ; Anders, Borthwick, T Pennington, W Jame., Ii Unsworth, S Halton, J Basnett, J Harwood, and RF S Twist, forwards. Recreation : C., Taylor, back ; R Langley, Seddon, and J Pyke, three-quarter backs ; W Parr and P Roberts half backs; T Rankin, 11 Gregeon, T Slater, P Finn. W Dean, W Cook, J Fletcher, W fli,gham, and T Green, forwards. LIVERPOOL CUP COMPETITION : SEMI-FINAL TIE— EVERTOR (CITPIIOLDERS) V. GOLROSNE.—The last stage but one in the Liverpool and District Cup ties was brought to an issue on the ground of the Bootle club, on Saturday' in the presence of about 1,000 spectators. The ground was soft and slippery; in fact, the mud was so plentiful that play had not progressed many minutes ere several of the players were hardly recognisable. Again, contrary to ex- pectation, the play was completely one-sided, so much so that during the latter portion of the second half the Ever- ton custodian was observed coolly sauntering down the fie:d with his great coat on, puffing a cigarette. In the first half Golborne made their effort, but, being completely out- manceuvred, were never dangerous, 'whilst in the second half they were fairly penned. If the spectators were not treated to a grand display of the dribbling rules, they, nevertheless appeared to enjoy themselves immensely, if we might judge from the hearty peals of laughter which greeted the puzzled looks of several of the visiting forwards,l who time after time were utterly non•plussed. The home' forwards played fine passing game, Richards, Whittle, and being specially conspicuous. The back division were quiet up to par. Findlay appeared to much greater advantage than usual. The visitors' goal-keeper deserves a word of praise, but the play of the remainder of the team does not call for special comment. At the call of time Everton were declared winners by nine goals and one disallowed to nil. Everton : C M Lindsay, goal ; T Marriott and R Morris, backs •, M Higgins, W Findlay, and J Pickering, half backs ; W Richards and J Whittle right wing ; J M'Gill, centre; C Jones and W Gibson, left wing. Gel- borne : W Jenkinson, goal; J Bate and J Waddington. backs; T Kay, P Ridyard, and J Barker, half backs; A Allen and S Morrie, right wing ; C Witlinall, centre, R Hemborough and J Clare, lift wing.

Elmatsrowx v. Boorut.—The Earlestown first team secured another victory on Saturday afternoon, when they succeeded in beating the Bootle first team by three goals to one. The match was played on the ground of the first-named at Wargrave Moss, and there was a large attendance of spectators, who witnessed a fast and exciting game. The home club turned out its full cup team, while the Bootle club was represented by its strongest eleven, inclading both Veitch and Hutton, late of the Dumbarton P.C. The visitors won the toss, and for the first hall choose to play up hill. Dagnall started the leather for the horns team, who bad the wind against them. After some even play the Earlestonians made a capital attack on their opponents' stronghold, and amid hearty cheere scored the first goal; Ellison shooting the leatker thrrAgh the uprights. On the game being resum„atb Liverpool men, and t home eleven still pressed the prolonged cheers greeted the scoring of the second goal by Dagnall fifteen minutes from the start. This double reverse woke up the Bootle representatives, and the Earlestown goal was seriously endangered, Jones, I Grayson, and Hutton made same splendid runs. Shortly before bait time an exciting scrimmage occurred in front of the home god, and Bootle scored their first and only goal. On changing ends Earlestown was ahead by two goals to one. but bad the ground against them. The visitors re• sumed the game with r,„ed energy, and for some minutes held a decided advantage. The defenders of the home goal played splendidly. however, and defeated the attempts of the Bootle forwards to score. The superior staying powe-s of the Earlestonians proved of great advantage, and to. wards the close they secured the upper hand. From a .free kick in front of the 'Bootle uprights, Sims again scored amid cheers. Bath teams afterwards worked hard to secure an additional poiet, but neither was successful, and Earles- town thus wen by three goals to one. Teams—Earlestown: J Appleton, goal; R Green and J Green, backs; J Dux- bury, R Bowker, and J Whalley, half backs; W Rich and J Ellisen, right wing; A W Dagnall, centre; J Sims and J Ogden, left wing. Bootle : J Jackson, goal; T Veitch and C Evans, backs; J D McMurray, J W C Rogers, and F Woods, half backs; J A Stevenson and J Johnstone, right wing; G Hutton, centre: J A Eyton-Jones and J E Gray- son, left wing.

div.head: WARRINGTON PUBLIC HALL COMPANY,
div.p: WARRINGTON PUBLIC HALL COMPANY,

On Monday the general annual meeting of this company was held at the Public Hall. There were present Mr. John White (in the chair), Messrs. J. Davies, C. J. Holmes, J. C. Whittle, H. N. :Houghton, Dr. Mackie, J. Hatton J. T. Picton, H. Greenall (solicitor to the company), and W. Johnson (secretary).—The report of the directors which was submitted stated that they had *Aire in stating that the income was again above the average. The total income for the post year (including piano and organ receipts) had bsen £,177 12s, and the total expenditure £327 3s Sid. This latter sum included= 3s 10d for completing the re- seating of the greater portion of the ball. As would be seen from the balance the amount available for dividend wee £l5B 4s 2d, out of wla'ch it was proposed to pay 'a divi- dend of 31 percent, carrying forward a balance of £7 Itle 21.—The CHAIIIII&N, in moving the adoption of this report, regretted the aosence of their chairman, Dr. Smith, who had been chairman of the company since it was formed 23 , years ago, and also of the vice-chairman, Mr. John Rylsnds, I and of Mr. Carter, Mr. Z, Armitage, and Mr. Long, who were directors. The revenue, he said, was very much about the average, though considerably more than the average of the last 20 years, and considering that they bad not been 1 passing through very good times they might congratulate themselves that the income from the letting ef the hall kept up as well as it did. The item of £l3O for meetings, lecturer, Ac ,was not altogether to be accmnted for by the meetings during the week days: On the contrary he thought their meetings on week days had fallen off, and the large sum he had referred to was owing largely to the fact that the Salvation Army had occupied the ball on Sundays. That was an item they could not always look forward to, and therefore their income must always depend in a great measure upon entertainments, Sze. The ball was now not 90 well suited to the kind of performances that- cams to War- rington as they ought to make it, and therefore the directors had employed Mr. Darbyshire, a well-known architect of Manchester, to suggest the alterations that should be made in the ball to meet the requirements of the people who came to it —Dr. MACKIE snonded the adoption of the report, which was carried.—Mr. DAVIES then moved" That a divi- dend be declared for the past year at the rate of Si per cent free of income tax, payab'e on and af er the let March."— Mr. HoLsrEs seconded the proposal, which was carried.—On the motion of Mr. WHITTLE, Mr. John White, Dr. Mackie, and Mr. Long were re-elected directors; and on the motion of Mr.Picrox, seconded by Mr. flerrox, Mr. Holmes was thanked for his past services as auditor and re-elected to the office. A vote of thanks was likewise passed to the directors. —A special meeting was then held for the purpose of con- sidering a scheme for the improvement of the hall. In the directors' report it was stated that these improvements were tube effected by a re-arrangement of the entrances and wait- ing rooms, and by the alteration of the platform, Ac., in ' in order that the same may be made better available for the various operatic and other entertainments upon which the income of the company now so largely depended. It is ex- pected that the cost, including an improved system of ven- tilation, will be from £3OO to £l,OOO, but the latter sum will certainly not be exceeded. The plans of the proposed ' alterations having been submitted and explained, the Cwarnstsw proposed the resolution That the directors ' may borrow in the name, or otherwise on behalf of the com- pany, such sum or sums of money for such times and such k rates of interest as the directcirs shall think fit by way of mortgage of the property of the company, but so that the ' aggregate amount of such sum or sums of money existing 3 at any time shall not exceed the sum of £l,ooo."—Dr. Itisortn seconded the propsal, which was supported by Mr. DAVIES, • and carried unanimously.—A vote of thanks to the chair- man brought the proceedings to a close.

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
EGYPTIAN FINANCES.

- - - CAIRO, SATITRDAY.—The Egyptian Government have re- ceived information from London that all the details of the Egyptian financial arrangement hive been agreed on be- tween England and the other Powers. THE FENIANS IN PARIS. Pants MONDAY.—A Congress of Fading and members of the dynamite party was held to-day in Paris. An account of the proceedings, alleged to be by an eye-witness, stated that there were eleven delegates, two of whom represented the Irish revolutionists in Great Britain' three others the extremists in the United States, two Ireland, two the Con- tinent, and two the Invincibles. James alcDerrnot, the in- former, was again condemned to death. It was also decided to despatch two dynamiter adquainted with military tactics to the Mabdi. FRENCH SOCIALISM.

PARIS, SIINDAY.—ArI international Anarchist meeting of working-inen was held to-day in the Salle Tivoli, at which four hundred persons were present, including several mein. bers of the Chamber of Deputies. M. Maret was elected president The meeting adopted resolutions declaring its implac ible hatred of tyrants, protesting against every policy having for its object a war of conquest, and expressing sympathy with the working classes of all nations. THE CONGO CONFERENCE.

BERLIN, MONDAY.—The Conference held a four hours' sitting to-day, under the presidency of Dr. Busch. An ap- plication from the International African Association to be allowed to give its adhesion to the Acte-G6neral was read. The plenipotentiaries of America, England, France, Get. , many, Italy, and Portugal made short speeches, refeaing in highly lau-datory terms to the association, and particularly to the King of the Belgians, its patron. Two small addi- tional amendments proposed by England were carried, and the final Acta was then accepted. It now only remains for the Ante to be printed on parchment for the signature of the Plenipotentiaries. FRANCE AND CHINA.—BARBAROUS PROCEEDINGS.

TAOISM (244 COLOMBO), JANUARY 25Th—The so-called " blockade " is only effective against European merchants. In Tamsui we are now without 10 males front Europe, and we cannot get away. Several French war vessels run along the coast, and sink every boat which they meet, taking the crews to Kalung, where they are treated tarharouslv. The proceedings of the French are unparalleled in the history of modern civilised warfare.
PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—GreueriI Bri6re de L'lsle telegraphs that he is preparing to undertake fresh operations aglinst the Chinese.

THE FRANCO-CHINESE WAR. PARIS, TlRTRSDAY.—lntelligence from Shanghai states that Admiral Conrbet will take up a position at a point at present unknown, but near Shanghai, with a view to prevent rice cargoes from leaving that port.

div.head: ITALIAN -RED EA EXPEDITION.
div.p: THE ITALIAN -RED EA EXPEDITION.

NAPLES, WEDNESDAY.—The third Italian expedition, consisting of 59 officers and 1,50 men sailed yesterday evening for the RA Sea. General Ricci, with a flotilla of six torpedo boats, will start to-morrow for the Same desti- nation.

div.head: GREECE.
div.p: GREECE.

ATHENS, MONDAY.—Failing to-day to obtain a vote of ; confidence from the Chamber of Deputiee, M. Tricmpia .read a Royal decree dissolving the Chamber. DISTURBANCES AT QUITTA.—THE ENGLISH GOVERNOR WOUNDED.

HAMBURG, MONDAY.—According to intelligence from the West Coast of Africa. serious disturbances have broken out in Quitti. The natives revolted against the English. and in the fighting which ensued the Governor received four gunshot wounds, one piercing the langs. A party of 60 men, und,r the command of a young officer, were still in possession of the town and fort.
TEM ALLEGED GERMAN ACQUISITIONS IN ZULULAND.
DURBiN, WEDNESDAY.—lntelligence received here states that Disizuln disclaims all knowledge of Herr Einwald's proceedings in Zululand. FRANCE.—THE CORN TAX.

Paws, TUESDAY.—The Chamber of Deputies to-day agreed by 316 votes to 175 to the proposed increase on the duty cn corn. This will make the total import duty 3f. It also adopted a proposal to levy a duty of Of. 60c. on corn of extra European quality imported into France from European entrepote. To-morrow the Chamber will dismiss the duties on flour.

div.head: ANARCHISTS IN SWITZERLkND.
div.p: THE ANARCHISTS IN SWITZERLkND.

GENEVA, WHDNESDAY.—At an Anarchist meeting. held here last nizht, speeches were delivered by ten Anarchists, and also by some Social Democrats. The former advocated the destruction by force of the existing state of society, while the German speakers favoured milder methods. The meeting dispersed ate late hour, but the proceedings passed off quietly. THE NEW AMERICAN MINISTRY.

NBA- Yong, THURSDAY:7 rhe World announces to-day from a source which it describes as unqaestionably authentic that the following appointments have been deci +tad upon— Mr. Bayward to be Secretary of State; Mr. Manning, Sec- retary of the Treasury ; Mr. Lomar, Secretary of the Interior ; Mr. Vilas, Postmaster-General ; and Mr. Garland, Attorney-General.

div.p: PRESCOL

CONGREGATIONAL BAZA&R.—As will be seen from an ad- vertisement in another column, a bazaar in connection with the Congregational Church will be held in the Assembly- rooms next Monday and Tuesday. • NovEsys.—Mr F Smith, coroner, held an inquest at the King's Arms Hotel, on Friday, on the body of Thomas Prange, pigeon dealer, New Brighton, Prescot, who died on the Thursday afternoon. He bad not been well for some days. but persisted in going to work again after dinner. His daughter took him some tea about four o'clock, but before he could partake of it he fell and died. The jury returned a verdict of "Died from natural causes."—Mr Smith also held an inquest on Tuesday on the body of a child of Anthony Sewell-street, who was choked by a nut on Sunday. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

TEMPERANCII SOCIETY.—The fortnightly meeting of the Church of England Temperance Society was held on Mon- day evening, in the Houghton-street school-room, when the roons was densely crowded. The opening address was given I by Mr J Goldsworth, after which the following programme was most successfully rendered :—Pianoforte duet, " Tan- orede," Misses Harris; song, 'When the tide comes in," Mr Loot; song, "The Sailor Boy," Miss Stead; piano and violin duet, Miss and Master Brandreth ; song, "Tell her I love her so," Mr D Goldsworth ; duet, " Hark the goat bells ringing," Misses Harris; recitation, "Nonplussed," Mr Berry; song, "The old wooden rocker," Mr Lunt ; song, 'London Bridge," Miss Stead; piano and violin duet, "Lee Cloches des Corneville," Miss and Master Brandreth ; song, Yeoman's Wedding Song," Mr D Goldsworth; encore," True to the last ; " song, "Pretty Jemima," Mr IPirry; duet, "I koyt a bank," MisßB Harris. .

It is stated that at least one-half the orders recently given by the Admiralty for new torpedo cruisers will be taken by Clyde firms. Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, who represents the moribund borough of Eye, is to contest a division of Sheffield in the Cooservetive intereat.

Cornertox OF CROFTER9.—Eight crofters residing at Valtos and Übr, in the island of Lewis, were convicted on Saturday at Stornoway Of assaulting and Obstructing a mes- senger-at-arrEs sent into their district to serve writs in December last. Sentences of from 30 to seven days' itn- prisonment were imposed. TR& SUPPOSED MURDER AT CRESTER.-00 Thursday morning, at the Chester City Police Court, before the May r (Mr. C. Brown) and other magistrates, the two women named Lloyd and Davies, who were charged last week with the murder of William Norris. a labourer at the Leadworks, Chester, were again brought up in custody. The adjourned inquest was held on Wednesday, in the magistratete-room, rown Hall, when further evidence was adduced respecting the occurrence, and the jury returned an open verdict. Mr. Fenwick (chief constable) now slated to the bench that all evidence available had been given in the case, and as the jury returned such a verdict he did not propose to offer more evidence against the prisoners. The Bench, after a consultation in the retiring room with the Chief Constable, decided that the case must be again ad- journed until Monday next. KAT% TIC PILLS, a specific in Neuralgia.
