div.head: NOTtS fl ?FIE WAY. .
div.p: NOTtS fl ?FIE WAY. .

On Saturday last the Warrington club were again Suc- cessful, administering a severe drubbing to Eccles. After the close game they played Raccarn a few weeks ago, at Eccles, the Warrington supporters looked forward to an even game, 'The " wirepullers," however, had matters much their mu way. Their success was in a great measure due to their collective play and sharp passing. Ampull are to be met to-day (Saturday), and they will prove to ba a very hard nut to crack, as they have not sustained a single defeat this season.

The match, Scotland v. Ireland, the premier fixture in the Scottish calendar since the withdrawal of the English game, wan played at Belfast on Saturday. Not more than 1,000 people put in an appearance. The Scotchmen, winning the toss, selected to play with the wind, which was blowing from goal to goal. Just half an hour after the start the ball was put into touch out of the loose. Maclagan threw out to Reid, who passed to Jamieson, and the latter got across the line very cleverly. Both teams now agreed as to the impracticability of continuing the match, and they left the ground, no arrangement being made for another meet- ing, and it is not likely to take place this year. On Saturday, at Hampden Park, Glasgow, the Vale of Leven and Renton met in the final tie of the Scottish Cup competition, but the result was a draw,neither side scoring; in the Birmingham Cup competition, the Wednesbury Old Athletic beat Nattingham Rangers at Derby, and Walsall beat St. George's at Small Heath ; In the Wedneabury Charity Cup competition, Aston Unity beat Excelsior; at Cambridge, the University beat Clapham Rovers, United Hospitals beat Upton Park, Westminster School beat Old Foresters ; at Kilmarnock, 3rd Lanark were beaten, Stave- ley beat Lockwood Bros., Bolton Wanderers beat Derby County, Great Lever beat Halliwell; at Burslem, Port Vala beat Small Reath Alliance.

The semi-final ties rn the English Challenge Cup compe- tition were drawn by the Committee of the Football Asso- ciation on Monday night, subjess to the absence of any protest, as follow :—Notts or Queen's Palk V. Notts Forest, Blackburn Rovers v. Old Carthusians. Both matches will have to be played on March 7, but, the plaqe for the former will not be fixed until after the decision of the match between Queen's Park and Notts. That between Old Carthusiane awl Black- burn Rovers is fixed for the Trent Bridge Ground at Not- tingham. The committee ordered the match of Saturday last between Queen's Park and Notts to be played over again at Derby on Saturday next. The final tie will be played at I Kennington Oval.
_GF,NERAI, NEWS.

. _------------,e, --- ----_____ , The di-abled transport Poonah WAS found, unOee sail, I , near Ballycotton on Wednesday, and was towed into Queenstown Harbour. It has been arranged that the debete in the House eft Lords on the Sanctity opening of museums shall take place' on the 20th of next month. The re-election of the Prince of Wales as Grand Master of English Fremasons will take place at the next meeting of the Grand Lodge, on Wednesday, March 4. At a meeting of the Yorkshire coalowners held at Shef- field on Thursday it was decided to take off the 10 per cent advance given to the oollieris in November,-18S2. Princess Louise of Battenberg, granddaughter of the Queen, was safely delivered of a daughter en Wednesday afternoon. The Princess and her child are doing well. Sir Watkin Wynn's pack of hounds whilst crossing the railway near White:lurch, on Wednesday, were overtaken by a passenger train, which killed eight of the valuable animals and injured several others. At a meeting of the shareholders of the Southport and Cheshire Lines Extension Railway en Thursday, sanction was given to a bill being introduced in Parliament to em- power the Company to raise £50,000 for the completion of the line. Txs MEN HANGED.—On Thursday morning the mail steamer Lagos arrived at Liverpool from West Africa. It was reported tbat the British authorities at Cape Coast had just hanged ten natives for riot and murders at Winnebab, on the Gold Coast. A woman named Hanratty was summoned at the Liver- pool Police Court on Wednesday for having exposed a quilt which had been used to cover a typhus-fever patient with- out having it disinfected. The Stipendiary described the case as " horribly disgusting," and fined the defendant 40e and costs. FATAL MINE ACCIDENT.—The Abersoch lead mines, on the Welsh coast, Pwllheli, have bees (boded by a sudden Inrush of water, and tbree of the miners, William Ellis, John Davies, and Owen Davies, are drowned. Operations to recover the bodies have been begun, but the water has risen . BO high that it is feared some weeksmust elapse before they can be reached. SHEEP STEALING IN CHESHIRE.—On Wednesday night some sheep stealers drove a pony cart into a field belonging to Mr. Weed, Lower House Farm, Audlesse, Cheshire. in which some sheep were grazing in a hollow. One of the finest sheep was killed, skinned, and cut up. The mutton was then put in the cart and driven clean away, only the maw being left to show the presence of the party. j THE WIGAN COUNCIL DIFFICULTY.-A majority of the Wigan Town Council on Wednesday again refused to declare vacant a seat which had been resigned by a coun- cillor who was a candidate for the office of Town Clerk. The Council was informed, without effect, that the seat was legally vacant by the act of the councillor; and it is stated that the Liberal party will apply for a maudamus to enforce the law. COMMERCIAL Law.—On Wednesday, the Lord Chan- cellor received a deputation from the Association of Cham- bers ef.Commerce, who urged the appointment of a Royal Commission to ioquire into the expediency of the codifi- cation of the commercial law. Lord Selborse replied that the Government would be willing to consider any well-con- I sidered scheme for dealing with codification in detail, but I not en Woe as proposed. TUX BIRMINGHAM MURDER.—At Birmingham, on Thurs- day, Henry Kimberley, tool maker, 53, was sentenced to death for the murder of Mrs. Palmer, wife of a publican in that town. A woman who had lived with the prisoner for many years but had parted from him was in the bar of de- ceased's house, and in a frenzy of jealousy Koneerley fired i a revolver into the, room, killing airs. Palmer and doing , serious Injury to the other woman. i I EXTRAORDINARY SHIT.—Tne hearing of the Ear. of Durham's i Durham's suit, be praying for nullity of his marriage on I I the ground that at the time the ceeemonv took place his wife was of unsound mind and incapable of centracting a 1 marriage, was commenced on Wednesday in the Probate : ' and Divorce Division, before Sir J. Herman. The respondent is now an inmate of the Barnswood Asylum. Lord Durham gave evidence, and was under cross-exemination when the• Court rose. On Thursday, the evidence of the petitioner as to the alleged insanity of his wife at the time of the marriage was cmoborated by a number of witnesses ; and the hearing was again adjourned. TERRIBLE ACCIDENT AT SHOEBURYNES9 —An appall- ing accident occurred on Thursday afternoon at the School of Gunnery, Shoeburycess. An experimental party, together with some members of the Ordnance Com- mittee of the War Office, were experimenting with sensitive fuses, and whilst they were screwing one of these into the nine-inch shell the latter exploded with disastrous results. Gunner Allen was killed on the spot. Colonel Fox Strang- ways, commandant of the School of Gunnery, bed one foot blown off and his leg shattered. Colonel Lyons, of the Ordnance Committee, had both legs blown off just below the thigh. Captain G. Adams, second experimental officer, had both legs blown off and his face terribly muti- lated, and Warrant Officer Daykin had one leg blown ofe from the thigh. None of these officers are expected to recover. Gunner Underwood had one leg blown off, and another gunner was wounded severely. Mr. Rance, a i civiliau, of Woolwich Arsenal, was severely wounded in the leg, whilst Captain Low and others had narrow escapes. Major O'Sally, who was 300 yards away, was struck by a portion of the shell and rendered insensible; but hie squad book saved his life. The untoward event has created quite a consternation throughout the garrison and village. Huesca OF PROMISE CASE.—A young lady of 34 winters was the plaintiff in an action tried in Dublin for a breach of promise to marry, the defendant being an "old sea-dog," who had arrived at the age of 04. The plaintiff deposed that she was proposed to in due form, and accepted the de- fendant. Her suitor had been thrice previously married, and at the time when the proposal was made the third wife was in existence. The plaintiff agreed, however, with much consideration, to "wait until the old woman died ;" but when that event happened Captain Barlow declined to fulfill his promise, and for this lapse the jury were requested to fine him in the aura of £3OO. The defendant, it appeared, had, displayed a curious pertiality for widows who were "well off," and on each of his three matrimonial ventures the bride had brought him a small fortune. Such was his , fondness for cash that it was broadly hinted that if the jury gave damages against him he would marry the plaintiff 'sooner than pay the amount. Captain Barlow, being heard In his own defence, denied that he had offered marriage. He was "a poor man." Being twitted with the undeniable fact that he had been able to support three wives, he ex- plained that he had not had to keep them "all stone time," and therefore the test as to his means was fallacious. The judge described him as" a mercenary old sea-dog," and hinted that £3OO was more than double his value. The jury Week even a more depreciatory view of the captain's merits, and assessed the damages at £2O only. BANQUET TO THE MARQUIS OF RIPON.--he Marquis of Ripon was on Wednesday night entertained at a banquet in St. James's Hall, London, by the National Liberal Club. The Berl Of Kirriberley presided, and there was a large and brilliant gathering, which included several members of the Cabinet. Lord Hartington responded to the toast of "The Army," and paid a warm tribute of appreciation to the [forces now serving in the Soudan, besides expressing his I Sincere regret for the lose of the gallant officere and men who had met their deaths whilst encountering a brave enemy. His Lordship also referred to the manner in which Lord Ripon had increased the efficiency of the English garrison in India and had conducted the operations in Afghanistan to an honourable close. The Earl of North- brook reponded tor 'The Navy." Earl Cowper proposed e" Her Majesty's Ministers." The toast was acknowledged by the Home Secretary, who defended the Government from the charge sometimes made that they bad no Imperial Sympathies, and that they were incapable of Imperial spirit OT of Imperial ideas. The Earl of Derby responded for "The House ef Lords," and Sir C. Dfike for " The House of Sommone." Letters were read from Mr. Gladstone and Lord Granville apologising for their absence aed "The health of Lord Ripon "was proposed by the Earl of Kim- berley. In responding the Marquis of Ripon, referring to the Afghan question. asserted that if threatening occur- rences should Wile ;anti upon per nerth-western flogger we Should now be in a batter Position in reepect to out relation with Afghanistan than perhaps at any previous period of 1 our history. The toast of " Prosperity to India" was pro. posed by Mr. John Bright. SESERE GALES, Loss OF LIFE, AND DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY.—In Scotland and the North of England on Saturday a severe gale raged, which resulted in direful con- Sequences. In Caithnesashire heavy snowstorms occurred, completely blocking the roads. At Scotscalder, on the High- land Railway, about ten miles south of Thurso, a passenger train raa off the metals and was buried in the snow, and it was not until Sunday noon the passengers were relieved. At Stornoway the gale raged with the fury of a tempest ; and in Orkney conveyances to and from Stromnese to Kirkwall stuck in the snowdrift, and the paeseragers had- to walk a distance of five miles for shelter. Some of the district mails had to be despatched by foot messengers, the vehicles being unable to proceed. The messengers were also storm- stayed, and had to seek the nearest refuge. Telegraphic 1 communication further south was broken down, and mes- sages between Edinburgh and Aberdeen bad to be conveyed by Inverness. A train from Inverness, which left at seven on Saturday night for Perth, was thrown off the rails near Dalwhinnie and the line was blocked for several hours. In Greenock considerable damage Was done to property. At Liverpool the gale sprung from time S S E. about mid-day on Saturday, and continued for nearly 24 hours. The flat Governor, coal laden from Gar ston, was sunk in the river abreast of the Albert Pierhead, on Sunday morning. The master, Jackson, and his crew of one hand narrowly escaped in their punt. The schooner Rosendale, of 13 mow, from Ches- ter, was driven on Holyhead breakwater and is expected to be- come a total wreck. Her crew were saved. The brigantine Camelia' of Cork, on Saturday was driven into Tramore Bay arid endeavoured to cast anchor under Drometorm Head, but her masts were carried away and she drifted towards the land. The Tramore lifeboat went out and made several attempts to rescue the crew, but was unable to reach her. The vessel drifted ashore and became a total wreck. The crew, nine in number, were loet. The Mirame, of London, from Philadelphia, arrived at Londonderry on Sunday with grain, after encountering a terrible storm in the Atlantic. Three boats were carried away and AS many sailors in- jured.—On Sunday night the barque Venus B. went ashore at Ballymacan, near Waterford, and became a total wreck. By the disaster, therefore, twelve lives will have been lost. Two of the hands were engaged in Liverpool—one of them, a boy named Frederick Wiley, beloeging to Liverpool, the other being a native of Deland. named Jeremiah Fitz- patrick. A GOLBOHNE GENTLEMAN AND EDS BEITCEIER'S BILL.— At a sitting of the Warrington County Court, held on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, Henry Hib- bert, butcher, of Newton, sued Mr. John Breads, of Gol- borne, to recover the sum of £3 Is Id for meat supplied. The son of the defendant appeared and admitted the claim with the iNception of an item of ZI 4s lid, which he said was for meat that bad not been ordered or supplied. Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for plaintiff, and stated the circumstances of the case. The defendant pro- duced an order book in which all orders were entered to prevent servants or others obtaining goods without being authorised to do so, and there was no entry showing that the meat in respect to which the item objected to referred had been ordered. Plaintiff, in reply, said that on some occasions be bad received verbal orders, Ilooctur, giving judgment, said that the precaution of giving written orders—which was a wise one—appeared from the book I handed in to have been for at least twelve months a custom in the house of the defendant. Judgment would be for the plaintiff, less the sum of de lid objected to by the de- fendant. Sr. Taciefes's T&SinItATICE. SOCIETY.—An interesting lecture on the temperance question was given in the Church School-room' Golborne, on Monday night, by Mr R A Naylor, of Cuerden Hall, near Wirrington. There was at good attendance, mad the Rev C 17 Quirk, M A (rector), took the chair, and spoke of the work of the Golborne Branch of the Church of England TgeremapteraasnsicsetaSooocolettybeiyn htabdat dpeartii:edh, lor's stamp, who tad travelled a af rnodm agceknorol ewrol eedogoe df itithre:s. number of miles to address their meetings. The lecturer dis subject in an interesting manner. He con- treaaeltt withedth h the Views working men held 50 years ago respecting the sustaining qualities of strong drink, and showed that it bad now ewes proved that colliers, farm labourer.% and others employed in daily toil could work better and foci fresher 1 without intoxicants than with them. He referred to Insur- ance Companies' statistics, which proved that teetotallers lived longer than moderators, and as a consequence their lives were accepted by Insurance Companies at less pre- miums. His own belief was that there was not a single • person in his audience but what would be better without drink even in a limited quantity, and the reason drink was taken at all was that people liked it He was glad to have seen the groat change on this question even in the Church itself, for 20 years ago people were looked down upon if they advocated teetotalism. He urged his audience to be- come abstainers themselves and to do all in their power to reclaim others. The address was listened to with great attention, and at its close Mr Naylor received a hearty vote I of thanks.

however large, would not have been be- grudged by the nation—but to the lives that Would have been needlessly but inevitably lost by employing English troops in a tropi- cal climate during the hot season. It is bad enough to see our brave soldiers and Generals cut down in fair fighting with semi- savages; but it would be worse to know that we were sending a large number of them to certain death by engaging them in an unequal struggle with a destructive Climate. If we are on the eve, whilst within striking distance of Khartoum, of suspending oPerations because of the approaching heat, What madness would it have been to despatch an expedition during the hot season of last Year! But, it may be urged, why not have done last year what it is proposed to do 4°4w—send troops to the Nile by a railway 1° be laid between Suakim and Berber? The 4nanswerable reply which Mr. GLADSTONE zsakes to this question is that the prepon- derence of military and engineering opinion Was against such a course. Further, it was r4cnight to he possible by taking the Nile route to effect the rescue of GORDON without 4luch bloodshed; and it is at least satisfac- tory to remember, in this almost wholly un- satisfactory business, that three-fourths of the journey to Khartoum was accomplished 414thout fighting. It would have been other- tvi'2, if an attempt had been made to lay a railway to Berber. , usual to have two curates to assist the Rector, and it is stated that Mr. MONTGOMERY is the 67th or 68th curate who has been engaged since the Rev.W. QUEKETT came to Warring- ton. The statement seems incredible, and it is obviously difficult to keep count; but we are as- sured that the number is not over-stated. Can it be that all, or that even most of the 67 have been at fault? Or is not more probable that there is something radically wrong in the treatment to which they are subjected? The Rector is over eighty, and he is too weak and ill to grapple with the work of a large parish. He has had his day, and has had his pay— ,6oo a year is no small sum—and what his best friends should urge upon him is the necessity of resigning. He is surely entitled to something of rest in the years that remain to him, while he will also be entitled to a re- tiring allowance which his 67 curates would regard, if granted to any of them, as a princely revenue. We know some will urge that it is out of place for us to make these suggestions; but the affairs of a Church which is a branch of the State are everybody's affairs. So long as we are called on to legis- late for the Church, and regulate its doings and misdoings, so long is it the duty of every citizen to see that Church scandals, which scandalise him, too, are reduced to a minimum. After the retirement of so many curate, we do not therefore hesitate to put the question—Would it not be best for the Church, and forall concerned, that the Rector should retire?

DISESTABLISBDIENr.—Mr. Peddie's Bill for the disestab- lishment of thr., Church of Scotland, which will-shortly be Issued, stands for second reading on Wednesday, the gt of May.—With regard to the motion respecting the Estab- lished Church in England, of which Mr. Richard gave notice last session, it is stated that it has been decided to bring it forward in the next instead of the present Parliament, it being supposed that the supporters of this motion will be considerably increased at the general election.—Mr. Dittwyn will bring forward a motion in favour a disestablishment ha Wales this session.

SIR R. 4, CROSS- ON EUUCATION.—On Saturday, Sir R. A. GfrlE,As, M.P., distributed prizes to the students of the tirbeck Literary and Sc:entific Institution, London. Ad. dressing the students, he said he knew nothing worse than a desultory education. The more young men applied them- solves to subjects outside their business in their idle hours the better men of business and the better citizens they would make daring the rest of their lives. Knowledge was a mighty engine and a weapon of enormous power; but it should b 3 remembered that it might be used for evil as well as for good, and that upon those who possessed it rested a heavy responsibility. (Cheers.) RAILWAY COLLISION AT WIDNES.—About nine o'clock on Friday night last week a collision occurred on the London and lsiorth-Western Railway at Widnes. A train of empty wagons from Garston to Wigan was crossing the points at the junction of the St. Helens line,when the latter portion of the train was ran into by a mineral train travel- ling from Warrington into Widnes station. The break van and several wagons were thrown violently frt,rn the metals, and dragged about a hundred yards. George Gear, guard of the St. Helens train, was slightly injured, and he was medically attended and taken home at once. Several wagons were completely wrecked, and the line was blocked for about two hours.

Remaly RATES —A correspondent states that at present, under the six miles " minimum" of 2d per mile, railway companies cannot charge mere than Is per ton for the whole distance of six miles; but they can charge that Is, or any proportion of it, for e'en a single mile of the six. By their bills they ask power, whilst reducing the nominal rate of 111 per mile, to extend the " mini- mum" to 20 miles. The effect of this would be that, while for 20 miles they could not charge more than 28 lid per ton, they could not charge the full 28 lid for any portion—even for a single mile—of the 20. Again, if they were allowed to have terminal charges legalised, they would add, probably, not less than another is per ton to the is lid.

RUNCORN COFFEE taID COCOA HOUSE CO., LIMITED.— The seventh ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of this company was held in the company's roomstligh-street, on Monday, Mr J 0 Jackson presiding. There were also present Messrs I Simpson, T Norman, P Speakman, T Handley, S C Beckett, R Norman, J Higgins, and B nive- ton (secretary). The secretary read the directors' report, which stated that consequent upon the extreme and general depression in trade the receipts were slightly below those of the previous year, but owing to the c ireful management the profits realised were considerably above last year. The nett profits amounted to £lO9 131 id, which it was proposed to deal with as follows :—£4 per cent, on paid up capital, £5B 17e 2d; write off balance of preliminary expense account, £47 65 7d; balance cirried forward, £3 9s 4d; total, £lO9 13s id—The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, remarked that he thought as business improved in the surrounding trades the trade of the company would be enlarged, and especially if that undertaking the Ship Canal were carried out. He mentioned with regret that their manager, Mr Moore, who with the aid di his wife had brought the company through its difficulties during the past seven years, was about to leave them at a time when their prospects were brightening. He had always been most civil mad obliging, and he retired with their best wish for his future welfare. (Applause.)—Mr. Norman ascended the motion, which was carried.—Mr P Speakman moved that a dividend as proposed should be paid, observing that from present appearances it looked as though in another year the dividend would be doubled. (Applause.)—Mr Handley seconded the proposition, whick was carried.-1r J Simpson and Mr T Norman wera re-elected directors. RUNCORN, WESTON, AN) HALTON WATERWORKS CON- PONY—The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of this company was held at the Runcorn Public Hall on Monday. Mr J Brundrit, J P; presided, and there were present Messrs T Bankes, J Simpson, W Whittaker, W Hayes, E Timmins, T Norman,J 0 Jackson, James Shaw, James Collier, and W F Salkelcl (secretary). The report of the directors read as follows :—" The revenue account shows a balance of £579 13s 7d, including £8 18s 81 brought from the previous half. year, out of which the directors recommend a dividend to be declared of four pounds per centum per annum, free from income tax, payable on and after the first day of March, this will absorb £572 15s 9d, leaving a balance of £6 17s 10d to he carried forward. The directors are happy to state that although the last summer was an exceptionally dry one, there was no diminution in the supply of water in the well, which still remains of the usual excellent quality. The advisability of erecting a reserve tank at the Pumping Station was abundantly proved during the time the reservoir was run ofY far repairs, as the supply over the whole district was kept up without any difficulty whatever. The ma- chinery and plant are all in good working order."—The Chairman moved tha adoption of the report and statement of accounts, and referred with satisfaction to the abundant supply of water during the dry weather, and the mainten- ance of its excellent quality. He pointed out that there- pairs to the reservoirs had been effectively carried out at a comparatively small cost, and said during the half-year a great saving had been effected in wages, fuel, etc. During the corresponding period last year the amount paid under that head was £790 185 11d, whilst this half-year the amount had been reduced to £692 2s, notwithstanding the fact that they had had to pay 3d per tan more for fuel. There had also been a decrease in the amount paid in in- terest on debenture and preference stock, caused by them having called up fresh capital to pay off the debentures which were at a higher rate of interest than they now paid. The repairs to the roof of the engine house he expected would save them from £l5 to £2O per annum, and the direc,ore hoped shortly to make a further reduction in their expenses. k Hear, Lear. )—Mr Bankes seconded the motion, which was carried.—On the motion of Mr Norman, seconded by 31r Shaw, the directors were thanked for their services, and a similar zompliment was paid to the secretary on the motiod of Mr Collier, seconded by Mr Jackson, and sup- ported by the Chairptan.—Mr Saikeld replied, and the meet, ing concluded. Watchmakers desiring to buy %Vetches advantageously send address for wheleeele prices to Byx 4, Post Othce, Blackbure.—A def.

MILTON LITERARY AND FRATERNAL SOCIETY.— Mr. R. Wilkinson delivered a lecture on geology to the mem- bers of this class on Tuesday evening, and he was heartily thanked. WIDNES IMPROVEMENT CLASS ASTI) GYMNASIUM.—Mr. A. Hankineon, of Runcorn, on Wednesday evening read an essay on " Thackeray " to the members of the above association. An inter...sting discussion took place, and the essayist was cordially thanked. BETHEsDA MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN. —At the weekly meeting on Wednesday, Mr. Akenhead read a paper on " Predestination." Afterwards a discus- sion took place, the Rev. D. Thomas, Messrs G. Lacy, I. Machin, F. Beck, and J. D. Jones speaking. RUNCORN Y.M.O A. HISTORICAL CLAXS. Before the members of this class on Thursday evening. Mr. S. Dun- combs Pink, F.R.H.S., read A highly interesting paper on "The Nile : its sources and its discoverers." Mr. S. Coventry presided, and the lecturer was accorded a rote of thanks on the motion of Mr. H. Fitton, seconded by Mr. 8. H. DAW9OII. WESLEYAN CfraPw., KINGSL:Y.—On Monday last, a ser- vice of sacred song entitled "Jessica's Fick Prayer." was given in the above chapel by the members of the Camden choir, Runcorn. The oonnective readings were rendered by the chairman, Mr. H. Randle. The programme was brought to a close by a vote of thanks being moved by Mr. J. Nor- cross, of Kingsley, and seconded by Mr. H. Faulkner. LECTURE AT RUNCORN.—To a good audience in Elles- mere-street Free Church, on Tusday evening, the Rev. .7. BiLtington, of Birkenhead, lectured on "Work and wages," his method of dealing with the subject frequently eliciting the applause of the assembly. Mr. J. Stubbs occupied the chair. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded the 'lecturer on the motion of Mr. Gandy, seconded by Mr. Timperley, and supported by the Rev. W. Vause. Mmairx.Missioxs TO SEAMEN Al RUNCORN.—Last even- ing there was brought to a conclusion a most successful six days' mission services organised by Mr Shaw, missionary to the Mersey seamen. The services commenced on Sunday evening, when Mr S Harvey, of Kingetey, delivered an ad- dress to a good congregation of boatpeopls. On Monday evening the Rev E J Robinson conducted the services, and on the following evenings the Revs E Williams, J D Thomas, T M Armson, and W Vause took a prominent part. On Thursday evening 70 boat people were given a free tea, and last Friday evening the seamen of the vessels in the dock were treated in a similar manner. ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT AT WIDNES. Before Mr T Sutton Timmis, at Widnea Police Court on Thursday, Wil- liam Hunt was charged with having, in April of last year, embezzled certain sums of money, amounting to about £8 12a from Messrs G-askell, Deacon, and Co. Mr W T Hus- band prosecuted, and Me J W Knowles defended. It ap- peared that the prisoner had been employed by the firm as a weigher, and it was part of his duty to pay certain wages. A few months ago, learning that an investigation of his books was to be made, he absconded, and it was then disc. vered that he had appropriated certain sums which he had obtained from the cashier by representing they were to pay men wages when the men were not at work. A warrant was obtained, and on Wednesday he was apprehended be' P.C. Murray in Liverpool.—The prisoner was remanded in custody until Wednesday. WIDNES Loner, BOARD ELECTION.—The rural ratepayers' associations are now marshalling their forces for the Lodal Raard election which takes place at the end of March, and a most exciting contest is expected. The retiring members ze Messrs J Midwood, D Wright, R Webster, E Manley, and j E Johnson, who were elected three years ago, as the notplase2, of the Owners' and Occupiers Association, the turmoil attend:2cr that election being very great. Since then Mr Wright tag elle over to the opposition and is now a member Of the Property L',,,-;:ers' and Ratepayers' Associa- ""• which Is lAmiliarly known a.;' the "Manufacturers' "" a T-bnson does nci: seek re- Association," ana at, e tdecidedenci to o election. The Property Owners as their candidates Messrs D Wright, B W T—,llurse" band, F Heyes, and John Taylor, whilst their rivals a bringing forward Messrs J Midwood, E Martley, R Webster ' (retiring members), J WHargreaves, and T Sadler. Mr McQuinn, who sought unsuccessfully to gain a seat at the , last election, may, it is thought, again offer himself as an independent candidate. BURNING FATALITY AT WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband, I the deputy coroner, on Wet!•uesday morning held an inquest 94.° .r.'crapes Hotel, on the body of Elizsbeth Jane Dia- moud, aged one year and eight monthe, the 3 daughter of I James Diamond, labourer, of 107, Midwood-street, Widnes. It appeared that on the afternoon 6 f Friday, the 30',h Jan., Mrs Diamond was engaged in washing, and placed the child on the rug in front of the fire in the kitchen whilst she went into the yard to empty a bucket of dirty water. When she returned she found the child's dress on fire, and lifting

the child up, she took her to the water tap and ex- tinguished the flames. Dr. McCambridge was called in, but the child was severely burnt about the abdomen, and suc- Cumbed to her injuries on Saturday afternoon last.—Evi- dea 2e was given by the mother, Mrs Mary Harvey, of Travis- row, and Mrs Rosanna Cane, of 50, Orford-street.--Mr. Thomas Sadler, a juryman, pointed out that placing a person suffering from burns under water rather added to the injury than otherwise. The proper way to extinguish flames oa any person was to wrap a blanket, or carpet, or some such article about the fire.—The Coroner remarked that in one month he had held no less than eight inquests on persons who had died from either burning or scalding.—A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned... .

„. -- CONCERT AT WIDNES.--A vocal and instrumental concert in aid•of the Widnes Sip Works Brass Bind was given in Widnes Volunteer Hall on Tuesday evening, under the patronaie of the local manufacturers and other gentlemen. The building was well filled by an appreciative audience, the concert in all reepects being a thorough success, owing in a great measure to the labours of the secretaries, Messrs John atvies and a Hufton. Under the leadership of Mr

W Jennett, the baud performed several selections of music in capital style, and the Cambrian Vcal Colon, conducted by Mr 1.) 0 Parry, of Birkenhead, rendered several choruses in a manner which elicited the hearty applause of the corn. pauy. Madame Graefe, of Eisteddfod fame, cmatributed " The Quaker's daughter," " Beloved again," and " Child- ren's home," and she scored an unmistakable success, being once heartily recalled. S'ae was also associated with Mr liumphrevs in the duet, " We come from the home of the *lee." Miss Kate Meredith sang " The little match girl " it an artistic and pleasing fashion, and she was encored. She also gave "Sunshine and rain," and in conjunction with the Vocal Union "Jerusalem." By desire. Mr Humphreys

sang" My blodwen," which be gs.ve in his usual finished manner. Ha was very successful in tha song' Thou art so near and yet so far." Mr Josef Cantor proved as great a favourite as ever, securing an encore for each e his efforts. The cornet solo, "Whirlwind polka." was listerrrd to with appreciative interest.—Miss M E Evans accom- panied in an accomplished Anner, and favoured the audi- . .

ence with a pianoforte solo. Ii WIDNES AND THE RAILWAY RATES BILL. —A. epec.al meeting of Widnes LOCat Board was held on Thersday to i consider the Railway Rases Bill. Mr E Carey presided, , and there were present—Dr O'ffeeffe, Mews J Midwood, T Handley, J Midwood, S Sadler, H Gaskell, junr, E Martley, R Webster, and J T Allen.(clerk.)—lt was decided, on the I proposition of the Chaieman, seconded by Mr H Gaekell, innr, that the Board petition against the bill, and that the following extract from the petition adopted ,by the Liver- peel Chamber of Commerce on Wednesday, should be in- serted in the memorial :—Upon a careful review of the bills referred to, the petitioners bdieved that their general effect would be to largely increase the ratans for the car- riage of all classes of goods, to the great hurt and restric- tion of the trade of thie,country. They were,unanhnously of opinion that the time had arrived when legislation as to railway administration and charges was urgently needed, and that a measure of such national importance coed be bestedealt with by a bill to be introduced at an early date by her Majesty's Government. The petitioners prayed that the House would not allow the apparently favourable as- pect of the bills to secure assent to them; but that, in view of the danger and restriction to trade that the increased and novel charges proposed would lead to, the House would not hesitate to forbid that the bill should become law.—On the motion of Mr Gaeltell, seconded by Mr Sadler, it was re- solved to forward copies of the memorial to the members of South-west Lancashire and to the President of the Board of Trade.—ln the House of Commons, on Thursday evening. Sir R A Cross presented a petition against the bill from the Widnes Traders' Association. WESLEYAN MUSICAL FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN.—A large audience assembled in Runcorn Public Hall on Monday evening, on the occasion of the annual musical festival of the Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School. The chorus, num- bering about 300 voices, was composed principally or children, and ()copied a gallery which had been erected upon the considerably enlarged platform. Mr T Simister, one of the superintendents of the school, presided over the proceedings, Mr John Simpson, the senior superintendent, occupying a seat by his aide. Previous to the commence- ment of a long and attractive programme of sacred musical excerpts, the Chairman delivered a short address, in which he referred to the fact that Brunswick -Sunday School had been in existence 80 years. There was, he said, every reason to believe that the echool was to-day as full of health and vigour as ever it was, and the audience tnat night was an evidence that the work that was being carried on was ap- preciated. (Hear, hear.) Handel's classical chorus, "Lift up your heads," was the Brat effort of the scholars, and, guided by the baton of Mr T Sitnkin, the conductor, was rendered its a meaner worthy of all praise. They were also highly successful in their render- ing of the other concerted pieces, the audience showing their appreciation unmistaka'ely. Miss Horton Bang Fawcett' "Bright blissful state" with much sweet- ness and expression, and later, in conjunction with Miss Sinakin, scored a richly deserved recall in the duet "Oh, lovely peace" (Handel), the voices of the vocalists har- monising admirably.—The duet "Low at Thy feet" was tastefully sung by Mrs Burrows and Mrs R Mcore, and the duet" the shall feed His flock" was successfully interpreted by Miss Jones and Mrs Hackett, who were loudly applauded. Mrs Hackett also sang the song " Heaven and Earth " (Pinsuti) withlaseefel appreciation of the beauties of the composition. Mr Id Morris gave an intelligent and pleasing rendering of "King David's lament," whilst Mr. J LI Har- rison contributed Gousod's song "Nazareth" in expressive style, and the hearty plaudits of the assemblage were well deserved. During the eveling Miss Yates recited "A city tale." and Miss C Littler The fireman's wedding very effectively. The capital manner in which Miss Littler realised the dramatic force of the piece was recognised by an enthusiastic encore. The festival concluded with a suc- cessful rendering of the Hallelujah chorus." Great praise is due to Miss Jukes (pianaforte) and Miss R Jukes (har- monium) for the eTcient manner Ito which they accom- panied, and Mr Simian is to bs congratulated on the entire success of the festival.

' num BY A SPY AN Rusconx.—Before Mr John Brun- drit, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, Thomts Abrams, 10 Tears of age, WAS charged with stealing a battle of 'Addeo and a pound of rice, the praperty of Richard Abel, of Duke's Field.—The prisoner was remanded until Monday.

SITTFOSED La.'s OF A RUNCORN VESSEL AND ALL HANDS. —lt is greaTly feared that the schooner Brodick Castle, of Rummel, has been wrecked and all hands lost during the recent gales. Early in the present week a name board bear- ing the letters "Brodick Gas" has been picked up near Milford, and another piece of wood with the letters " Corn" has been also found. Mr Peter Sinnott, managing owner of the vesselphits gone to Cardiff to make inquiries. His son, Mr John Sinnott, was the captain of the Brodick Castle. LECTUNE ote Da. Joansos.—ln connection with the Hal- ton Mutuallmprovement Society, the Rev S Mees, the pre- sident, delivered a very able lecture on Tuesday evening, in the Trinity Wesleyan Schoolroom, the subject being" Dr Johnson!' Mr John El GAMOG occupied the thair. Oa Wednesday evening the rev. gentlem in delivered the situ° lecture before a large assembly at Weston Wesleyan School. The chair WM occupied by Mr G S Hazlehntst, of Rnyl. A hearty vote of thanks wts accorded to the lecturer on the motion of Mr I W Kirkham, seconded by Mr James Ball. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A WIDNES GENTLEMAN —Tele- grams have been received in Widnes, stating that Mr I Har- greaves, secretary to Messrs Elargretves and Robinson, of Ditton Chambers, Ditton-road, has been seriously iniared in France, but there are no tidings as to when and hew. He left Widnes on Tuesday night for the south of France, and it is surmised that he has been injured on a French railway. His wife and brother, Mr. John Hargreaves, have left the town to go to him. We understand that Mr. R. Davies was travelling with the injured gentleman. THEFT OF PIGEONS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Robert Gaul, a boy, WAS brought up on remand charged with stealing two pigeons, the property of Thomas McManus, 14 years of age, of 2, Walmsley-street. On the 18th inst. McManus discovered that his cote had been broken into, and two pigeons worth 24 f3d taken away. Subsequently P.C. Pitt found them at the house of the pri- soner's father in Midwood-street, and the prisoner admitted having stolen them.—He was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch-rod. ILLEGALLY PAWNING AT WlDNES.—Esther Beesley, a middle-aged w0c0a..4 was summoned by William Smith, of 4,:Timperley-street, for unlawfully pawning a dress, value 2s.—Mr. J. W. Knowles defended.—lt appeared that the defendant was sister-in-law to the complainant, and for a few days the daughter of the complainant, aged 17 years, had been living with her aunt. Whilst the girl was stay- ing there the defendant pawned the dress at Mr. Neil's. It was contended that the girl had authorised the pawning of the dress in order that her aunt might pay the rent, but this was denied.—The Magistrates ordered the defendant to return the dress and pay a fine of Is and costs, es di, CRUELTY TO A PONY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Eiamblett Gill, a hawker, of War- rington, was charged with cruelly illtreating a pony by allowing it to be worked whilst in lan unfit state. Jams Lee was summoned for working the animal.—lt appeared that on Friday, the Bth jest, Inspector Greenwell, of the R.S.P.C.A., met Lee driving the pony, which was attached to a cart laden with salt and whiting, along Hale-road, Ditton. It was extremely lame on the near forelimb, and when at rest stood on three legs. The animal was examined by Mr. Robinson, veterinary surgeon, who diszovered that it was suffering severely from an old prick in the hoof. It was totally unfit for work.—Gill was fined 5s and costs. Lee was dismissed.

THEFT AT RUNCORN".-- kt Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday Patrick Morgan, a labourer, was charged with steal- ing a pair of boote, value els 01, the property of William Croley, shoemaker, High-street. About one o'clock on Saturday afternoon Mrs Sarah Price, of Halton, was near Mr. Croley's shop, when she saw the prisoner take a pair ,;f boots (produced) from a book at the door. At that time a nissing and the prisoner remarked to him " This - replied " Thr
ley are,
is a nice pair of boots." The nu.-- . and walked on. The prisoner then placed the his arms and went towards Church-street. She inforaked Mr Mutch of what had occurred, and he went in pursuit and

captured the prisoner, who was subsequently given into the custody of P.C. Bason.—The prisoner pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour. THE 80:1A•11DE TRAVELLER Qrto T Rutircortx.— At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Messrs W. Bankes and James Handley, William Tinsley and Geo. Walton, young men, were charged with having on Sunday, the 15th Februry, unlawfully obtained intoxicating liquors from Henry Jackson, landlord of Wilson's Hotel, during prohibted hours by falsely representing themselves to be . .
, travellers. Between three and four o'clock en the afternoon

of the day in rptestion the defendants went to Wilson's Hotel, where they represented themselves to Hr. Jacksm's eldest son as travellers from Northwich. He produced a book in which they signed themselves as William Sutton and George Egerton, of Northwich. Upon this represents- tation they were each served with two glasses of beer, and
it was afttrwards disc)vered that both defendants lived at
Weston.--Superintendent Leah said Tinsley was appre• headed the same evening for being drunk and disorderly and had been fined.—Each _defendant pleaded guilty and _ _ _ _
was Ened lOs and costs, 93 ed. - - LARGE ARREARS OF RATES AT WIDNES. Mr. J. W. Carlile, builder and contractor, was summoned to appear at Widnes Petty SkAsions on Wednesday. for nou-payrnent of

rates. lie did not appear and P.C. Pitt proved the service of the sunimons,—Mr. Whitfteld, rate c,dlector to the Local Board, said the defendant owed. £l. 24 41 for gas, £5B Os 71 for water, and £233 us 91 on account of general district . _ _ _ . .
rate, total £2:32 143 81. Ile had made repealed application
, for the rates but he bad been unable to obtain therm. Mr.
Carlile had had some negotiations with the Board on the muter—Mr. Fletcher : Why wont he pay ?—Witness : I conk say. He added that he was instructed to ask for
an order for. immediate payment.—The Clerk: How is ...it
the amount is so large?—Witness: Re owns about 404 houses in Widnes.—The Bench made an order for payment

in seven days.—Mr. Goff, assistant overseer, also Elpp- eared to ask for an order to be made upon Mr. Cirlile for the pay- ment of the oors rate amounting to £755 Ss 6d. The de- fenlant had made repeated promiges to pay, but had not itene so up to the present.—The Bench made an order for
payment in seven days. THE ROBBERY FEOM A JEWELLER'S SKOP AT RUIWORN. —Francis Kelly, Annie Price, EliZ4 Nash, Fanny J.ennion, and Margaret tirambl !, were charged at Runcorn Police

Court, on Monday, with stealing 2-4 silver finger rings, 12 silver scarf rings, and a silver glove stud, value ..C4 7e, the property of Mr James Button, jeweller, Church-street, Run- corn.—Saperintendent Leah remarked that Kelly was the man whom tke prisoner Price said gave her two rings, but her statement had ;seen found to be untrue, and he asked that Kelly should be ,discharged.—The Benno at once dis- charged Kelly, Wilk, asked that he might be recompensed for the anxiety and suspense be had suffered through his im- prisonment.—Evidence was given by Mrs Sutton as to the disappearance of the rings, and P.S. McMichael proved find- ing a portion of the stolen preperty in possession of Bram- ble, Nash, and roice.—Superintendent Leach read a corres- pondence which had passed between Janoion, who was supplying the prisoners with food, and Price, the letters being secreted underneath a basin. " Dear Annie" was ad- vised to " stick " to what she said at •-first, and " Dear Fanny" was asked to tell Eliza Nash" to mind what she says."—On Ws evidence the prisoners were remanded until

Monday next. ALLEGED EfldGillNG AT CRONTON.—Thomas Ellaby, tool- maker, of Cronton, appeared before the Widnes magistrates, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of being in possession of a net used for the purpose of taking and killing game.— P.C. Durkin stated that about twenty minutes past one on Sunday morning, the 15th just, he met the defendant in Chapeblaxe,'Cronton. He discovered that he was carrymg a net, which was wet, as though it had been recently used. He took charge of the net, and said he should have to re- port the matter. The defendant said, "Don't do that. lam only a porr man, and I shall have to go to gaol." The de- fendant appeared to come from the land of Job Glover, at Cronton. The net was 96 yards long and four feet deep.— Mr Knowles, for the defence, -stated that the defendant w a ateohsto make a hen-pen, and on the night in question he, in company with a man named Critchley, went to several places ic order to obtain a net. About midnight they ar- rived at the house of Thomas Roberts, who produced a net he had had for some years, and told the defendant he could use as much as he wanted. They did not leave this house until one o'clock, and on the way home the constable met the defendant. The net was damp because it had fallen into a dish of water.—John Critchley corroborated this state- ment.—ln reply to Inspector Wood, he denied that he had boasted of catching with other persons 286 head of game since Christsnas.—Thornas Roberts, labourer, who had been a gamekeeper for 13 years, also gave evidence. He stated the net was his. He also denied boasting of the head of game he had obtained since Christmas.-- The .13-2nch dis- missed the case, but Mr Fletcher said there was great sus- picion against the defendant. A WIDNES CASE AT Sr. HELENS.-4 special sitting of the Sc. Helens County Court was held on Mosley, when, before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge, and a jary, the action by Wm. Grace, farmer, Upton Rocks Farm, Fainworth, for the recovery of £2O 5s from Samuel John Francis, greengrocer, Widnes, was resumed The case was opened at the ordin- ary sitting of the court on Wednesday week, but the plain- tiff had only just given his evidence when the court rose. At the resumption on Tuesday, Mr. W. T. Husband again appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendant was repre- sented by Mr. J. 0. Swift. The plaintiff alleged that the sum of £2O 5s is the balance due for cabbages sold, the price agreed upon for a field of which was £4O. The de- fendant had a counter claim of £33 Ps 61 for breach of con- , tract. Some time last year the defendant agreed to par- chase a field of cabbages from the plaintiff for the sum of £lO, and in various instalments the sum of £l9 Iss was paid, leaving the balance, to recover which the action was brought. Ties defence was that the plaintiff had failed to comply with the • terms of the bargain, namely, that he should menu e the field if it was found that the cabbages were not growing in a proper crop. The plaintiff promised to ace that the cabbages were grown te a marketable condition, but this, Mr Swift contended, he had failed to do, although his attention was called to it. If this was net done then the bargain had to ha considered at an end. The defendant kept an account of the cabbages he took and had paid a sum amply sufficient to cover their cost. The cabbages he had left in the field were absolutely worthless, and the defendant had entered the counter claim in respect of the loss he had sustained by Grace notsarry- ing out his part of the bargain. Several witnesses were called on behalf of both parties' and his Honour ultimately gave a verdict for the plaintiff for £l9 15s.

• THE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT RIINCORM.—The physicist , condition of Mr James Craig, who a fortnight ago attempted to commit suicide by cutting his throat, is considerably , improved, but on the advice of the medical attendant it has been decided to remove him to a place where he can receive proper attention. Itounmay AT WlDNES.—Michael Kelly was charged at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, with stealing a mug, value is 31, the property of William Caldicut, a labourer, living in Elizabeth-street. The prisoner and hic wife live apart, the latter zaining a livelihood by hawking. On Sat- urday she sold Mrs Caldicuta mug, which the prisoner a few days afterwards fo-cils'y took possess;on of and carried away from the house. The prisoner was apprehendeo P.O Davis, and was now remanded until Monday. SHOCKING ACCIDENT KO A HORSE AT RUNCORN.—Yester- day afternoon a dreadful accident occurred to a horse be- longing to Mr. John Williams, of Top Locks. The animal, to which was attached a cart, was proceeding along Waterloo Bridge, when it became alarmed, and started off at a rapid pace. Upon coming to the corner, the horse being un- managable, ran upon the spiked railings, which pierced its breast to a considerable extent. The occupants of the cart, Master Albert Williams and another youth, narrowly es- Caped being thrown out. The Brae, suffering great agony,: remained upon the spikes until the railings were taken down. Its flesh was fearfully lacerated, and even it it re- covers it will be permanently injured. The animal was a valuable one.

THE Honsit OF COMUONS AND THE SWF CANAL, &C, —ln the House of Commons, on Tuesday, in reply to Mr. Jacob Bright, Sir A. Otway said that in accordance with an arrangement the Manchester Ship Canal Bill had been re- ferred to the House of Lords, and would go first before a Committee of that House. Any proposition for referring the bill to a jaint committee of the two Houses must, there- fore, originate in the House of Lords. The project was no doubt one of great importance not only to Manchester, but to Liverpool and the whole of Lancashire. It bad in 1883 and 1884 been before two Committees of each House, and between £100,030 and £200,000 had been spent. Consider- ing the exceptional character of the scheme, he was of opinion that it ought, in ancordance with precedent, to be referred to a joint Committee. He should be glad to give his co-operation in bringing about an arrangement of that kind.—Runcorn and the Ship Canal Bill.—Teere is con- siderable interest manifested as to the fate of the resolution of tha Board of Commissioners to oppose the Ship Canal Bill. During the week handbills have been circulated argu- ing the question from the Cammissioners' standpoint, and two letters from the Staffardshire Pottery district which have been published have reoaived much attention. It is widely considered that thn poll will be favourable to the Board. The voting papers will be collected to-day, and the result will be made known on Monday afternoon. Yester- day afternoon Mr. Leader Williams, engineer to the Man- chester Ship Canal Scheme, and several members of the Provizional Cutnmittee, and other genremen, vi itel Runcorn and surveyed the proposed course of the canal from the Old Quay Canal along the river side.

Before Mr. A, Fletcher and Mr. W. Bllnkhorn, at Widnes Petty Sessions on Wedneselty, Henry l'ythian, of Ditton, was brought up under a warrant charged with assaulting his wife, Ellen —Mr. Knowles, wilt appeared for the com- plainant, acid if the evidence Nras ettisfac:ory to their worships he should ask to- a judicial separation, as the case was a very serious ass. During the whole of their married life, extending over a period of 30 years, the parties ha t had a miserable existence through the defendant's brutal conduct. He had frequently Mused her, on ono occasion breaking her arrn, for which he suffered three months' im- prisonment. For the past four years he had acted more like am td man than a sane being He was in the habit of go'ng on the spree" for several weeks at a time, and he would then corns home at all hours of the night and turn I the family, even if in bA, into the open air, and leave them to sleep under the hedges or anywhere they could. He had I often threatened to kill the complainant, and it was utterly , impossible for the woman to live with him any longer—her life was in danger. Only a few weeks ago he was com- mencing to kick her when the eldest daughter, aged about twenty - seven years int.lrfered. He knocked the daughter to ths floor, and "laid" into her face with his fists in a most ferocious fashion, black- ing her eyes and otherwise injuring her—in fact almost killing her.-the complainant stated that on the 21st inn the defendant came home at half-past two aed asked for his dinner. The servant girl, Mary Evans, gave him his dinner, and then be commenced to call the complainant very bad names, and ran at her. She just escaped into the lane, and her brother-in-law managed to shelter her in his house from the defendant's fury. Ile threatened to kill her, and she was afraid of her life. She bad not slept in the house for a week. The children were all frightened of him. The family had to keep him —Lucy Phy- thian, the daughter, corroborated. The defend- ant admitted that he had been in gaol thee times for ill•uding his wile.—Jona Phythian, de- fendant's brother, said the defendant was a very pessionate man in drink, which was the cause of all the trouble. When sober he was very quiet. He thoeught the complainant's life in danger. It was not safe for the family to live with him.—Asked by Mr. Lewin if he had anything to say, the defendant said he did not want to leave his wife He pro- mised that ifthe Bench would discharge him he would not taste drink as long as he lived.-111r. Knowles pointed oat that the complainant and her family were able to maintain themselves, and they did not ask for any payment tram the defendant.—After several minutes coffsultation the Bench Sentenced the defendant to 14 days' hard labour, and gran- ted a separation order.—The defendant said he had pur- chased all the things in Me house with £250 that was left him, and he wished to know if he could take the geois.—Mr Lewin.: if you bought the things you are entitle to them.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD. Thc monthly meeting was held on Thursday. Mr T S Tinomis,J.P., presided, and there were present—Revs Father Clarke, Father Finegan Dr O'Keeffe, Messrs Bradshaw, ' Deacon, and Danby (clerk). TEN COST OF WARRINGTON•ROAD SCHOOL—AS di2CIISSIOII took place upon the cost of teaching at Warrington-road School, which was considerably more than at West , Bank and Simms Cross. The gross cost of teaching per I head at Simms Cross for the year ending August 31st' 188.! was Li lie GU, at W.sr. Bank LI. 17s lit-I, and at Warringtou-roa.Z.£2 33 83. An exptenatioi laws now re- quired why the cost should be greater at West Bank than Situin3 Cross.—Dr O'Keeffa, as chairman or the Finance , Committee, explained that West Bank School would not hold the number of children in attendance, and the Boa-d ! had been compelled to engage an additional sultool and em- ploy a head teacher and pupil t-achers, which caused the expense to he greater than lithe children were all taught in one building. With regard to Warrington-road there was a great difference between last year and this year in the salaries paid per head. The amount paid per head last year was ..£l. 9s 21,1, and this year it reached £1 153 51 I. This was a great loss to the school, and whatever it was owing to he could not say, but he hoped the School Man- agetnent Committee would provide a remedy as soon as possible. There were also losses anon the earnings of the scholars. For instance, in 1882 the earnings of the boys' school at Warrington.road were 183 OP per head, and the girls department at the same school 1832 D, as compared with:lBe 7±' at Simms Cross and 183 81d at West Bank. In 1883 the earnings were stiil less, being Ids 811 in the senior bays' deportment at Warringtsn-road, 18s Sd in the girls' department, whilst at Simms Cross the earnings were 1.93 4±l, and at West Bank 20s 411. Triers was a slight improvement in 1884, when the earnings at Warrington-road were :—Boys' department 17s 5.1 d, girls' department 20s ; and at Simm's Cross 21s Bid, and West Bank 21s SD. There was very little to be found wrong with any of the other schools except Warrington. road, and he argued that as their pupil teachers had now only to work 25 hours each week, the schools ought to be as efficient its any in the kingdom.—The Rev Father Fine- gan also explained that the cost of carrying on Warrington- road school was increased by having to epen a new depart- ment and supply a staff of teachers, and also the necessary books. He would not say that this explained everything, but it must be borne in mind that Warrington-road sines it was opened had cost more than the other schools. Toe School Management Committee would be prepared when the proper time arrived to take action which would meet the wishes of the Board and further the education of the district.—The Chairman thought with that explanation they might adopt the report presented last mcnth.—Mr Deacon pointed out that the largest increase in the earnings at the schools this year had been made at Warrington-road, so that although the teachers might not be perfect, still they had improved considerablr within the p ist year. He thought it just to point that out.—The Chairman ; Still there is more TOM for improve. merit in a low standard than a high one.— Mr Deacon referred to the high cost of books, 4.m., per head at Warrington-road School.—Father Finegan said they would always find that a small school would cost more in proportion to a large one. He was far from saying the state of things were satisfactory at Warrington-road, but things were not an bad as they looked at first sight.—Th.s report was adopted. DISTRICT EDUCATION.—The District Education Com- mittee reported that there had been 168 applications for school fees, and they were recommended for payment in

(164 cases. There were 279 persons summoned to appear before the committee, and 44 were convicted before the magistrates.—Mr Deacon, in moving the adoption of the minutes, remarked that the applications for school fees were on the increase,and this would seem to show that there were many persons out of work.—Tne -hairman : Are these strangers or residents.—Mr Deacon said when the Local Board gave employment to stonebreakers, &c., a number of strangers entered the town and were found work.—The Rev Father Carkre remarked that the applicant for fees were mostly labourers earning small wazes.—The minutes wefe passed.

Scwoor. MANAGEMENT CommirrEE.—On the recommenda- tion of this committee Miss Ethel Payne was appointed certificated assistant mistress, senior girls' department, West Bank School, at a salary of £55 per annum; and the resig- nation of Miss Clayden, as teacher of drawing at the cen- tral class of pupil teachers, was accepted. THE EXTENSION or WEST BANK SCHOOL—The Sites and J3uilding Committee recommended that the Board accept, aubject to the approval of the Education Department, the tender of Messrs. Roberts Brothers for the additional accom- modation required at West Bank School, for the sum of £l,lOO. It was also recommended that the senior girls' cloak room at Simm's Cross school should be enlarged, and that the tender of Mr. 'l'. Sailer bs accepool.—The minutes were passed on the motion of the chairman. FINANCE.—The Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £529 191 lid. There had beemeceived during the past month sums amounting to £206 10s 3d. The committee recommended that the Board be empowered to obtain a loan of £1.300 from the Public Works Loan Commissioners for the additional an- coinmodation required at the West Bank School, and the necessary furniture and fittings, repayable by instalment of principal in 50 years, with interest at 41 per cent—The minutes were passed on the motion of Dr. U'Keeffe. THE BOARD AND THE OVERSEERS: MONEY WANTED.— The following letter, addressed to the chairman, from Mr James White, an overseer, was read .—Dear Sir,—The over- seers have received your precept dated January 22nd for £3,000, ohieh you require to be paid into the bank to your credit on or before the 28th February. The overseers have already collected and paid to the School Board £3.500, or 70 in the £. during the year ending 31st March next. If you insist upon the wording of the precept we shall be compelled to levy a special extr.t rate of another V,: in the £ to be collected within one month, and making the School Board rate Is 3d in the £ for the year. This would be almost ruinous to rainy property owners. We consider the wording of the precept sheuld be altered, making the £3,600 "payable from time to time as required by the Board during the year ending the 29,1 i September next." I am requested by the overseers to ask you to be good enough to bring the matter before yours Board, so that the over- seers may know how to act.—The Chairman had replied to the effect that it the precept were acted upon literally, no doubt it would be necessary to levy an ad iitional rate dur- ing the present financial year, but he was sure he correctly , interpreted the wishes of every member of the Boa-d when he said there was no such intention. The course pursued (exc,pt that the date named for payment was ante-dated one month) was exactly same as in previous yeav, and the course taken in nqui,ing plyment in former years would be followed this year.— Dr O'Keeffe was called upon to explain the precept. He said it was made out for the 28th January, because the amount in the bank to the credit of the Board was so small 'that they would have been unable to pay the salaries for March. The speaker pointed out that in former years the precept had been dated the first January, and for the five or six years it had been dated the first of March, so that there was not much difference between the twenty- , eighth February end the first March. There was no inten- tion whatever to hurry the overseers and through them the 1 ratepayers by getting in this money at once. The Finance ' Committee only intended to net the money as they had done for the past five yeam He was sure they wanted to carry on the business of the School Board as carefully and economically as possible, and to live in amity with the overseers and the ratepayers.—The Rev. Father Fine- gan thought the Board ought to make a lefs demand at the commencement of the year.—The Chairman was of opinion the precept ought to be worded differently.— The • • ••••• Friday there would only remaruen " " in be £7 lOs 4.1 to the credit or Loa the hank. They had nothing to depend upon but that precept.—Mr Deacon said the form., of pre- cept had remained unaltered for ten years, and if Mr White understood it last year he did not see why he could not understand it this year. The overseers were Raked to pay the rate in March last year, but they did not pay it in that month, and they said nothing about IL—The letter was then referred to the Finance Committee, and Mr Denby was in- structed to wait upon the overseers and make the necessary arrangements for the payment of the money. AN Menem Law.—At the conclusion of the business the Rev Fa her Finegan referred to the fact that according to the Education Code the Board schools nor de- nominational schools were not paid a grant of over 17s tki per head unless a certain amount of money had been spent ppon the schools during the year. He thought it was within the province of the Board schools to consider this subject and endeavour to prevail upon the Government to pay schools grant according to their earnings. He knew deaominational schools had been fined because they had not spent sufficient upon their schools for the amount at grant earned. It was astonishing that such a law should be in ex- istence under this enlightened Liberal Government.—The Chairman thought the law somewhat unjust, and wanted altering.—The Rev Father Clarke said he had suffered in cane' venal of that law, and he thought it a great hardship. —The Rev Father Finegan said he would bring the subj.ct forward at a future meeting, and the subject dropped. There was no other business of public interest.

A Pcintabes's DISPOTE.—A case as heard before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, at a sitting of the Warrington County Court, held on Thursday, in which Mrs Ann Ker- shaw, formed 7 landlady of the Hop Pole Inn, florsemarket- street, sued the now landlord, James Hill, for the sum of .£3 103, the value of an hydrometer, under the following circumstances, as detailed by Mr. P. Davies, who represen- ted the plaintiff. Seine time ago Mrs Kershaw left the Hop Pole and Wd9 sucoeeded in the businesi by the defendant The goods left in the house were valued by two valners, one appointed by each party to the transaction. The claim made by the plaintiff was for a hydrometer, valued at the sum set down in the claim. After the defendant had taken the Hop Pole be refused to give up the hydrometer, and said that a wasbhandstand he had paid for was broken when be took possession. In reply to this defendant adhered to that statement, but on a clerk in the employ of one of the 1 valuers deposing that the washband stand was broken at the ' time of the valuation, and was valued at its then worth, his Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff.

A WARRINGTON YOUNG MAN'S " LANES" AT Sr. HELENS. —John Ash, a young man, was brought up at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, on a charge of stealing an 'overcoat, value £2, the property of Arthur J Robinson, of Warrington.—PrOsecutor stated that he was a clerk in the employ of the Castle Rebber Company, Warrington, and he lived at 18, Bridge-street, Warrington. At 11-15 on Saturday night he and several others were waiting for the train to Warrington. when the prisoner struck him. They prepared to fight, and he (prosecutor) took off his overcoat and hat. They were separated by Detective Wright, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and when the train was abeut to start he missed his overcoat. The prisoner was spoken to about it, but tie denied that he knew anything about it. The i overcoat was afterwards found in the possession of the prisoner, who was wearing it beneath his own overcoat.—ln reply to Mr J 0 Swift, who defended, prosecutor said be and other young men had been to St. Helens to play a hil- -1 hard match. He (prosecutor) bad nothing to do with any "lathing" that took place at the station.—Detective Wright stated that he saw the prosecutor and prisoner fighting amid 20 persons. He separated therm and prosecutor complained of having missed his overcoat. Witness found that the prisoner WAS wearing it.—The Bench stated that they would give the prisoner the benefit of the doubt in the case, and he would be discharged. berunmEmena Issux —At Warrington County Court, on Thursday, an interpleader issue was heard before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, in which the parties concerned were Thos. and Henry Brett, brothers, and Edward Kellett, of Tib- street, Manchester, who was the execution creditor. Exe- cution was sought in respect to some furniture in the pos- session of Henry Bate, and the circumstances under which the claim was made were detailed by Mr A Browne, who appeared on behalf of Thomas Brett, the claimant.—alr Browne said that his client was a jeweller and watch jobber carrying on business a', 47, Regent-road, Salford. The debtor, Henry Bratt, was his brother. Au action had been instituted in Salford Hundred Court of Record, and judg- ment went against Henry Brett. Execution was issued, and levied at Lymm, where the defendant then lived. The bailiffs of that court took all the furniture in the house, and the debtor in consequence explained his circumstances to his brother;who lent him a certain number of articles that were absolutely his own, and were the articles mentioned in the schedule. Claimant also took a house 'n his own teeme, for his brother, paid the rent, and got a receipt.—Several witnesses were called to prove having been present when Thomas Brett lent his brother the furniture, and attesting as witnesses a document in which the particulars of the loan were set forth.—Mr P Davies, who represented the execu- tion creditor, after reviewing various aspects of the case and criticising the evidence, asked his Honour to discredit the witnesses called by claimant.—His Honour, having ex- amined the document referring to the transaction, said that interpleader actions were such as constantly cropped up, and they were matters of difficulty, because claims of that kind were very easily mode and arrangements were effected between people who were in difficulties, and their friends, in expectation that such an occurrence as an execution i might happen, and with a view to evading it. Therefore n every case a claimant should make his claim out by. clear and satisfactory evidence. Apparently the transaction in question was that the brother getting into difficulties, in- formed his brother, who told them that he lent hiin goods. After the evidence that bad been given he thought that the transaction was not a loan, but a sale on credit, and that Ike paper was a concoction on the part of the brothers in order that it might be shown to any officer who might be put in to levy an execution. Other circumstances countenanced that view of the matter. He thought a contrivancr had been made to shield Henry Brett, and that being so he could not say that there had been a bona fide claim made Out for these goods, and therefore he must give judgment for the execution creditor.

LONDON, TRURSDAY.
