With occasional /lashes in the pan and one memorable explosion the debate on the Vote of Censtr e has been plod- ding its dull way through the House of Commons. It must be gratifying to the Governinent, and equally depressing for the Conservatives, to note the almost absolute ference with which the process of unloading speeches in watched. It was settled from the first, in accordance with a vicious principle of a very recent growth, that the whole of the week must be given up to the debate. '1 he House of Lords, which in this matter, at least, always shines by com- parison with the House of Commons, settled with equal promptness that two nights would be quite sufdcient for it to exhaust argument on the topic. In times within recent memory, before obstruction had sapped the business energies of the House, two nights were in the Commons considered ample for such a purpose. But, as Major O'Gorman once said, one does not need to be a Cassandra to prophecy that to-morrow night efforts will be made to carry the debate into next week. For all practical purposes it might have closed. on Monday night. Sir Stafford Northcote.supported an invertebrate resolu- tion with a weak-kneed speech. There is something in the personal position of the leader of the Opposition that must excite sympathy in the least kindly mind. I suppcse the last thing in the world Sir Stafford would voluntarily do would be to move a vote of censure on anybody or anything. At the present crisis such an action can bring nothing but fresh disaster upon the Opposition. They are avowedly de- pendent for any impression they can make upon the Par. nellite vote and upon any stray support they may receive from the Whigs, who live in a conditi.m of perpetual poll- cal discontent.. Having submitted his motion and sup- ported it in a painstaking speech, Sir Stafford has the sat. isfaction, first of hearrng Mr. Gladstone, amid much cheer- ing, point out the simple fact that what Sir Stafford says on the 23rd of F. braary, 1885, he had said almost in the same phrases on the 13th May, 1884. Not a single new fad, not a solitary novel argument, an hardly. anyibing fresh in the way of travesty of history. liars is the opinion of a political opponent, and might be borne if it stood by itself. Bat it was immedittely followed by reproaches and con- temptuous remarks from the organs of his own party, fol- lowed immediately afterwards by a squabble at a party meeting, whereat a dead set seems to have been made upon the hapless leader. All this is very melancholy, and must make Sir Stafford sometimea turn with tender thoughts to the retirement of the Pynes.

One victory the Conservatives have oblaintd this week of , which they may or may not be proud. They have practi- cally defeated the authority of the chair and have made it exceedingly unlikely that the Closure Rule will be again en- forced in whatever desperate circumstances an over-ridden House may find itself. The eveut of Tuesday night is not a political one, and may be discussed without suspicion of political animus. Thus freely judged it must be pronoun- ced one of the most discreditable things ever achieved by a great party. They had themselves dem andel opportunity for debating a Vote of Censure. The minister indicted had set aside all Government busiress in order to give the op. portnnity. In accordance with custom he had moved to postpane notices of motien till the debate went forward. This had been opposed for obstructive purposes by the Par- nellites. The Speaker had courageously put in action an unpleasant authority shifted to his shoulders! by the House itself; and then the Conservative party sided with the oh- , stractionists to affront authority and, give wider scope to license. Lord Salisbury, not a scrupulous man in political warfare, has expressed his unbounded disgust at this proce- dure, not because it is a crime, but because it is a mistake. If there is one thing upon which the English people have a strong and united feeling it is on the subj,ct of obstruction in the House of Commons. Yet here is the Speaker at last screwing up his courage to deal with the evil, and the party of Order either run away or side with the Obstructionists. And these are the men who propose to displace Mr. Glad- stone and his colleagues, and take under their control the destinies of the country This is comparatively a small thing. That Lord Salisbury shrewdly appreciates its effect ',non the Popular mind, and its bearing upon larger issues, _• and does well to be The dinner given by the National Liberal Club to the Marquis of Ripon was a great political success. For per- sosal comfort the place was a little crowded. But sensible people do not go to festivals of this kind for their dinner but rather for the feast of reason and the flow of soul that comes on with dessert. Of this there was plenty, possibly again too much. The influence of the National Liberal Club is so widespread and so powerful that the most emi- nent leaders of the party are always ready to appear under its auspices. Mr. Gladstone himself would have presided, but for the interdict placed upon his rnovemeets by his doctor. As it was there were Lord Derby, Sir Chas. Dilke, Mr. Bright, Sir W. Harcourt, and the Marquis of Ripon, any one of whom would of himself have proved an attrac- tion for a meeting like this. The consequence was that it was very late before the speakiug was over, rind the audience were perhaps a little surfeited. Poor Mr. Bright did not get his innings till half.past eleven, and very naturally showed an inclination to let Mr. Lalmohnn Ghose "answer ' for India," which was a little hard en the mild Hindoo. But of course the audience would not let Mr. Bright go, and he had to make a speech, though he was evidently much fatigued. These little incidents supply evidence of the club and of the popularity of Lord Ripon. To my mind the most striking and important speech of the evemeg e-as Earl Cowper'e. This nobleman, though ranking as a Liberal and but lately a member of the Government, has always been a little shaky. In one of the many votes of censure that have been brought on in Orel-louse of Lords he absented himself from the division. He was by no me ins enthusias- tic in his tone when proposing the health of her Majesty's Government. What is significant is that he, a cautious man of highly developed Whig tendencies, has made up his mind to stand by Mr. Uladstme at the present juncture.

The annual reports of the various London Co-operative Associations now being published are calculated to make the month of the honest trader water. Here is the Civil Ser- vice Supply Association, for example, turning over close upon two millions sterling in a year. On sales amounting to £900,000 in the last half year the gross profit was a trifle over £109,000. This and kindred institutions must, it would seem, affect the business of shops. But as for as informa- tion is attainable in individual instances this does not appear to be the case. There are, of course, complaints of slack trade. But those are perennial, and were in full cry long before co-operative stores were started. The fact seems to be that the case of the shopkeepers and the stores is an. alagous to that of omnibuses and the underground railway. Omnibuses were to be ruined when the unElemround railway' was opened, whereas they are doing business tenfold what it then was. Shopkeepers were all to be ruined when the stores opened, and yet in many shops to-day customers stand or sit at the counters two deep.

'Mr. The statement 'which appears as a postscript to Charles Williams's graphic descripeion of the battle of Abu Klee has created a very painful sensation through the wide circle of Colonel Burnaby's friends. It was, Mr. Williams sap, Burnaby who gave the order to the Heavy Cavalry to advance and meet the onrush of the Arabs, thus breaking the square and making an easy opening for the enemy. I for one, among scores with whom I have spoken on the subject, take leave to doubt this stateteent. In the first place, not a whisper of it has been heard before; whether in official or unofficial descriptions of the inciden's of the day. Secondly, such an action would imply that Burnaby had lost his head, and bad suddenly gone cen- Vary to the soldierly instincts which formed a lexileg feature of his nature. He was not in command of the Heavies; he knew that wantonly to break a square from the inside was to hand himself and, the men over to the mercies of the enemy, Therefore, he could have taken that step only in a moment when absolutely devoid of preeence of mind. Now, everybody who knew Burnaby know that in the face of danger he was impeiturable as a rock. The- greater the danger the more supernatural became his cool- ness. Re was the last men in the world to outrage through military etiquette, and in a moment of hysteric ti excite- ment to break up a square and madly lead other men to to certain death. It will be well before accepting it :o await confirmation of this incredible statement, and in the meantime we may regret that it has been circulated. Many accounts have been printed of Mr. Wills:leo, w Ten o'clock," and all as far as I have seen have succeesfullv hidden the fact that it was a failure, that is to say, it was a failure from the point of view of the audience. For Mr. Whistler it was a great seceess, since every seat was occu- pied and every seat,. without a single exception it is said, represented half a guinea. The fact of the matter is that beyond the first four row of benches the lecturer was abso- lutely inaudible. In private conversatiou he has not the clearest form of enunciation. When it came to reading people anywhere near the back manuscriptthethe was position hopeless. f o But there has not been loud cm- plaint. The room was pleasantly lighted, " everybody " was there, and nearly everybody knew everybody else. -It w to go, and those who did net catch the string atnrgohfesrmtahre thing and strained efforts at epigram which made up the performance' were content to know that they did not miss much. Whistler is undoubtedly a witty. man. One or two or his sayings really and honestly fliseed forth in conversation, have from time to time been recorded with due appreciation in this column. Bat the effort to ' provide witty sayings that would Last over an hour was too much for him, and he gave instead of the true metal, hands- ful of showy and glittering coins which hid not the true ring about them. However, everybody was pleased,"James " with his half-guineas and the audience with themselves ar.d each other.

Strangers are beginning to return to the House of Com- mons like a flock of pigeons temporarily frightened away. It is very odd to see this part of the House, hitherto crowded in the dullest times,empty and forlorn. The re- strictions in the House of Commons, enacted it is well un- derstood under the personal direction of Sir William Har- court, are in great danger of defeating themselves. Tne last hampering edict with respect to the press (that winch closed the corral)r as a passage batween the House of LordS and the House of Commons) has already been abrogated. The real danger lay in tiv indiscriminate admission of un- identified strangers, and it is to be feare3 that in.the reac- tion against stupid regulatiMs salutary precautions may finally suffer.

POLICE INTELLIG.

--- WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Tbere was DO business. MONDAT.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), in the chair, and Mr. John Fairclongh. MISCELLANEOUS.—The following charges of drunkenness were dealt with :—Robert Scanlen, in Legh-street, on Sat- urday evening, fined 53 and costa ; Michael, Mannion, in Bridge street, on Saturday evening, fined 5s and c )sts ; Jane Runcorn, in Bold-street, at midnight, on Saturday, fined 103 and costs; Henry Crosby, in Mersey-street, on the 14th inst., fined 53 and costs; John Hardman, in Winwick- street, on the 14th inst., fined 53 and costs.—James Leonard, charged with begging in Winwick-road on the previous afternoon, was discharged on promising to leave the town.—John Kearns was fined 103 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, for being drunk on the licensed prem- ises of James Kenyon, on Saturday, the 14th inst. DISTURBING THE Pr...Km—Thomas Lee and David Smith were each bound over to keep the peace for six months on a charge of fighting in Winwick-street, on the 14th inst., and Lee was fined Sc and costs for drunkenness at the same time.--Three young girls, named Carey, Perrier, and Nolan were charged with disturbing the peace in Bridge- street, on the 15th inst. They were described as members of the Skeletm Army, who followed the processions of the Salvation Army, and caused considerable annoyance.—The Bench fined them 23 each, and ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months. UNREGISTERED LODGING-HOUSES.—William Heaton, 2, Mottram's yard, off Scotland-road. was fined 5s and costs, or seven days' imprisonment, for keeping lodgers without having his house registered, and Isaac Bate, 14, Dial-street, was fined 403 and coats, which he paid, for a similar offence. THE SUAKIM-BERBER RAILWAY. The view we give above will give our readers an idea of the nature of the country wnich the Soudan Railway will traverse. The Times says :-The construction of a broad gau,ge line f rom Suakirp to Berber appears to be decided up- on, and considerable interest will attach to a work which will be a great engineering feat. Not since the American War has engineering on a grand scale formed a feature in a campaign. Military engineering has grown in im- portance of late years in several respects. The intro- duction of the_breechloading rifle has enhanced the de- fensive value of earthworks. The increased range and shell power of field artillery has entailed the provision of bomb-proof accommodation, rendering the field-works of to-day not more complex as to general plan, but cer- tainly more intricate as to internal arrangement. The rapidity of movement which characterises the later campaigns not only entails the pOwer of hasty bridge- making and restoration on the strategic assailant, but necessitates facilitates for demolitions on the part of the defence. The immense present importance of railways in war has opened up a wide field for the engineer,whil aalidmotshteallputrpheoscsosienoctesmhze .INulaten t-' campaign nail - and The Soudan • - _ perhaps, be remembered in connection with a great engineering work, calculated to confer great and lasting advantages upon the country. When the railway line touches Berber the Soudan difficulties will assume an altogether different aspect. The purely en- gineering obstacles which have to be overcome will be those of gradients and sharp curves. It may probably be assumed that the northern route from Suakim to Berber will be adopted. This route passes through Tambouk, Es Sibil, Haratri and Ariab. The southern route passes through Sinkat and Hor- mareb, striking the first in the Wady Laemeb, 15 miles , from Obak and about 75 miles from the Nile. Two in- termediate cross routes connect the two main tracks, and other practicable passes doubtless exist. The northern route to Berber has U. known groups of wells , "along its course, the longest waterless distance—Ariab , to Obak—being 53 miles. The wells are, in some cases, , mere shallow, scooped holes in the sand, and in others deeper excavations, riveted with wood or stone. There has never been any real attempt to increase a water supply which just suffices for the needs of caravans, and there seems to be every reason to suppose that, with time and the necessary appliances, a considerable ,de- velopment is possible. Starting from Suakim in a north- easterly direction, the railway would reach Tambouk, 27 miles distant, with little difficulty. The height attained is I,Booft. ; but the gradients are not excessive. Follow- ing the Wady Omareg, the route reaches Es Sibil, 2,300 ft. high, and 20 miles from Tambouk. After ascending to the height of 2,700 ft., a wide, gravelly plain is passed with an easy descending gradient, and a pass is entered leading to Haratri, 2,85.0 ft. high, and 22 miles from Es Sibil. This is the highest point of the route, and the pass, which is narrow and steep, will be one of the prin- cipal engineering difficulties of the route. The track now descends to another wide plain at 2,300 ft. level, and another mountain pass leads to Wady Kokreb, 33 miles from Haratri. Here also there may be difficulties of curve and gradient to overcome. From Kokreb the route descends to Ariatr at I,Booft. level and 27 miles further on. For 110 miles from Ariab there is a gradual descent to Berber at 1,250 ft. level. Throughout this dis- tance the only constructive difficulty is a belt of soft sand at Obak about five miles broad. This may have to be turned by bending the- track to the northward. While it is impossible with the information at preseut available to predict the rate of progess of the line, it is evident that much will depend upon the effect produced by the operations against Osman, Digma, and upon the success with which the water supply difficulties are overcome. If it is possible to send out working parties to prepare the track at Efaratri and Kokreb much time will evidently be gained; while if the neighbouring tribes settle down an supply labour and camels the work will be considerably lightened'. The rate of advance on a de- sert line necessarily diminishes with the distance from the base on account of water transport.. Thus, for the purposes of the railway alone it will be most desirable to develop the natural supply, or„.bylaying pipes, to relieve the line of water transport. From. Suakim two routes lead to Sinkat, which will probably-be General Graham's first objective. Of these one strikes nearly due west and the other taluas a south-westerly direction and passes through Tamanieb. Sinkat, at a height of 3,080 ft. above the sea, is only about 33 miles from, Suakim, so.thatwith 3 well-equipped transport column the British force-vrill soon be able to strike a blow- at Osman Digma's power. The reports point to a fight in the neighbourhood of Tama, or Tamanieb, and this will be followed up by a rapid advance to Sinkat, where it may: possibly be de- sirable to garrison for a time. Sinkat is comparatively cool, and would form a healthy summer station,.the oc- cupation of which would probably paralyse the action of the tribes and enable the railway pioneer force to. ad- vance along the northern route unopposed. It has gene- rally been believed that the movement of a small force to Berber would have been possible after Gen. Grahairds victories last year, and this is still more likely to be the ease now, when after defeat the Arabs, will be at once followed up to their stronghold. The probability seems to be, therefore, that after one battle the, military situa- tion in this portion of the theatre of war will clear-itself, while there can be little doubt that the final suppression of Osman Digma will produce a moral effect at Khar- toum.

ATTEMPTED EXECUTION OF THE BABBICONIBE MURDERER. —A SICKENING CENE.—The execution of John Lee, con- victed at Devon Assize for the murder of • Miss Keyse, at Babbicombo, on November 15th, was to have taken place on Monday, at Exeter prison. Berry, of Yorkshire, was the executioner, and the gallows was erected In a building used as a coach-house and situated on the left of the prison. The rope was fastened to a beam in the roof, and the trap was let into the floor, the idea being that whet the bolt was drawn the body would fall into the pit. The trap has bees used before, and on Saturday was tested by Berry, the ese- cutioner, and answered all right. Since then there have been two wet days, and this has probably caused the wood- work to swell. The rope was adjusted and the bolt drawn, but the trap stood firm. Berry and the warders tried to start it by stamping, but to no use. and Ls e was taken cif the trap and the rope removed. A second attempt was made, the chaplain meantime continuing to read the service for the dead. The lever was pulled and again the trap remained firm. A few minutes after Lea was agein placed on the drop. By this time he was in a pitiaMe state. His face was destitute of colour, his hands were blue with cold, and his eyes were half closed, though he had previously stood and moyed without assistance, but now he had to be supported on his way back to the prison, and had to be helped by the warders up the steps. '1 here was much ex- citement among the crowd outside the gaol while all this was going on. The delay in hoisting the black flag had caused a great deal of comment, and when the idea that something was wrong had occurred the crowd rapidly swelled. This time it was decided not to try again, but to communicate with the Home Secretary. A telgraphic reply was received in the evening, stating that the Home Secretary had obtained the consent of the Queen to a respite in consequence of the condemned nun having twice under- gone the pangs of imminent death.
THE SOUDA_N CAMPAIGN.
THE ATTACK ONT GEN. BULLER.- RE PULSE OF THE ARABS -NEWS FROM KHARTOUM.

HEAD QUARTERS, KORTI, SIINDAV.—Major Wardrop has arrived at (*Adel with _despatches from General Bailer. As the riflemen on the hills around Abu Klea continued to an- noy the camp with their distant flee, General Bailer opened a shell fire upon them, the Gatling gun also playing upon their position. Some of the shells burst among the enemy, and our field-glasses showed that they suffered severely. Major Wardrop, with three Hussars, made a circuit, and by tiring upon the enemy, now-from one ridge, now from another in their rear, always keeping out of eight, he im- pressed them with the idea that a large force was surrounding them. This completed the effect produced by the accuracy of our shell-fire, and the enemy presently drew 6ff, 4ed tirely evacuated their position, retiring tor & Meigorneh. Our losses, in addition to ogee mousaio en e rai Sul- -.let's former denPatY 3. Doi.- - was tome ten men wounded. Oienerial now occupied the high ground from which the Arabs were annoying us. He will probably remain at Atm Klea until joined by the Camel Corps and Mounted Infantry fromGakdoi. Yesterday, 230 of the black troops from General Gordon's steamers, with a few women and children, arrived here. The medical officer who came down with them re- ports in very high terms of the cheerfulness and willingness shown by these troops on the march, which was a heavy one, at they carried the wounded with them. A convey of camels of Kabbthish tribe started yesterday for Gakdal to replace the camels which have broken down. A inessengec who was sent to Khartoum on the 6th inst. returned to-day, having failed to get through. He was stopped at Nausea, where he intended to cross the river. A number of the Mandi's men were there, and these exami ed every one who wished te cross. He was asked the name of his Shiekh and the colour of his banner. Managing to satisfy them on these points, he was allowed to go on. On arriving at Kerreri he saw a Yaalin tribesman who was known to him, and who was at the taking of Khar- toum. This man told him that General Gordon was not shot, but was killed with swords and spears. The soldiers had consulted among themselves whether to take him alive or not, but they decided npm killing him, because if they took him alive to the Mandi he would be spared, and that they did not wish, as they thought that he ought to be killed, as he was the cause of all the trouble. The regular ddiers were spared, except the men holdiag the Boon i Gate. These were killed, but the man who made cartridges for the rest was kept alive. No women or children were killed. The Mandi has ordered his people to collect all the animals they can and to prepare large numbers of water skins, as they would soon move again. Animals were very scarce both in and around Khartoum, and our messenger's infor- mant thought it would be a long time before the main body of the Matadi's force would be able to advance. The mes- senger ascertained that no reinforcements have as yet been sent down the river from Khartoum to Metammeh. all that branch of the Kabbabish tribe Inhabiting Waled Geralbh are with the rebels. Food is said to be dreadfully scarce all along the banks of the Nile, as General Gordon's foraging parties from the eteamers and the bands of the Mandi had swept away everything edible from the villages for a great distance above and below Khartoum. The mes- senger has brought back with him many sovereigns. He says they are sold by the rebels at three dollars each. The man did not go farther than Kerreri, as he was afraid, and had found out from the Yaalin man all he was sent to die. cover.—Staaard.

KORTI, MoNDAY, 5 1.31%--4. despatch from Sir Evelyn Wood, dated from Gakdul, reports that all is quiet there. The rebels near Abu Elea are apparently disinclined to renew their recent attacks on the British, not venturing to advance in face of the commanding fortified posts established by General Buller, and defended by a detachment of the Royal Irish Regiment. The despatch adds that seven of the Mandi's men who formerly belonged to Hicks Pash.a's army have surrendered. They state that the Mandi had started to come down the Nile to Metammelr, but subsequently turned back.

THE SUAKIM-BERBER EXPEDITION. CAIRO, MONDAY.—Iii military cirzles it IS expected that Brigadier-General Braokenbury's column will advance as far as Abou Hamed, in order to secure command at the desert route to Korosko. The force will intrench itself at Abou Hauled, where it will pass the summer. it simulta- neous advance on Berber and Khartoum would be made in the autumn. It )8 believed that the Suakim-Berber expedi- tion will considerably exceed 2,000 men. Sir Gerald Gra- ham will, in all probability, encamp at Sinkat. The 2od Battalion of the East Surrey Regiment has left for Suakim. The 2nd Battalion of the Durham Light Infantry Regiment arrived here this morning. Summt, MONDAY.—The Egyptian despatch-boat Jaf- farieh left yesterday with two hundred natives of the friendly Amara tribe, to carry out a raid upon the cattle of Osman Digna's followers. The steamer returned here to- day after a most successful trip. She landed the natives during the night at the mouth of the river Klor, which comes down through the llandoub country. The Amaras succeeded in capturing and embarking three hun- dred cattle belonging to the Hadendowae after a slight skirmish with the enemy, of whom one was killed and two wounded. Stumm, TUESDAY.— The troopship Hurialbert, with Brigadier-General Davis and. 200 men of the, East Surrey R-giment, arrived here today. She will sail early to- morrow.

GIBRALTAR, Trusniv.--The hired transport Qu?erax, with Enginoers and Commissariat Corps, sailed to-day for i9uakim. Five ships of the Channel Squadron arrived here at midniaht. Koart, TUESDAY.—Brigadier-Geueral Brackenbury ex- pects that his advance guard will reach Abu, "lamed to- morrow.

_ 150 navvies belonging to Messrs. Lucas and Aird's staff embarked at the East and West India Docks on Tuesday, in the 03wrey, with materials for the Suakim-Berber Rail- way. THE REINFORCEMENTS-INSPEC- TION BY. THE PRINCE OF WALES. The seoond battalion of the Scots Guards lett Westminster for embarkation at Gravesend in the Pembroke Castle en route ts Suakim on Saturday. The battalion were conveyed down the river from Westminster Pier in three steamers. The troops par.iie4 at half-past anren in the barrack-square of the Wellington Barracks, and a few minutes after the half-hour EI.R.H. the Prince of Wales, the Princess of Wales, Prince Albert Victor, and the three yoing Princesses, accompanied by the Princess Louise, drove up. The troops presented arms, and H.R.H., in the undress uniform of a Field Marshal, marls a minute inspection of the troops.. Ad- dressing the Colonel, the Hon. W. It. Treble, the officer in comm met, H.R.H. said be had come to wish them good bye. The condition of the Scots Guards was well known. Their services were a matter of history, and they would, he was sure, sustain their high reputation. Ho wished them good health under fatigue and trials, God speed, and a safe re- turn. Men and officers fell in, starting from the barrack yard as the clock struck eight. The crowd had taken pos- session of every vantage point and the enthusiasm was un- paralleled. Many past officers of the Scots Guards accom- panied thq battalion to Gravesend.

The Donlace sailed from Woolwich Arsenal on Saturday afternoon with more than 1,000 tons of provisionsovbich she will tak3 to Soakim direct. Tke first of the railway transports, 2.uricb, left East India Docks on Saturday. 0 Ning to the works constructed at Suakim since General Graham last commanded a farce against Osman Digtna, no difficulty will be experienced in landing the troops forming tip present expsdition. The first transport conveyin4 troops to arrive at Suakim will be the steamship Arab, which

left Southampton on the 17th just, conveying commissariat and medical staffs, artillery, and stores. She will arrive at Suakim on Much 6th, after taking in additional troops at Gibralter. Other transports will follow in rapid succes- sion. In the course of the next fortnight or three weeks the force already at Suakim will be thus augumented by 197 officers, 4,611 men, and 616 horses. It is expected that the Indian contingent, numbering about 3,000 of all ranks, will arrive about the 10th of March. F2.lr Charles Tupper, the High Commissioner for Canada, has received a communication from the Secretary to the Colonies, stating that her Majesty's Government highly appreciate the patriotic offer made by the Dominion Govern- ment with respect to a force for foreign service, but that the length of time before it could be embarked for active service is an obstacle to the immediate availing op It. It is anticipated that the force already under orders will be sufficient for the military operations which are to be immediately undertaken, but if they are prolonged until the autumn the Government will gladly take the offer into consideration. A similar message has been sent to the Governors of the other oolonior excepting New South Wales.

SIDNEY, MONDAY.—An enthusiastic meeting WAS held here to-day, attended by 8,000 persons, at which resolutions were adopted urging the NtiV South Wales Government to despatch the troops to Egypt with all possible promptitude. Sir James Martin, Chief Justice, New South Wales; the hon. Edward Barton, Speaker of the Legislative Assembly; Mr. Jennnings, and other speakers addressed the meeting. The Patriotic Fund now amounts to £30,000, including a oontributidn of Z 5,000 from the Railway Department, and several individual subscriptions of £l,OOO. PRIVATE LETTER FROM GORDON. Canto, Fan 24.—The following letter from General Gordon, addressed to a friend is Cairo, and dated Khartoum, Dec. 14, was received to-day : " All is up. I expect a catastrophe in ten days' time. It would not have been self our people had kept me better in- formed as to their intentions. My adieux to all. "C. G. GORDON." Ills remarked that the scrap of paper received by Lord Wolseley from General Gordon with the words " Khartoum all right" bore the same data as the above letter.
DECORATION OF THE •MUDIR OF DONGOLA.

KOUT/ TUESDAY EVEN/NO.—A grand durbar was held here to-day on the occasion of the investiture of the Mudir of Dongola with the insignia of the Order of St. Michael and St. George by Lord Wolseley. The brevet of installa- tion WAS read by an interpreter in the Arabic language, after which Lord Wolseley placed the collar of the Order round the Modir's neck. The Mudir delivered a short soeech, in which, he begged his lordship to convey to the Queen his thanks for the distinction conferred on him by her Majesty. The chief sheikhs of the Kabbatrish, Romareir, and Sowa- rob tribes with their followers were present. The West Kent Regiment formed a guard ef honour. The latest intelligence from Abu Klea states that the wounded are doing well, including Captains Walsh and Paget, who were wounded on the lesh inst. The whole force, in- cluding 780 animals, guns and equipment complete, bed then crossed to the right bank, and was to advance on Abu Hazed, 40 miles distant, at daybreak on the 22nd.

There had been no deaths since the I2th inst. The health and spirits of the troops were excellent. Exclusive of the wounded, there are only 18 sick in the total force. . _

div.p: Wttttro to the 41t0r.,

_ . TEETOTALISM IN EARLESTOWN. Sir' —" Tee Tee" is evidently annoyed that I decline his little help, and do not take np the pertinent points he sug- gests. I beg to inform him that I feel quite capable of dis- cerning pertinent points and when to take them up, so I re- spectfully decline his asssistance. If he would be a little less officious and give more attention to the points already [before him, this discussion would be much more profitable reading. Further than this I will not refer to his last let- ter as it is not worthy a reply. I am sorry he has so far I descended from his first letter, but I hope he will soon re- gain himself.

Just a line or two on the "New wine "theory. Did the Jews possess as good a knowledge of chemistry as "Tee Tee?" Or does ancient and present custom support his explanation of the "New wine skins? " Archbishop French says no prudent man who means to keep his wine for tire feast pours it new and not yet having worked off its fer- menting strength, into skins old, and therefore weak and stiff, not capable of expansion. Burdillon says bottles were then made not of glass, but of skins of leather, and the leather in time grew weak and could not bear the motion of fermentation of new wine, though it [sight still be strong enough to held old .wine safely. New wine must be put into new and strong bottles. Should my good friend carry out his threat for the benefit of yeur readers, I purpose troubling you with one short letter, stating as concisely as possible my reasons for thinking Christ was not an ah- itainer.—Yours truly, MODERATOR.

div.head: FAIR TRADE.
div.p: FAIR TRADE.

Sir,—l notice you wiLS.-a:lea:d-i-n-6;-f.irticle upon the Fair Trade question in your issue of the 21st inst. It is un- necessary for me to wade through the whole of that article, but I will at once come to the practical point, and deal with matters as they are. First then I ask you whether the people of England pay the revenue of this country now at the present time ? You must answer, yes. Very well then, what advantage have we in taxation over the tariff sys- tem of foreigtr nations ; if we ply out own revenue, other nations can do no more. In the second place, I ask you who now pays the largest proportion of the revenue of our country ? Does not the British working-mao, through the customs duty upon tea, coffee, cocoa, and tobacco,and the inland duty upon beer ? in other words, is it not more than half the revenue of the country raised from customs and excise duty principally paid by the w)rking population in their retail purchases ? Give a direct reply, and again you must answer, yes. It will serve no useful purpose to argue that working-men need not buy so-and-so; there re- mains the fact that they do buy, and in baying they pay the greater part of the revenue. I ask, does each working- man know that when ha pays 2s for a pound of tea that he really gets is 6d worth of tea and 61 worth of taxation, or that when he pays 31 for an ounce of tobacco that he get d worth of tobacco and 2l of taxation? Yet, this is true, and it proves that the working-men of England bear a large burden of taxation, under our present fiscal policy, and are moreover fobbed of employment and wages by the foreigner into the bargain, through the free importation of foreign manufactured articles.—Yours
BRITISH WORKMAN. Warrington, February 23rd, 1885. [Our Correspondent :will see that we have dealt with his difficulties in our leader columns.—En. Ex.]

div.head: MR. NORMAN, SEN., AND ECONOMY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: MR. NORMAN, SEN., AND ECONOMY AT RUNCORN.

Sir,—The Itttepayir" makes of the good joke about " facilitating expenses" is a fair in- dex of the incapacity and misrepresent ition which charac- terises the v:Lcrie of. his attack on Mr. Norman. "A Rate- payel3s friends Should prevent him rushing into print, as his electioneering purposes would be better served by keep- ing his misleading information outside the range Of offiCial contradiction.

To begin with, the Wesleyan schools are not an incubus on:the denomination, for, without private subscription, pub- lic collection or popular entertainment, the managers promptly discharge all their liabilities, and hand over to their trustees a substantial rental for the buildinge they occupy. The NOS "it Ra,tepayer " knows, Or ought to and yet be Ventura tbo 3nsinuation that Mr. Nor- man would be benefited by their traier. Again, the ma- chinery of the School Board at present is nifitaiy employea Idriving poor people into the merciless clutches of denomina- tional officials, and it is the harsh conduct of tkese officiaia (iide recent proceedings of the Board) that has driven Mr. INorman to assume his present attitude. These facts also "A Ratepayer" knows, or ought to know; and yet by mis- representation he seeks to obscure the issue. The policy Mr. Norman foreshadows, as an alternative, may be highly objea!onable to the narrow circle which owns "A Ratepayer" as its leader, but those whom the Ellie ition Act was framed to benefit will no fail to appreciate its worth. "A Ratepayersi vereton of the Commissioners' proceed- ings is equally misleading. Recent events have demon- strated the necessity for an alteNtion in the conduct of the business of the Board, and Mr Norman proposes—not tLe garbled arrangement "A Ratepayer " publishes, but that Mr Dutton shall be made chief of the Sanitary Department, with an assistant to superintend the market, and a working foreman to take charge of the scavengers. One hour per day at his office in the market would suffice for the super- vision of this branch; and then free for the inspection of nuis- ances and lodging-houses' he could readily visit every part of the town, ordering the scavengers to whatever point he considered necessary. This arrangement, easy to work if efficiently carried cut, would ensure the town being thor- oughly cleaned, and its sanitary condition maintained at the highest possible point. "A Ratepayer's" idea that ten men are necessary for the performance of these duties is too absurd for consideration, while his strictures on infection display an ignorance of tke elements of sanitary science, which I shall not attempt to dispel. I suppose he imagines that after contact with infection, nothing remains for either doctor or inspector but to withdraw from the pale of civilisa- tion, with the mournful cry," Unclean, unclean." Mr Nor- man has, indeed, a feeble hold on the Runcorn public, if at the next election the pitiable epistle of " A Ratepayer" in- fluences his return.—Yours truly, Runcorn, Feb. 19th, DM. VERACITY.

div.head: REDISfRIBUrION_AND REORGANISATION IN
div.p: REDISfRIBUrION_AND REORGANISATION IN
RUNCORN.

Sr,—Through official bungling the name of the new electoral district of which Runcorn—by far the largest and most important town—is to form a part, is to be Northwicb. It were mere waste of time to find fault with our political godfathers and godmothers whose saline proclivities have led them to clog us with such a name. "What's in a name?" we may resignedly ask, and seek how we can best help forward the cause of Liberalism under the altered state of affairs,

It may be that in addition to losing the honour of calling the district by its own name, Runcorn will have to submit to the greater humiliation of seeing the centre of political influence set up in Northwich, instead of in its natural home,. Runcorn, where active Liberalism is indigenous, as all who are acquainted with paat Mid-Cheshire eleotioas will readily admit. Again we are willing to submit to the inevitable, after first expressing a hope that the scriptural injunction, "Remember Lot's wife," will be attended to, lest, by a b ick- ward movement the party to which we have the honour to belong becomes paralysed and stiffened into a " Pillar of Salt."

It is quite time that steps were taken for the reorganisa- tion of the Liberal party in Runcorn. A meeting should at once be held to which every Liberal should be invited; at which a strong and representative committee should be elected—a committee of men, not of names. There has been too much of the "figurehead business in the past in the shape of names that were meant to look well and no more. The man in moleskins will soon have the vote, and he must be encouraged to cast in his lot with the Liberal party, or the unscrupulous party of bribes and baubles will certainly lure him to his political ruin. Having formed the committee, the heavy task of preparing for the coming election must be commenced in earneet. This iq a work that is never fully finished; for, one election won, prepara- tions for the next must be taken in hand, and followed up with unflagging energy; so that the district need never be taken by surprise.

To faCilitarte this all-important work a club or set of rooms should be established, and thus provide a rendezvous for the workers and an educational institution where the principles of Liberalism could be fostered or instilled, mak- ing it a centre of political activity.. lam not sufficiently informed as to who is likely to be the candidate. I hope that politics will not be made sub- servient to salt. If amidst the rock-pits and brine-pits there is naturally an inclination among the ignorant (politically) to write salt with a capital 8, we in Runcorn are not en- tirely oblivious to its claims, seeing that vast quantities of it are shipped from the port and used moor chemical man- ufactures; while at no distant date salt itself will be made here. Nø candidate who tvould neglect the great salt in- terest, however suitable he might be in other wave, would have a ghost of a chance of being returned. Liberal and Tory are agreed on the question of salt. What we require in a candidate is a man who wtll sturdily stand by the prin- ciples of the great Liberal party—" Peace, Retrenchement, and Reform.' The first and second have certainly been under a cloud of late ; but the last has not by any means received the least attention. To particularise—the candidate to suit us must be prepared to support the demand for a scheme of land-law reform, such as shall ease the croaking burdens on the a4rieultural classes especially the labourers, i and the Scheme for prohibiting the cometen sale of itatox.H 'eating liquors. Those stand head and shoulders above every other question before the public mind. Soudan twonbles, Afghan difficulties, and Boer question', crop up DOW and agaio,and for a tires attract public attention, but these too, like the " poor," we" have always with us." The others are planples on the body politic; these are cancers. Our candidatamust be prepared to support • the proposals for free elementary education, and a more equitable method of taxation, and thus help to form, in the words of that erratic but patriotic Tyneside Tribune, J. Cowen," a robust, higb-spiriUd, magnanimous democracy, that will unfold the nation's worthier naturu and protect the highest properties of honesty and truth ; that will dissipate the moral inert- ness that at times grows parasitically over England's energies and cramps her pristine vigour."—Yours,
SPiRO .MELIOR.A, Rancorn, Febrgary 24'6, 1885.

" The latest football invented has a can of dynamite inside of it. What is left of the contestants is gathered up in a clothes basket. A lady said to a gentleman suffering from inflaenza, "My dear sir, what do you take for your cold ?" "Five pocket handkerchiefs a day, madam." Gabbing says that ladies ambitions of platform popularity I would indignantly deny the truth of Whately's assertion that "woman is a creature that cannot reason, and pokes the fire from the top." Scene—Army competitive examination. Examiner: "If I King ALLred were still alive, what part would he probably take in the politics of the present day?" Competitor: "If I King Alfred were still alive, he would be much too old to take part in politics." A good etory is told of a punctual host and would-be- polite but =punctual guest. Arriving very late the visitor took his seat at the table, and was profuse in his apologies. "Please excuse me, my dear sir," he said, "and allow me to go on with whatever is new being served; don't have any- thing brought up again for me." Taking him at his word, his host courteously assented, and the unpo.nctual one dined off apple tart." For a wary and thrifty business man commend us to a Jewish commercial traveller who the ether day received from a wealthy acquaintance in Frankfort a proposal to marry his daughter. The letter added—" Be sure ti come; my daughter is an acknowledged beauty, and is sure to please you." The commercial traveller wrote back that he was willing to come, but cautiously inquired, " Suppose, however, she does not please me, will you pay my travelling expenses home again l" A HORSE'S TRICES.—A Liverpool tram-car horse shot out with his heels the other day, and hit the driver with one, and the cash-box with the other, and an investigation showed that he had knocked six shillings and fourpence into the driver's overcoat pocket. Such wonderful sagacity on the part of the horse unfortunately in the long run caused the discharge of the driver. Wan Lrzzug SANG AMID TRH FLOWERS.—A few days after the first performance of the opera Blaise et Duvet, in which occurs the charming air, " Lizzie sings amid the flowers," a party of young fellows, says a French paper, went at night to the house of Mouvel, the composer of the opera, and shouted his name at the top of their voices. At last the sleepy composer appehred at the window, and his nocturnal visitors asked him to he kind enough to inform them what it was Lizzie sang amid the flowers. "Wait a moment," replied Mouvel ;"1 will tell you." He soon re- turned with a jugful of water, which he emptied over their heads, crying, 'The rain it raineth every day !" "I was once," says a writer in Tracity Fair," at a 'big ' shoot ' where a beater had been specially detailed for three days to carry the ammunition, the macintosh, the drinks the cigar case, and the other paraphernalia of one of the guests who had not a reputation for generosity. When the last beat was over, this gtulet gave the man half-a-crown. Said the man to one of his con;Yadee, 'Bill, want a sob?' Don't mind if I do, Sam.' 'Well, azenl—throwing him all the ungenerous one's traps—' take the 'll things to the Lodge for this 'ere genleman, and 'ere's 'arf-a-crs:7°l2 for Your trOnhie Tableau!' "You mustn't touch the top of the baby's hed," said A mother to her little four-year-old, "she has a soft spOt there that is very tender." The youngster gazed at it curiosOlY for a moment, and then asked: "Do all babies have soft spots on their heads ?" "Yes." "Did papa have a soft spot on the top of head?" "Yes," replied the mother with a sigh, "and he has got it yet." And the old man, who had Overheard the conversation from an adjoining room, sang Out: Yes, indeed, he has, my dear boy, or he would be a single man to-day." Mrs. Stowe gives a characteristic account of a gramma- tical exercise at which her brother Henry Ward assisted in his school-days. Young Beecher was about eleven years old, and as full of fun and mischief as possible. The teacher was drilling her pupils in the rudiments. "New, Henry," said she, " ' a" is the indefinite article, you see, and must be used only with the singular. number. You can say 'a man,' but you Can't say Men/ Can you 2" "Yes, I can say 'a men,' too," was the rejoindef, "Father always says it at the end of his prayers." "Come, Henry, don't be joking. Decline 'he.'" Nominative possessive 'his,' objective 'him.' "Yon see, 'his' is possessive. Now you can lay 'his book,' but you cannot say 'him book.'" "Yes, Ido say hyttn-tint,' too," said the impracticable pupil, with a quizzical twinkle. Each one v: these fiallieS made his young teacher laugh, which was the victory he wanted. I "But now, Henry, `aeriously, just attend to the active and passive vole,t, New 'I strike,' is active, you see, because, if you strike, you do something. But 'I am struCle is paSsive, you see, because, if you are struck, you don't do anything, do you r "Yes, I do—l strike back again." After about six months, Henry was returned on his parents' hands, with the reputation of being an inveterate joker and indifferent scholar.

THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.
ALLEGED MISMANAGEMENT, AND PROSE-

div.head: CUTION FOR LIBEL.
div.p: CUTION FOR LIBEL.

At Warrington Police Court, yesterday morning, a case I Was heard in which great interest was taken in political cirelee. M,..1-oseph arks, 13, Rylands-street, wassammoned by Mr. Speakman, manager of the Conservative Club, on a charge that he "unlawfully and maliciously did publish a certain defamatory libel of and concerning one Thomas Orrell Speakman." Oa the case being called, the magis- trates on the Bench were the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), who presided, Captain Reynolds, Alderman Burgess, and Mr. John White. Mr. Wharton, barrister, Manchester, instructed by Mr. Jeans, solicitor, Warrington, appeared for Mr. Speakman ; and the defendant was repr-sented by Mr. Arthur Browne, solicito-, Warrington. The proceedings, 'which were held in the County Court during the progress of repairs at the Borough Court, were watched with interest by a large number of politicians of the neighbourhood. Before the case was entered upon, Mr. Browne s ;id :1 appear on behalf of the defendant. I never do like making objections, but one of our borough magistrates sitting-- Captain Reynolds : Let me anticipate you. I came here to-day at a little inconvenience, knowing that I may be wanted to give some evidence. I think I should be known well enough in Warrington for you to know that I never sit on the Bench under these circumstances. If I sit here (on the Bench) it is only for convenience. Mr. Browne : I do not object to you sitting there. Captain Reynolds : I don't suppose it would matter much if you did. Mr. Browne : I believe one of your worships is one of the club committee. Mr. White : Yes, lam not going to take any part. Mr. Valatton: If your worships please, this is a summons against the defendant for publishing a defamatory libel in an issue of the Warrington Examiner on the 31st January hat. I will real YOU the libel before commenting upon it:—

THE WARRINGTON CONSERVA T EVE CLI7B. Sir.—lt is now ever two months since the committee of the new Conservative Club placed it under its present manage- ment, and by this time anyone would suppose that it would have been carried on to the s.itlefaction of all concerned, but, alas I how blindfolded were the e emmittee when they made their selection out of 10) applicants, with the result that com- plaints ace the order of the day. lam not blaming anyonabut the club committee for all the irregularinies that have taken place; they ha turd cm place it on others if they think proper. We, the members, hold the committee responsible for the good and efficient working of the club; and I will ask them to look round tee large billiard rce m and examine the card tables, chairs, stools, and spittoons, and see if they are kept in a fit state. A little s iap and warm water judiciously applied would produee a good effect, and would at the same time materially add to the respeetability of the establishment. We have had to complain of these things before in the first-class card room, and It was immediately attended to. Then why not attend to all the rooms alike, and not wait for complaints to be made? Again, we have to complain of the way the ref esbments are served out. If we call for a glass of beer, it is carried to us in the hands of a little lad, which are certainly very often un- clean. For my part, when I require a glass of refreshment I like to see it served on a tray, and the glass lifted therefrom In a proper manner, and not with the fingers round the top of the glass, but near the bottom. We are told that " cleanli- ness is Lest to godliness;" it this maxim is true, then we must be very ungodly when we an surrounded by the things I have mentioned At other establishments in the town, sach as Wa'ker's, we find these in charge are not afraid to display the colourof their shirts, and are not within lending a helping hand to s care what we as Englishmen so much p:ize, viz., cleanliness. For 2d we get a small portion of cheese, and three biscuits. ow these biscuits ale sold in the shoes at 61 per lb., and there are about 56 in a lb , so that we pay at the rate of nearly Is 7d per lb., a profit that any tradesman might envy, mud ap- proaching the rate that was charged to the ball c mmittee on the night of the Cetservative Ball for refreshments for two police rfficers and two door-keepers, viz., lOs for a ditto corned beef and bread etch. At the time it was said that it Was not the quantity they were eating that was objected to, but the space they occupied. Now when the late respected managerees, Mrs. Hannah, Was in charge of these things, we received six biscuits in the place of three now received, every oat was perfectly satisfied, and a legitimate profit was secured. We have also to complain of the unequal temperature male- tamed in the !arge room; sometimes we are lam!. eee'eyscle. ted ; at others the temperature 7.7. L low. I also hear filial those who five:teat the readine-room that there are complaints of every day occurrence. In conclusion, I appeal to the committee to deal with these things with a firm and unwavering voice. Warrington, Jan. 261 h, 1885. ANTI-HL'elEteae The Meyer That is a very unique and humourous pro- duction, Mr Wharton. (Laughter.) Mr Wharton : It is, sir, and a very skilled produc- tion, because, as I deducted from a movement of my friend when I sold, " We appeal to the law to deal with these things in a firm and unwavezing voice," I saw at once my friend's defence, and he, like his client, will be prepared to say that he does not wish to reflect upon anybody except the committee, and that he wishes to reelect upon the corn- mutes in order that they may do their duty. I venture to say that I can paint out that that Was not his intention— die intention was a totally different one. First of all, I would point out to you that with regard to libel any dis- paragement of a parson is sufficient. I Can preduce cases, if necessary, and lean do so at another time. There is quite safficient disparagement of some one in this letter, so long 29 I can show that it was intended to refer to the plaintiff. I will c ill your especial attention to the worde, "Placed it under its present management." The manager of this club is the plaintiff, Mr SPeakman, and therefore "placed it nn- der its management" can only have reference to Mr Speak- man. ‘• Sat, alas," further if goes on, " how blindfolded were the committee when they made their selectien," obvi- ously Mr Speakman, for that was their selection," out of a hundred applicants, with the result that complaints are the order of the day." That can only have one meaning, that by their selection, namely of Mr Speakman," complaints are the order of the day," obviously that Mr Speakman can- not manage it properly. This letter would not have quite so mach force if it were not for one little fact, and that is that the defendant was also an appli- cant, one of the hundred applicants for this situation, and this letter is the result therefore, I submit to you, of personal sp'te on behalf of the defendant, because, being an applicant, he was refused the post. Now, my friend has pro- duced a packet of biscuits for an obvious reason. I suppose he wants to prove the truth of the libel, or rather, to prove that the place is mismanaged; but I venture to think that you will not listen to that for a moment, and for this reaeon. If a man requires, being a member of a club, to put an end to any improper conduct in the club or manage- ment of the club, he usually writes a letter to the commit- tee, who are the persons which should attend to the matter, and he does not as a rule rush right to a newspaper that Supports the opposite side in politics. If a man wishes to complain of some public matter, such as the improper state of streets, or anything of that kind, he naturally writes to the newspaper; but he does not write to a newspaper that he wants to have his club properly managed, and certainly be would heeitite before writing and making these com- plaints to a newspaper which would naturally for poli‘ical purposes be only too delighted to let the public see the members of the Conservative Club washing their dirty linen in public. And that is the idea that bas actuated tee de- fendant throughout the whole of this transaction, because when this letter is published, signed "Anti-Humbug," the application is only made to the publishers for the name, and they have very properly given up the name, and have expressed regret in their next issue if they had made any suggestions which would in any way injure Mr. Speak- men, and are wiling to pay the cests incurred. That is perfectly satisfactory, and if the defendant had been pre- pared to do the same you would never have heard a word about this case. But his spite goes a little bit further, for a very proper letter is written to him by the solicitors as follows : '27. Winve'ek-streat, Warrington, February 18,1885.—Sir, —ln consequence of proceedings which have, been taken against the publisher of the Warrington Examiner fora libel is respect of a letter signed "Anta-Humbug," published in that paper on the 31st of January last, you have been dis- closed to us as the writer of such letter, and we have instruc- tions from Mr. Speakman, the manager of the Conservative Club. to take legal proceedings against you as the writer of alien libel, unless you forthwith sign an ample apology to be published in three Warrington:newspapers on Saturday next, and pay all expenses. Unless we hear from you satisfactorily before twelve o'clock to-morrow, we shall set the necessary Proceedings in motion.—Yours truly, W. D. JEANS and CO.— Mr. Joseph GI-rice, 13 Rytands-street." In reply one would have thought if his object had not been to interfere with, or injure Mr. Speakman, he would at once have said "I have not the slightest intention of in- juring Mr. Speakman, I am merely making what I think fair and legitimate complaints against the management of the club." That is what an honest man who did not wish to injure Mr Speakrnan would have done. He addressed a letter in which he said : Werrington, February 19th. 1885.—Gentlemen,—I beg to acknowledge receipt of yours of yesterday, and in reply I beg to say that it Is not my intention to apelogise, or retract a single word I wrote in the letter to The Eramitzer eigqed .• Anti-Ht mbug." You can new proceed to carry out your instructlans to the full extent, and you may rest assured that this ease will be ably defended when the props,. time arrives.— lam, gentlemen, respectfully yours. Josamr 6RICE All correspondence and any documents received I shall pass through the columns of The Examiner to keep the public in. formed of what Is going on, (Laughter.) He his not bean able to carry out that portion ' St the threat, because the proprietors of The Examiner have exercised their usual common sense. (Laughter.) The next point, and which aggravates this case more, is that anticipating that this strong letter in answer to Mr. Jeans and Company would not have any effect, he writes to the Secretary Of the Conservative Club, thinking that he could di& this matter by frightening the Conservative Club into the belief that they were going to have all their affairs ven- tilated, biscuits produced—(laughter)—dirty shirts, and all the rest of the things. Mr Wharton then . ead the letter in question, which warned the secretary that he would find it necessary if the ca 33 went into court "to disclose on that .occasion facts that had better be suppressed." The letter added, If possible, we shell have the case carried to Liverpool As- sizes," commenting on which Mr. Wharton said:— if that is all that is wished for by the defeudent it will save me from speaking- further and we can stop the case, although. here you will have to receive some formal evi- dence before you can do what he desires. Just one word so as to complete the matter upon the question of law. All - you have to discuss here to-day is the question of publica- tion and the question whether it lea libel. Reading from a learned authority are words supported by the cane of Fray v. Fray, to the effect that "the publication of anything in writing which can by any conetruction be shown to be dis-

paraging to the character of another may be libellous, and the plaintiff has a right to take the case to a jury." That is if you find that this letter may by any construction be shown to be disparaging to Mr. Speakman' and you find that it is published, you are bound to commit him for trial. It may be suggested that it was not intended to apply to Mr. Speakman, but it is not at all necessary that Mr Speakman should be mentioned. If a party can publish a libel so framed as to describe persons without naming them, or specifically describe them by express form of words, and so describe them that it is known who they are, and that those connected with the circumstances may come to the same conclusion and have no doubt that the writer of the libel intended to mean those individuals, then that would open a wide room for defamation. That is the dictum of Lord Cottinghara in a case similar to this. Therefore we have to look into the suggestions of this letter in order to ascertain whether or not it applies to Mr Speakman. After quoting and commenting on certain passages in the letter to show that they referred to Mr Speakman, Mr Wharton said: To say of Mr Speakman that he has neglected the managing of the club, but I do not blame him but the committee,iis just the same. I will only submit formal evidence, and sin satisfied you will send the case for trial. Mr. Browns: I wish to know under what section of Lord Campbell's Act he is now proceeding ; the summons is not very precise. Mr. Wharton : I sin not bound to give any information as to the section. The summons is there; the information has been properly laid, and if my friend has any objection he is entitled to put it. Mr. Browne : I shall object to the form of the summons; there are two different sections in Lord Campbell's statute under which it might be laid. Under one section I should be entitled to call certain evidence which I could not under the other section. Mr. Wharton : •Under which of the sections can you call evidence? After a further search in his books, Mr. Wharton said the section was obvious for the summons itself. It said that be maliciously aed unlawfully, not falsely, published a defama- tory libel. The Mayor : I presume the case is rightly before the court ? The Clerk : Oh yes, sir : I cannot see what the section has to do with it. Mr. Browns: It is not; in the one We I can produce witnesses, which I cannot in the other. Mr. Wharton said if the summons had been issued under one of the sections the word " falsely " would have been put in the summons. Mr. W. D. Jeans was then called, and said he was a solicitor practising in Warrington. He produced a copy of The Warrington and Mid-Cheshire Examiner which he had purchased at the Examiner office on the sth February. In consequence of information he received at the Examiner office' he wrote the letter of the 18:11 February (already cmoted) to the defendant. Mr. Browne objected that no notice had been given to produce the original of this letter. Mr. Wharton said he could give secondary evidencs. A copy of the letter was then put in. Mr. John Walker (editor of the Warrington Examiner) was then called, but said : 13,fore being sworn, I ask for expenses. lam here at very great inconvenience, as we have two newspapers which go out this morning. lam summoned here on behalf of the prosecution. Mr. Wharton: I don't want him to be sworn; I want hint to produce the original letter. The Mayor: But still he is entitled to be paid before be opens his mouth. Mr. Wh Won: No, sir. A witness is nat entitled unless he be sworn ; I don't want him sworn. Mr. Browns: He cannot produce any document without being sworn. Mr. Wharton: Oh, yes. Mr. Browne : I may say I represent Mr. Walker in this case. In order to bring a witness into court and cause him to produce certain docummts there muet be a Crown office subpcena, dacestecum, not an ordinary witness summons. An ordinary witness 91.131K10ns is only to bring a person before a court to give evidence. I submit that before pro- ducing any document he meet be sworn to say that docu- ment was the document. Mr. WhattOil : I dtT.'t ctilt him sworn. 1 want to know What he wants to be paid for? Mr. Browns: We do not say we have the document yet. Mr. Wharton: &toot so tar as bringing the doca- ments is concerned the witness need not have attended. My friend is quite right about the Crown office subpoena being necessary, but all I ask is that he may produce the copy. If he will not do that we must allow him to go down. The Mayor : Of course, you know, it is quite easy to take a horse to the water, but you cannot force him to drink. (Laughter.) Mn. WALKER : I shall not drink, your. worships. (Laughter.) Mr. Wharton: If he won't drink I cannot help it. Mr. Walker: It he would stand drinks, I would not ob- ject. (Laughter.) Mr. Wharton : Have you got the libel letter ? Mr. Walker : lam not sworn yet. (Laughter.) ' The Mayor : We conot take his word : I think he ought be sworn. Mr. Wharton : There is no doubt in the world that if he had been subpcened by the proper subpeena, I could have had the document produced. Mr. Walker : I asked to be snbpconecl, so there could be no doubt about that. After a pause, The Mayor said : Unfertunately the road seems to be ob- structed by a sort of pons asinorunt. Mr. Wharton (to the Mayor) : I am sorry von should ' call the witness such a nasty name, sir. (Laughter ) Mr. Walker : I understosel it to apply to counsel. (Laughter.) Mr. Wharton then agreed on behalf of the prosecution that Mr. Walker should be sworn and raid expenses. The Mayor: I should think half-a-guinea would be sufficient. . Mr. Browne : Mr Walker is the editor of a journal. Mr. Wharton : Bat he will make his fortune out of this. (Laughter.) Mr. Walker, having been paid half-a-sovereign for ex- penses, was sworn, and said he was the editor of the War. rington Examiner. He received the letter signed " Anti- Humbug " on, he thought, the day previous to its publica- tion on the 31st January. lie believed it came by post, but he could not say. Mr. Wharton : Have you the original letter ? Witness said he had not the letter. It was sent to Pres- ton to Mr. Toulmin, the proprietor of the Examiner. He sent it himself, but he believed Mr. Toulmin brought it with him on the day they went to see Mr. Jeans. As soon as he heard from Mr. Jeans again, he wrote to Preston asking if they could produce the letter, but their answer was that when they had settled with Mr. Jeans they put the letter into the waste paper basket, and it had been put away with the rest of the waste paper. He thoroughly believed it had been destroyed. Mr. Browne said that before the next witness was called he w mid submit that by their own witness, Mr. Walker, the prosecution bad proved the publication of a libel on the 30th. They were summoned for the 31st. The publi- cation of the libel was to Mr. Walker by letter. The Clerk said there might be half-a-dozen publications, and the prosecution might deal with any they liked. Mr. Wharton : If a newspaper was sold every day for a month it would he a publication every day to every person who bought the paper. Captain Sylvanus Reynolds was next called, and said he was a member of the Warrington Conservative Club Com- mittee. He knew the defendaat's handwriting, and the letter produced was in his handwriting. He received that letter on the date mentioned on it or thereabouts. Mr Wharton said this was a letter lee had not read before. It was a letter which showed still more strongly the animes and the reason for writing the letter to the Examiner. The letter, which was dated Dec. 19, 1884— some weeks before that published in the Examiner—cotn- plained to the euh committee that Mr Speakman had asked Mr. Grice to withdraw from the "guinea-room" when he was there on business, because he was a "51. member." It also referred te certain irregularities which, he said, he was "in a position to substantiate," and spoke ef the spleen of Mr Speakman towards him. The writer concluded by saying he would remain at the club to answer any question the com- mittee might wish to out. Captain Reynolds, continuing his evidence, said he had been on the club committee, and was acquainted with the applic ition3 for the management of the new club. The de- fendant was one of the applicants. Defendant had before written to him (Captain Reynolds) stating what he thought were his claims to the post. He was not the successful ap- plicant, the complainant being appointed. Mr. Browne : In this letter, he says that he told Mr. Speakman that if he had done anything wrong be would de- fend himself before the committee. The until course is that any member having any complaint shouldgo to the com- mittee ? Witness : Yes, but I should say that 10-30 was a later hour than the meeting existed ; it was broken up before that. Ile could not call to mind whether or not they bad a meeting that night, and he did not know whether or not that subject was mentioned. They bad never had any com- plaints about the management to his recollection lie thoneht he had attended every meeting but one. He could not tell how often, if at all, Mr. Speakman had been up before them for irregularities. He did not think he had, as a / member of the committee, received any other complaint from Mr. Grime than the one just read. Ile did not rernem. ber having been present at any committee meeting when any other communication from Mr. Grice had been brought forward. They tad exnelled Mr. Once from the club. Re did not remember any letter vjrittert by Mr. Grice to the secretary of the club, Mr. Wright, five or six weeks ago. Mr. Browne asked if it was not a fact that many members of the club had left. This question, however, was objected to and not an- swered. Questioned by Mr. Wharton, Captain Reynolds said that from inquiries he had made the previous night he found that Mr. Grice had not paid his subscription to the club. He was a 5s member and not entitled to go into the guinea

room. By Mr. Browne : Be could not say whether or not defen- dant had tendered his subscription and, that it had beet re- fused. BY Mr. Wharton: We expelled defendaot for writing to the -Examiner. Mr. J. E. Wright, architPct, said be was hon. secretary to the Conservative Club Committee. He deposed to bay-

div.p: THE EXAMINFR, SATURDA.Y, FEBRUARY tB. 1885. LATEST NEWS.

ing received the letter from the defendant in which he threatened to expose the club. By Mx. Browne: Ile could not say whether or not be bad received a complaint from the defendant five or six weeks ago. Hedid not remember the complaint. Mr. Wharton objected to going into the question of this complaiee. The Mayor did not think it ha anything to do with that case. .

Mr. Browne thought it had, for the reason that if a member I of a dub had a complaint to make, and made it to the management committee of that club, and they took no notice of it, his remedy was to write to the newspapers. Mr. Wharton: A • Liberal newspaper in particular? (Laughter.) If a man makes a complaint to a proper quarter and gets no remedy he is to make it to an improper quarter. Mr. Browne: No, a public newspaper is open to all fair comments. Mr. Wharton: If a man objects that he cannot get a fresh law passed, he is to break the law; that is my friend's ob- jection. Mr. Browne: No, it is not; my contention is that my client, not getting his remedy, from the committee, therefore went to the paper. The Mayor: He did it on his own responsibility. Mr. Wharton said if a man asked a corporation to carry out a public improvement, and they did not do so, he was justified in writing to the papers, but a Conservative Club was a private matter. The Mayor asked Mr. Browns if ho could see his way to ask his client to make an apology, The Defendant : You would not get one. Mr. Browne : My client has refused to apologise. The defendant was then charged and replied "I am not guilty." Mr. Browne then addressed the Bench. He said that be- fore they decided as to whether they would commit the de- fendant for trial at the forthcoming assizes upon that trivial libel he should ask if, on the evidence, the libel, bad been made out and brought home to his client. In the first place the libel itself must be produced. In the second place what was the definition of a libel ? A libel was a malicious defamation of any person made public either by printing, writing, or by signs or pictures in order to provoke him to wrath, or to expose him to public hatred, contempt, or ridi- cule. Ha asked whether in that case one of those things bad been proved. He submitted there was no intention to injure the complainant's character in the letter. It was simply a letter on the management of the club for the purpose of causing an investigation into facts in which the defendant was interested. He (Mr. Browne) contended that his client being a member of the Conservative Club, and one of those who elected the man- agement committee, Mr. Speakman, being a servant of the management committee, was also therefore a servant of his client, and the letter which he wrote to the paper, if he did write was privileged. But his chief contention was that the libel ought to be produced. The Mayor asked if he did not remember the case many years age in which the Duke of Cumberland commenced an action against the editor of the Weekty Despatch. The duke went to the one of the Despatch and obtained a copy of the paper, not without a great amount of trouble, and he sacceeded in getting a considerable amount of damage. Mr. Browne said that was a case against a newspaper. Mr. Wharton then quoted to show that where the writing was not in existence secondary evidence might be given. The Bench then retired, and after a short absence they returned. The Mayor said he nerd hardly tell them that their de- cisions were purely ef a ministerial character; and on the evidence that had been produced, they being only a court of first instance, they had no altereative but to commit the defendant to take his trial on the charge laid against him. At the same time, they should be ready to accept bail, him- self in £4O and two sureties in £2O each. He was sorry that that had not been made an end of by a more peace- able mode of procedure; but the defendant was not inclined to let it do so. Mr. Browns: I have asked my client again In apolo&se, but he won't. The defendant NC) white feathers here. Ivir. Beane applied that one surety in £4O should be aacepted in place of the two in £2O each, and having men- Cooed the name of Mr. Connor, Sankey-street, as this surety, the application was granted,
