REDASTRIBUTION.—The report of the Boundary Commis- sion (Ireland) was issued on Friday evening,. They re- solved,. as a primary rule, in the division of counties, to adhere as far as possible to existing baronial arrangements, the barony being a well-known land division. With regard to division of boroughs they mode special local inquiries. The whole number of county divisions they hove mode is 84. The only boroughs requiring division were Dublin and Belfast.

THE ALARMING EXPLOSION AT SHOEBURYNESS. SIX DEATHS. In adding to the particulars given in another column of this catastraphe we learn that Captain Geoid Adams and Sergeant-Majer Daykiu have succumbed to their injuries, and that there are seven other officers and men at present under the care of the surgeons. On Friday one of Colonel Strangway's sons arrived at Shoeburyness by the 6-20 a.m. train, but was too late to see his father alive. General Hay, Assistant Adjutant General of the Royal Horse Goards, arrived at Shoeburyness from the War Office shortly before eleven o'clock on Friday morning, and was received by Lieutenant-Celonel Betty and Lieutenant Acland. The cir- cumstances connected with the explosion were explained to him, and he afterwards proceeded to make further in- quiries. Gunner Underwood succumbed to his injuries on Friday afternoon, making six deaths from Thursdav'e disaster. The remaining five who are injured are doing well, and no fur- ther deaths are anticipated. Mrs. Lyons was present at the death of her husbmd, whb passed away quietly. The Central News correspondent says :—I learn that there were altogether seventeen officers and men engaged 111 experiments with Colonel Lyons' fuse. Four experiments had already been made with the fuse without mishap or hitch of any kind. The fifth attempt, however, gave trouble; there was a difficulty in screwing the fuse into the shell, and all those on the ground gathered round to witness the preperetions for the experiment. Sergeant-Major Daykin I commenced to hammer the lead pellet which fits over and , Into the bIV of the fun hole, and gunner Allen was assist- ing him when the shell exploded. The result was terrible, every one of the seventeen being thrown vio:ently to the I ground. Colonel Lyons and Colonel Strangeways suffered : fearful injuries to their legs. Major Belly was struck by a ipiece of suell, and besides a deep flesh wound sustained a severe injury to the spine. Captain Adams had both his feet blown off, and carried eeveral yards away. Mr Rance and Mr Low both sustained severe injuries to their legs. SergeanteMejee Daykin was terribly wounded, ORO of his legs being blown clean away. The Gunner Allen was blown to fragments, his head being almost severed from his body; his limbs were blown off, and his remains were scattered over the ground. It is indeed a wonder that the casualties were not even greater. Both Colonel Fox Strangeways and Colonel Lyon succumbed to their injuries and the exhaustion which followed upon amputation. Mr. Superintendent Hawtree, of Southend, has received instructions from Mr. J. Harrison, the coroner, to call the inquest for Saturday afternoon at two o'clock at Kirkwood, Shoeburyness Tavern. The bodies will be formally identi- fied and the inquiry will be then adjourned. The following is a complete list of the killed :—Colonel W. A. Fox Strang. wave, Colonel F. Lyon, Heti Captain Geoids Adams, Ser- geant-Major Daykin, Gunner Allen, and Gunner Under- wood.

• A court of inquiry into the causes which led to the ex- Olosion was opened in the Orderly Room at two o'clock on Thursday, after which the survivors who were able to at- tend gave evidence. Colonel Lewis presided, assists by Major Latham and Major Downing. The inquiry was strictly private, and it is understood that a detailed report will be forthwith submitted to the War Office. The Queen has sent messages both to Mrs. Fox Strange- ways and the Hon. Mrs. Lyon expressing her deep sym- pathy with them in the terrible bereavement. Her Majesty has alo telegraphed to the commandieg officer at Shoebury- ness asking to have all particulars of the accident sent to her. A large number of telegrams of condolence have been received.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met at 4 o'clock. Both Houses of Parliament are crowded. The utmoEt excitement prevails, it being generally believed that the C+overn-nent majority, if any, will be small. Several men:- bell of both Houses have been brought down in inval4 sham.

rIOTICNS AND Qtrnsnows.—Sir J. Parma gave notice of his intention to call attention to ths cumulative penalties inflicted under the ` Vaccinson Act.—Mr. LABOUGHHEN gave notice that when her Majesty's message referring to the army Reserve forces was considered he should move an [ addition to the address in answer thereto regretting that her Majesty's Government should have thought it neces- sary to recommend the calling out of the Militia and pre- venting certain persons from joining the Reserves when entitled to do so for the purpose of interfering with the in- tarns.' affairs of the Soudan..-.-Mr. ASHLEY', replying to Sir G. Campbell, denied that a Royal Commission had an- nexed Damaraland.—Mr. SEXTON asked Mr. Gladstone if he could now answer whether it was intended to renew or allow the Crimea Act to lapse.—Mr. GLADSTONFI said he could say nothing further than he had already said on the subject. —Lord HARTINGTON said a telegram had been received that day from Lard Wolselay stating that a message had been received from General Wood, Gakdul, February 25i Buller will be here to-morrow with his whole force. All wounded, including Captain Walsh, doing well. THE ADJOURNED DEBATE.

The adjourned debate on the Vote of Censure was re- sumed by 84 M. BoAco, who contended that no attempt had been made by the Government to contradict the else that had been made against them in regard to the fall of Khartoum and the death of General Gordon. By declining to utilize the victories of General Graham for the relief of Gordon, the Government had made the expedition of Lord Wolseley necessary. Re insisted that Khartoum and GrJr- ' don had both been lost because the Government delayed m tking up their minds to act.—Mr. COMITNES contended

that there was no necessity for the expedition that had been I resolved upon. He objected to the policy that had been advocated of holding our own in Turkey. it was difficult from the varied statements that had been made by Ministers to discover what were the.intentions of the Go- vernment as regarded the future of the Soiulan.—Lord E. Fvrxmaunrcu defended the action and policy of the Government, detailing the measures taken te rescue General Gordon. Mr. TYSON AIVLBURST opposed, and Mr. H. BaCTIARDS, who said we were in the midst of a great crisis, supported the amendment. Mr A BALFOUR refused to allow the Government to plead that they had been unfortunate 2—Mr LABJUCHERE sup- ported the amendment, as be failed to see anything to justify our now entering upon an aggressive campaign.— Mr. CLARKE supported the motion, and condemned the amendment of Mr. Morley as a sham.—Mr. W. E. FORSTER knew General Gordon's mind would have revolted at the idea of a party struggle over his suffering and death, and hoped the self-sacrificing spirit of that gallant man might have its influence over the debate.— Lord HA.RTINGTON said whether the Government was de- feated or sustained, the expedition now in progress would go on. The Government might have been wrong in send- ing General Gordon to Khartoum, but it was only fair to remember that at that time public opinion protested against the abandonment of the Egyptian garrison without an attempt at rescue. We owed it to our Indian empire not to show the Mahome- dans the spectacle of civilisation retiring before barbarism and fanaticism. He did not think the House would en- dorse a policy that contemplated the government of a new Indian empire in the heart of Africa, and if gentlemen op- posite were prepared with a light heart to undertake so heroic a task, he doubted whether the country would sup- port them in it. The House divided : For Vote of Censure 283 Against 302

VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES TO DUBLIN. —lt is officially announced that the Prince and Princess of Wales will visit Dublin early in April, and hold a levee and draw- ing-room on behalf of her Majesty in Dublin Castle. In consequence of this arrangement, the lark fixed by the Lord-Lieutenant for March 3rd has been postponed.

BULLER'S FORCE EXPECTED AT GAKDUL.

Lord Wolseley telegraphs to the War Office as follows:— The following message was received last night from General Wood :—Gakdul, February 25. Buller has sent in Khasnelome, and will be here to-morrow with his whole force. He Iva three wounded officers, 16 of other ranks, and 15 sick-34 invalids in all—the wounded including Captain Walsh, doing as well as possible, Major Poe, Lieut Crutchley, and all the wounded here are also doing well." CAIBO, FRIDIV.—Major-General Sir Redvers Buller, with his whole force, was expected yesterday at Gakdul, where Kaslum il Moss Pach3 has already arrived. florae, FRlDAY.—latelligence was received here last night that Major-General Buller, with his whole force, was within a day's march of Gakdul. No casualties occurred on the march. All the sick and wounded were doing well. They are expected to arrive here next week.

SCAHIM, FRIDAY EVRNlNG*—Lientenant Royal Engineers, wilt setting a dynamite mine this after- noon, when it exploded, killing hina on the spot.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. VOTE OF CENSURE DEBATE. The debate on the Vote of Censure was resumed by Earl CAMPERDOWN, who called earnestly on the Government to say frankly what they intended to do in the Soudan after smashing the Mandi. If they intended to occupy the Sou- dan until a stable government was established, then the country would support the Government, our military posi- tion would be strengthened, and the power of the Mandi, Osman Diana, and the hostile Arab tribes would be weakened. If the Government would not make such frank declarations of policy, then he should vote for the resoln- lion of the Maroms of Salisbury.— Earl Catateenvox intended to vote for the resolution- on the ground of the shameful treatment which General' 'Gordon had received at the hands of the Government. He urged that it was not creditable to the prudence and ' sagacity of the GovernFnent to allow the flower of the British Army to be locked up for months in the Soudan. Although the Conservative party had no desire to take office at the present juncture, they would not shrink from the responsibility if called on to do so.—Earl KIMBERLEY yielded to no one in admiration of General Gordon, but he was not infallible, and was mistaken in his calculations. After going to the Soudan he changed his views, and came to the conclusion that nothing would answer but an exten- sive military expedition. The Government, knowing what was passing elsewhere, could not conform to his advice, especially with regard to Zabehr Pasha and sending Turkish troops to the Soudan. The Government denied that they had abandoned Gordon ; they believed that Gordon had a reasonable chance of success, and that a ;military expedition would be unnecessary. Lord Napier of Magdala, the Duke of Norfolk, Earl Den- bigh, and Earl Ca.dogin continued tha debate.—Earl GRAN.. VILLE denied that the Government had sacrificed General Gordon. The Government policy now was to secure the salletv of the Euglish forces, destroy the power of the Mandi, and defend Egypt proper. If the tnotion was successful in both Houses, and Lord Salisbury succeeded to responsi- bility, he exceedingly doubted whether he would propose such a policy as the retention of the Soudan. If he did, he would be forcad by the country to wriggle out of it at the earliest moment —After further discussion, the Marquis of SALISBURY con- demned the Government for announcing their intention to evacuate the Soudan. As to future occupation, unless they retained pawr in the &Avila sufficiently long to give secu- rity and good government, all the blood and treasure would be expended in vain, and Egypt would be exposed to all the danger they desired to avoid. The House divided at 11-30 on Lord Salisbury's motion.. For Against
Majr,rity l2l The result was received with Opposition cheers. The Home rose at a quartet to twelve o'clock,

COIIIIT.—At n Occasional Court held at Mr Buckton's office, on Tuesday, before Mr James Tinsley, two militiamen named Thomas Harrison and James Ryan were charged with damaging straw in a shed beloqging to John Smith, farmer, Orford, and two girls named Elizabeth Esstham and Catherine Duffield, of Rose-yard, were charged' with sleeping out. The men were each fined 203 and costs, er 14 days' imprisonment, and the girls were committed for 14 days. THEFT OF CLOTHING.—Annie Jordan, a single woman, described as a field-hand, who resides in Flagg-lane, off Cockhedge-lane, was sent to jail for a month by the borough magistrates, on Monday, for stealing clothing to the value of ss, the property of Mary Kenny, a widow' who lives in Dial-street. The two women were acquainted, and prisoner alleged that Mrs Kenny lent her the clothing to pawn. Mrs Kenny admitted having given prisoner certain articles to pawn, but denied that those enumerated in the charge were given for that purpose. ALLMON!) TFIEFF OF TOOL9.—At the Borough Court on Thursday, a young man named George Frederick Walker, was remanded on a charge of having stolen from a work- ' shop on the premises of his employer, Mr. Thomas Flet- cher, gas engineer, Thvnne-street, on the 9th inst, and on ' other dates, a quantity of tools, of the value of £3. Pri- soner, who lives in Aiken-street, had excited the suspicion of the police, and on Constable Neale visiting his house in I reference to some matter not connected with the charge, he saw the tools in question and took possassion of them. They were afterwards identified as the property of Mr. Fletcher. UNFIT FOB Foon.—At the Borough Court on Monday, William French, Golborne-street, was fined 40s and costs for having in his possession Eilbs of veal that was pro- nounced to be unfit for human food. Mr. Wallhead, from the To an Clerk's office, prosecuted, and Mr. A. Browne ap- peared for the defence. The veal was discovered in defen- dant's shop by Inspector Norman, and afterwards certified as being unfit for food. For the defence it was contended that the defendant bought the meat before he saw it from a man who said that he bal sold similar portions to several people' and that he had no guilty knowledge of its condi- tien. The Bench, however, were of opinion that he must have been aware that the meat was not fit for food.

A VIOLENT RAILWAY PASSE/O.:MR.—A young man who gave the name of John Keys was brought before the borough magistrates on Monday, on a charge 'of riding in a third- class carriage from Liverpool to Warrington, on the London and North-Western Railway, on Saturday, without having paid his fare.—On a ticket being denim I.ed at Bank Quay station, prisoner refused to give one up, or to give his ad- dress, sad also assaulted a railway detective named John Hale. Afterwards a ticket from Chester to Widnes was found in his possession, and he now told the magistrates that he had got drunk and been miscarried.--lie wai allowed the benefit of the doubt as to his having had intentions of fraud, but Was fined 20e, or a month's imprisonment, for as- saulting the detective. WARRINGTON WIRE ROPE COMPS.NY.-ISSIZE CASE.— At the Liverpool Assizes on Tuesday,. before Mr. Justice Mills, an action was brought by the Warrington Wire Rope Company against Evey and others. Ur. Fickford appeared for the plaintiffs, and Mr Bighani, Qie , and Mr Segar for the de- fendants. The action was brought to recover £BB, the price of a wire haulage rope supplied to. the defendants, who are colliery proprietors at Castleford, near Viz'akedeld. the de- fendants denied their liability on the ground that the rope was not of the quality ordered. They also put in a counter- claim for £5O, for damages alleged to have been sustained to their machinery owing to the rope breaking. After hear- , lug a large number of scientific witnesses as to the quality and texture of the rope, his Lordship, gave judgment for the plaintiffs, with costs. SERIOUS DISTURBANCE: TWO MEti STAZBED.—it the Borough Court on Monday, a young man named John Fal- lon, who lives with his parents in Rose-yard, off Dial.st., was charged with cutting and wounding his' father, Patrick Fallon, and P.C. Singleton, in Rose-yard early on the pre- vious morning. Shortly before midnight on Saturday, Mrs Fallon went to the police station and asked Singleton, who was standing outside, to go with her to Rose-yard at once, as her eon was "canting on" in a shameful manner, and had been using threr'lning language, and that she and her husband were afraid for their lives. Singleton went to the house and heard prisoner threaten to take hie father's life. Prisoner made for the fire place, apparently with the inten- tion of taking the poker. An attempt was then made to se- cure him, and in the scuffle that _ensued the father was stab- bed on the shoulder and the constable in five or six different places. Prisoner was eventually placed lit safe custody, and the knife, an ordinary pocket one, was secured. P.C. Singleton gave evidence regarding.the affray and Dr. Smith described the nature of the wounds of the two men, from which he did not anticipate serious results„ and, on the ap- plication of Chief-constable Hunt. a remand until Monday was then granted. _ _ _

Eetarssur, Cnortem—On Thursday evening the second anniversary of the dedication of the above church was cele- brated by a special service. There was a large attendance The sermon was preached by the Right Rev Bishop Gregg, who took his text from the sixth chapter of the 2nd Kings. In the course of his remarks he saki that that was the second anniversary of the opening of that church, and be thought they might safely say that that church had been faithful to the principals and practices laid down for the guidance of the branch of the Church of Christ to which they had the honour tabelong. fie felt very thankful when he was permitted to open that building for the service of God, and he felt thankful for having been spared to meat. them again and to learn from their worthy vicir of the pro- gress of that place. Referring to the methods of encomia' working in connection with churches, he said they heard a great deal in this world of trades unions. What was the secret of the success of trades unions, and even of the banding together of masters?' It was co-operation based upon individual respon,ibility. The secret of failure was ' that in many instances the work was left to be done by a few individu as. He therefore strougly advocated us- operation in Church work, and said where that was wanting there would also lie wanting a measure of success. Special sermons rail be preached to-morrow (Sunday) by the pastor.

TRH OLD MILITIA BARRACKS.—ID view of receiving the Army Reserve, these barracks are now undergoing consider- able alterations, the Government having taken the building on lease from the county authorities. It is expected that in about three weeks the barracks will be ready to receive about 120 men. Mr Iledgcockt of King-street, has the work in band.

BRICK-STREET AND,Fsleas GREEN BAND or HOPL—The fourth entertainment was held in Brick-street Schoolroom en Tuesday evening, when Mr G Jolley occupied the chair. A capital programme was provided, which gave great satis- faction to the audience, keeping up the interest from begin- ning to end. The meeting concluded with the dialogue en- titled "Will Wildar's birthday party." WYCLIFFE Currnot.—ln this church, on Sunday evening, another of the special people's services was held,,and was largely attended. The Rev J ouge preached on "Man- sions in the skies,'" taking as his text part of the second' verse of St. John "In my Father's house are many mansions." After the sermon the beautiful hymn, "The palace of the Kingrwas admirably sung by Mr W H Wal- lington.

WARRINGTON RADICAL CLUB —The weekly meeting of the members of this club HAS held at the temporary club- room, Park View Coffee Tavern, Sankey-street, on Saturday evening. when there was a most encouraging muster, the chair being occupied by Mr. H. Whitham. After disposal of formal business,. an interesting discussion was opened on the "Government policy in the Soudan," and continued until near ten o'clock, at which hour the meeting and discus- sion were adjourned. WORKMEN't•CLUE —Another family party in connection with this club eras held in the clubroom on Monday evening. Alderman Davies presided, and there was a god attend- ance. Songst be, were contributed by Mr G archer, Miss ' F A Baker Mr D Ikin, Mr Bellian, Mr G Parr, Misses Dalton and Stirrup, Miss K Lawton officiated at the piano- forte., and the band of the 9th L R.V. was•aleo present. A vote of thanks to the chairman, moved by Mr T Morris, and seconded by Mr Robinson, brought the entertainment to a close. WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB.—The• annual meeting of this club was held on Thursday evening, when the accounts were submitted for approval and passed. They were con- sidered very satisfactory, a balance being carried to the new pavilion fund. The officers for the ensuing year were elected, arid Mr. James Fairclongh was chosen as pres.. dent. A committee was also appointed to superintend the affairs of the club, which is now in a flourishing condition. The corning season gives promise of being a successful one, a number of important matches having been arranged. PENKETH WESLETAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIL. TION.—On Wednesday evening a well attended meeting of the members of the above Society was held in the Wesleyan School-room, when a most able and comprehenaive paper was read to the members by Mr. Edwin Hankinson on " America." Mr. Hankinson having visited America, was enabled to give some very interesting facts about the culti- vation of land, allotments of land, conveyance of land, and fees, etc. The paper was highly commended by Messrs R. Garnett' C. E. Parker, W. Pickton, A. J. White, B. Hobson, and the President. Mr. David Garnett occupied the chair. Sr. Para's Carom —On Sunday evening, after the ser- vice at at. Paul's Church, a number of books, kindly con- tributed by Mr Thomas Morris, were distributed to several of the chair boys for regular attendance and general good conduet during the past twelve months. The presentation took place in ths vestry, amongst those present being Mrs Wilkinson, Mrs Morris, and several other ladies, and Messrs Thomas Morris, 'l' Sutton, D W Finney, and Smethuret. Mr Finney explained that there were altogether about half a dczen recipients. The condition upon which the prizes were given was attendance 200 times and upwards at the Sunday and week-day services. He had carefully gone through the attendance list, and he found that the boys who would receive books had fulfilled the condition, one lad, Albert Oxley, having attended no fewer than 248 times out of a possible 251. The books having been distributed, each boy receiving two, a hearty vote of thanks was ac- corded to Mr Morrie, on the motion of Mr Smethurst, seconded by Mr Sutton. Mr Morris returned thanks, and the proceedings terminated. Ores Linesmen (WARRINGTON) VOLITSTEERS.—On Saturday afternoon this corps paraded at their headquarters e,—The jr _pre at the Drill Hall, for a march out under the directioa of the Adjutant. Owing to the extreme coldness and threatening nature of the weather, the mnsterwas not quite so good as might otherwise have been expected. The following officers attended the parade, with the Adjutant :—Major Boltoe, Captains Ridgway and Gooch. and Lieutenant Buckton. Before the men marched off the column was closed, and the names and performances of the corps marksmen were read out by the officer commanding the parade. Ro•cial men- tion was made of the fact that whilst in 1883 there were only three marksmen, in 1884; no less than 22 men had qualified themselves by their scores for the marksman's badge. A score of 58 had been made by Sergeant T A Ward, as against 42 in 1883. This last was equalled by no less than eight men in 1884. The march out was by way of Bold-street and Wilderspool, into the country. A short halt was made on arrival at the "Mulberry Tree," on the Cheshire side. where the men were each supplied with a refreshing drink, and the march was then resnmedty way of Latch- ford horns. Altogether the corps had a meet enjoyable march-out, reaching their quarters about 6-45 p m —Sub- joined we give the marksmen and their scores for 1884 a Sergeant T A Ward, 58 paints;' Sergeant T Jolley, 51; Private G Smith, 50; Sergeant G Watmough, 49; Private T Sloane, 45; Private J Nicholson, 42; Lance-corporal G Davies, 42 ; Corporal J Lace, 42; Sergeant J Bennian, 40; Sergeant-Bugler D Plinston, 39; Sergeant H Gernon, 37'S; Sergeant G Painter, 37; Pioneer E 'll,l ores, 35; Private T Rayenacroft, 35; Cerpoml J Dobson,. 33; Private J'Smith, 31; Sergeant S A Tunks, 31; Corporal T Brobbin, 30'; Private W Ashton, 27; Private J Standish, 27 ; Corporal J L Kidd, 25; Private R Bennett, 25. THEATRICALS AT ORFORD BARRACKS.—Dramatic enter- tainments were given in connection with the Bth and 40th Regimental Districts at the Theatre Royal, Orford Barrrcke, on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings. The attendance on both occasions was flattering, and the performances excel- lent. Wednesday evening was staff night. Although small, the theatre is comfortable and adapted to mast its re- quirements' and the stage effects are pretty and appropriate. Sergeant-Major Cope, as genera/ manager of these theatrical representations, always distiormishes himself by the com- pleteness of his arrangements. The programme opened with a selection by the orchestra, and a summer evening ketch, "Ruth's Romance," was thon enacted. Rath Carey, the child of rich parents, in compliance with the terms of the will of an eaeentric relative, adopts for a time the life and work of a humble country maiden, and in the same neigh- bourhood live? Captain Wilton, Ruth's brother-in-law, a pleasant enough fellow with a spendthrift reputation, who meters the solitude of country life as the only means of avoiding his creditors. The third character in the romance Is Jack Dudley, of good birth, who woos the rustic maiden, and successfully. Theie.troth is plighted, when an unex- pectedetermination to their bliss threatens when Jack, wit- nessing an interview between Ruth and the Captain, allows in hisignorance of their relations. jealousy to assert itself. Finally, of course, al/ is explained and happiness ensues. Mrs, Kavanagh, as Path Carey, was easy, and natural and wait suited to her part. Quarter-Master Sergeant Flynn,. tea Captain Wilton, was both amusing and interesting, enter- ing thoroughly into the spirit of the character. Sergeant- Dr: O'Brien mada.a sufficiently ardent lover, and took Jack Dudley's part with credit. Another selection having 3-,een ;given by the orahestra, Sergeant /Cavanagh commence 4 the ,secend part oi*tbe programme with a humorous reading "Mickey Frees Father on Sentry„" well delivered, and a Huts duet, which was encored, was then given by Sergeant- D Burgess and Mr ilrimelow, Colour-aergeant Neild, in giving the comic sketch "The Quack Doctor was very characteattic, and provoked much laughter. Sergeant-D. O'Brien gave a cornet solo "The Lost Chord" in a splendid manner; a repitition was at once demanded. Sergeant Kavanagh again Proved a favourite in the comic song" The Dublin Carmen," given in character, which was encored. "MV Uncle's," or "No. 1 round the earner," a farce,wa given in conolusion, the parts being well represented by Coleur-Sergeant Neild. Colour-Sergeant Sullivan, and Mr Jones Pita Smith (norm de p!unzt.l Sergeant-D, Burgese acted as musical conductor.
